text:
In January 1919, Alice Evans met her second husband, Foster Bailey, a lawyer and Freemason from Massachusetts born into a distinguished family of politicians and lawyers, hailing on the maternal line from founding father of Fitchburg, Amos Kimball. The couple soon took on key administrative roles in the TS, Foster as secretary and Alice as editor of the sectional magazine. 

Around October of that year, Alice began writing as amanuensis for The Tibetan or Djwhal Khul, one of the Theosophical Masters of Wisdom. The Tibetan had also been Blavatsky’s master, from which her seminal text The Secret Doctrine arose. Reluctant at first, Alice took on the role of writing for The Tibetan, a role that would culminate in twenty-four volumes of esoteric teachings and commentary, a number written in her own right and many published posthumously. The collection became known as the Blue Books due to their indigo covers. 

A year later, an organisational row resulted in both Alice and Foster being ousted from their roles in the TS. They moved to New York where Foster was offered work as secretary of a Theosophical association. The couple quickly married and settled in Ridgefield Park, NJ. While Foster continued to campaign to change key organisational practices of the TS, Alice continued writing as she visioned their future. 

She established a Secret Doctrine class held in a room on Madison Avenue, which became an outstanding success. Interest grew and grew from all over the United States and beyond, and correspondence mounted. In 1922, the Baileys established the Lucis Trust and published the first three volumes of her opus. In 1923, they founded the Arcane School – an esoteric training school delivered by correspondence to disciples around the world. 

Alice Bailey would dedicate the rest of her life to laying the foundations of a new age of spiritual enlightenment, in the hope of countering the continued rise of materialism, hatred and greed.

The Blue Books
Alice Bailey’s body of work is in part a reformulation of the Theosophical current of Western Esotericism, composed in language accessible to the contemporary mind. Central to Theosophy are: a belief in the existence of the soul, reincarnation and the interconnectedness of all existence; an epochal view of evolution that includes consciousness; the transmission of an Ageless Wisdom from master to disciple; and a commitment to humanitarianism. 

There is nothing fluffy between the pages of the Blue Books. The atmosphere the teachings evokes is business-like, with an emphasis on responsibility, leadership and executive management. The volumes are instructional texts for aspirants and disciples of the spiritual path. Some are harder to read than others. The volumes include A Treatise on Cosmic Fire, an intricate cosmology drawing on Neoplatonist metaphysics and Eastern philosophy. Other works provide instructions for disciples on how to live, think and behave. A Treatise on the Seven Rays provides a detailed formulation of human psychology and advice on meditation and healing. 

Cemented in Alice Bailey’s particular version of Theosophy are Christian ideas of goodwill and good works, and she sought to make these basic principles the cornerstones of her teachings. She made it her mission to elevate occultism from the lower reaches of charlatans and counter the left-hand path some occultists follow. For Alice Bailey, esoteric thought and practice needed to be oriented towards selfless, altruistic goals and always for the good of the whole. 

Controversies
Despite these noble aims, during her lifetime Alice Bailey aroused the wrath of purist Theosophists, Christians and Jews who all took issue with her body of work.

Purist Theosophists accused Alice Bailey of false claim-making over her assertion that the source of most of her writings was none other than Blavatsky’s master Djwhal Khul. That she was merely a conduit in telepathic rapport receiving the next outpouring of the Ageless Wisdom provided her with a handy disclaimer should any issues of copyright or plagiarism arise. Some even alleged Alice Bailey made use of secret Theosophical teachings only available to members of the society’s Esoteric Section, a matter that cannot be proven as the teachings have not been made available in the public domain.

US President Donald Trump says his Special Envoy to the Middle East, Steve Witkoff, is working on a potential agreement with Iran and is “doing very well”, while indicating that a deal is not his preferred outcome.

“He’s working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn’t really something that I want to do, but they’re willing to offer us anything to stop,” Trump told supporters at a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas.

Trump said Iran would “never have a nuclear weapon” and praised Witkoff as “a great negotiator.”

He also said he expected the war to end soon.

“That war ends – it’s going to be very soon. It’s got to be very soon,” Trump said, describing Iran as “a failed nation” with “a little spunk left, but not much.”

text:
Mike Malone on the @UNC_Basketball  coaching job: It's more than just basketball! - 10.7.26 at #ACCTipOff

📷 Michael Malone Discusses UNC Basketball, Recruiting, Team Development and Coaching Philosophy
📷 International recruiting whirlwind: UNC head coach Michael Malone described extensive international travel during his first three months, including trips to France, Spain, Portugal, Turkey and Mexico. An impromptu trip to Spain helped UNC recruit Sion Kéïta, illustrating the differences between college and NBA coaching.
📷 Adjusting to college basketball: Malone called his first two months a whirlwind of recruiting, hiring assistants, assembling a roster and adjusting to Chapel Hill. He said coaching on the practice court remains the most enjoyable and rewarding part of his job.
📷 Cameron Boozer's eligibility situation: The transcript identifies the player as Cameron F., whose eligibility remains unresolved. Malone confirmed the player would miss Friday's exhibition despite practicing daily and expressed hope for a prompt resolution. The player's full name and status should be verified before publication.
📷 Managing young players' workloads: Malone emphasized that coaching 17- and 18-year-olds requires greater attention to academic schedules, recovery, physical demands and personal well-being than coaching NBA professionals.
📷 Patience with player development: Malone acknowledged having to adjust his expectations after 25 years in the NBA. College players require more individual instruction, repetition and encouragement, but he finds their improvement particularly rewarding.
📷 Positionless basketball philosophy: UNC will use multiple players to initiate offense rather than relying on a traditional point guard. Terrence Brown, Henri Veesaar and several other guards and wings are expected to share ball-handling responsibilities.
📷 Defense and rebounding come first: Malone said his primary concerns are defensive stops, rebounding, limiting turnovers, sharing the basketball and improving teammates rather than determining who plays specific positions.
📷 Three exhibition games provide valuable tests: UNC's exhibitions against USC, Indiana and Charlotte will allow Malone to evaluate combinations, experiment with strategies and establish the team's identity before the regular season.
📷 Reconnecting with Carolina basketball tradition: Malone wants to honor UNC's history by welcoming former Tar Heels back to Chapel Hill, including coaches Wes Miller and King Rice, while maintaining relationships with former players.
📷 Former players reunite: More than 150 former Carolina basketball players attended a reunion organized to strengthen connections across generations. Malone particularly enjoyed meeting Charlie Scott, Jimmy Black and Bobby Jones.
📷 Former Tar Heels remain involved: Malone praised the willingness of former players, including Tyler Hansbrough, to attend practices and support the program. He believes their involvement helps current players and recruits understand Carolina's basketball tradition.
📷 Recruiting 'connectors': Malone wants selfless players who make teammates better. He cited LeBron James and Nikola Jokić as examples of elite players who elevate everyone around them.
📷 Leadership remains a work in progress: With 11 newcomers and five returning players, UNC is still developing its leadership structure. Malone wants players to hold one another accountable rather than depending entirely on the coaching staff.
📷 Different leadership styles are valuable: Malone said effective leaders do not necessarily need to be vocal. Some lead through their actions, while others motivate teammates through communication and accountability.
📷 High expectations for Neoklis Avdalas: Malone praised the Greek transfer's size, court vision, passing ability and unselfishness. He believes Avdalas can become an important contributor after improving his strength and conditioning.
📷 Sion Kéïta's impressive adjustment: Malone described the young international recruit's transition from Mali and Barcelona to Chapel Hill as remarkable. He praised his maturity, adaptability, length, athletic ability and potential.
📷 Jarin Stevenson's offensive development: Malone wants Stevenson to become more aggressive offensively through transition opportunities, post mismatches, offensive rebounds and attacks toward the basket.
📷 Respecting individual personalities: Malone emphasized that Stevenson should not be forced into becoming an outspoken or emotional leader. Instead, the coaching staff wants him to demonstrate confidence and aggression through his performance.
📷 Practice statistics guide coaching: UNC charts practice performances, including shot attempts and turnovers, to identify improvement opportunities and hold players accountable.
📷 Playing fast without playing carelessly: Malone wants an up-tempo offense built around disciplined decisions. He emphasized that speed cannot come at the expense of ball security or shot selection.
📷 Turnovers are a major concern: Malone stressed that successful teams cannot afford self-inflicted mistakes, declaring, "Good teams don't beat themselves."
📷 Daily improvement over championship talk: Malone said UNC's primary objective is building winning habits through productive practices rather than repeatedly discussing championship aspirations.
📷 Preparing for postseason success: Malone believes consistent daily improvement will put the Tar Heels in a stronger position when conference tournament and postseason competition arrive.
📷 Official recruiting visits offer personal connections: Malone joked about recruits' appetites and the number of Chapel Hill restaurants he has visited. More importantly, he sees campus visits as opportunities for recruits and families to experience the program firsthand.
📷 Authenticity drives recruiting: Malone refuses to change his personality when recruits attend practice. He believes honesty, approachability and genuine relationships help prospective players determine whether UNC is the right fit.
📷 Lessons from an NBA championship: Drawing on his championship experience in Denver, Malone wants to establish a culture where players work extremely hard while enjoying basketball and their relationships with teammates.
📷 Influential coaching mentors: Malone credited his father, Jeff Van Gundy, Mike Brown, Monty Williams and Gregg Popovich with shaping his coaching philosophy.
📷 Defense and attention to detail: Malone identified Van Gundy's defensive principles and meticulous preparation as particularly influential in developing his own coaching approach.
📷 Empowering assistant coaches: Lessons from Mike Brown helped Malone understand the importance of trusting assistants, giving them meaningful responsibilities and allowing them to contribute to decisions.
📷 Gregg Popovich's lasting advice: Malone recalled Popovich encouraging him to remain authentic while ensuring players understand that demanding coaching comes from genuine care and respect.
📷 Overall takeaway: Malone's first UNC team will emphasize defensive accountability, rebounding, disciplined up-tempo basketball, unselfish play and daily improvement. Although eligibility questions, roster chemistry and leadership remain unresolved, Malone believes the program is making progress toward establishing a sustainable winning culture.

The World Health Organization is still trying to gather information regarding the death of a lab worker in Siberia. There have been reports out of Russia that the 28 year old’s death on October 2nd may have been from the plague. Maria Van Kerkhove is the Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management at the World Health Organization. She says they don't know what the "causative agent" was behind the woman's death.: “This person worked in a high threat lab. So there are a lot of provisions in these labs related to biosafety, biosecurity. This individual would have had training, would have had vaccinations related to some of these pathogens. Um, this is the type of information that we're seeking. ”
The Russian government has blamed pneumonia for her death but also initially quarantined about two hundred people.

The FBI has arrested a suspect who they say was orchestrating a mass shooting plot at Minnesota's Mall of America.
NewsNation's Elizabeth Vargas reports federal investigators were communicating with 18-year-old Shake-doon Abdu-llahi Mohamud for two years before moving in: “During that time, the teenager allegedly sent hundreds of messages detailing his support for ISIS and his desire to kill non-Muslims. More than a year ago, when the suspect was still a minor, the FBI became so concerned it sent agents to his home. According to the criminal complaint, his parents wouldn't talk to them and brushed them off. They say he eventually chose the Mall of America as a target because he said it's owned by Jews. ”
Prosecutors say the suspect had planned to carry out that attack on October 24th.

Two lawsuits have been filed challenging president Trump's recent federally-funded TV ads. The Democratic National Committee and a coalition that includes nonpartisan watchdog group Common cause argue the ads violate U.S. propaganda law. The ads promote the president's political message, and cost taxpayers $12 million out of a contracted $20 million.
**********
The lawsuits are asking the courts to block the use of federal funds to pay for the ads.
The president has said he'll pay for the ads going forward through his super PAC.

The number of shingles cases among younger adults has dropped sharply.: “The firm Epic Research credits the relatively new chickenpox vaccine. The virus that causes chickenpox can remain dormant and later reactivate as painful shingles. The vaccine became available in 1995. The number of shingles cases in people born from 1996 to 2000. Was 62% lower than in those born in the five years before the vaccine came out. The researchers say childhood chickenpox vaccination could offer a lasting benefit in reducing shingles, but they still recommend people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce the risk. Michael Wallace, Worldwide News Network. ”

In Major League Baseball:
The Tampa Bay Rays eliminated the Bronx Bombers from post-season play with a 4-to-3 win to complete a 3-game sweep. A potential game-tying homer was overturned after a fan caught the ball in the left field stands.
Tampa Bay will play the winner of the Chicago-Cleveland series in the American League Championship Series.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are going on to the National League Championship Series after eliminating the Atlanta Braves 4 to 1 in game four of the Division series tonight.

The U.S. trade deficit hit a 17-month high in August.: “The Commerce Department says the gap between what America buys and sells overseas grew to more than $105 billion as the AI boom drove up imports of computer chips and equipment. Chip imports jumped sharply in August and are up more than 80%. This year, the increase comes despite President Trump's tariffs, which are aimed at reducing the trade deficit. Still, the deficit is lower overall this year than it was at this point last year. Stacy Lynn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

🪔 SARVA PITRU AMAVASYA — 10 OCTOBER 2026, SATURDAY  
Last Chance of the Year to Seek Pitru Blessings

Amavasya Timing: 9th Oct 9:36 PM → 10th Oct 9:20 PM  

This is Sarva Pitru Amavasya — the final and most important day of Pitru Paksha. It’s considered the last opportunity in the year to honor all ancestors (pitrs) and receive their blessings for peace, prosperity, and removal of Pitru Dosh.

THE 4 MUST-DO UPAY FOR SARVA PITRU AMAVASYA:

1️⃣ WATER OFFERING WITH BLACK SESAME (TARPAN)  
Mix black sesame seeds (kale til) in water and offer it while facing the South direction.  
This is the traditional way to offer tarpan to satisfy ancestral souls.

2️⃣ LIGHT A SESAME OIL LAMP AT THE MAIN DOOR  
After sunset, light a diya with sesame oil or mustard oil at your home’s main entrance.  
This is believed to guide ancestors and remove negative energy from the home.

3️⃣ FEED CROWS, COWS & BRAHMINS  
Prepare food and specifically set aside portions for:  
Crows — believed to be messengers of ancestors  
Cows — considered sacred and a medium to ancestors  
Brahmins — for spiritual blessings  

4️⃣ DONATE GRAINS (ANN DAAN)  
Donate food grains or rice according to your capacity. Cooked rice donation is especially considered highly auspicious on this day.

Washington State 

WA State Dept. of Health (DOH)

Building Skills in Sexual Health (BSSH) 

Office of Infectious Disease (OID)

Oct. 7, 2026

Building Skills in Sexual Health (BSSH) Web Training Series:

Please join us as we partner with the MWAETC and the NWPCA for year FIVE of the BSSH Web Training Series. This training series works to engage our FQHCs/CHCs in supporting and promoting sexual health delivery in the community health center environment, in hopes that the barriers to access to care are decreased, allowing for the increase of positive health outcomes for all Washingtonians.

"Sexual Health History Taking"

We are honored to welcome back Dr. Carrie Horwich, who has been incredible champion in this work! 

This "Sexual Health History Taking" session will provide brief epidemiological data that demonstrates why taking a thorough sexual health history is so important to the overall health of Washingtonians.  By gaining a full understanding of a client's health, practitioners can help to combat the transmission of preventable infections and offer aid and guidance for treatable conditions.

REGISTER

https://t.co/m8H7WJycmh

Learning Objectives:

Upon completion of this training, attendees will be able to:

Discuss integrating the 6 Ps: the modern Pleasure domain, alongside Partners, Practices, Protection, Past history and Pregnancy, to normalize sexual health wellness and improve the disclosure accuracy to enhance health outcomes.

Employ open-ended, non-judgmental questioning techniques to discuss sensitive behaviors, actively reducing clinical stigma and overcoming patient discomfort.

Structure history-taking to efficiently identify patients eligible for Doxycycline Post-Exposure Prophylaxis, (DoxyPEP) under current Washington clinical protocols.

PLEASE NOTE: When you log into the session, please make sure that your first and last name are displayed.  Participants who fail to display their names will be disconnected from the session.

ID Badge

Learn More From Our Expert:

Dr. Carrie Horwich

Carrie A Horwitch, MD, MPH is a board certified internal medicine physician. She has worked as an outpatient primary care physician for over 25 years.  She is also credentialed as an HIV care specialist from AAHIVM.  Dr Horwitch graduated from University of Arizona, College of Medicine. She completed her Master of Public Health at University of California, Berkeley. She is a Clinical Associate Professor of Medicine at the University of Washington. She has presented on multiple different topics such as taking a sexual history, HIV care, medical ethics and professionalism, medical improve and laughter. She has done training for HIV care in the United States and Internationally – including several countries in Africa.

text:
Jeff Samardzija is criminally underrated!

Jeff Samardzija's decision to pursue professional baseball instead of football started with...a coin flip!

Jeff Samardzija used a coin flip to help decide between the NFL and MLB, and when it landed on football, his immediate feeling of disappointment made him realize he actually wanted to play baseball.

The Coin Flip: At the end of his career at the University of Notre Dame, Samardzija flipped a coin in his apartment to decide whether to attend the Senior Bowl for football or sign with the Chicago Cubs.

The Gut Reaction: The coin landed on football, and his immediate emotional response was frustration and feeling "ticked off," which revealed his true preference.

The Rationale: He felt he had already reached his peak and potential in football, whereas baseball offered more room for physical and skill growth, greater daily autonomy, and a longer career.

The Deal: He turned down a potential 1st Round NFL career to sign with the Chicago Cubs on a lucrative contract.

Samardzija was twice selected as one of the three finalists for the Fred Biletnikoff Award, for the season's outstanding college football WR in both 2005 & 2006.

Although initially planning to play both in the NFL & MLB, Samardzija announced after being selected in the Major League Draft that he would take his name out of the NFL draft and play baseball.

Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji‘un.

With a heart full of grief, I received the news of the passing of my beloved teacher, Hazrat Maulana Dr. Saeedur Rahman Al-Azami Nadwi (RH), Principal of Darul Uloom Nadwatul Ulama, at the age of 92.

I was in Durban, South Africa, when I received the news, and it deeply saddened me. Hazrat was one of the most influential personalities in my life at Nadwa, a man of profound knowledge, wisdom, taqwa and remarkable punctuality.

I was blessed to receive his duas on many occasions throughout my journey at Nadwa. I still remember that when Hazrat himself was taking my admission, he said to me: “You will raise the flag of Nadwa throughout the world.” His words and duas have remained among the most precious memories of my life.

May Allah (swt) forgive Hazrat, elevate his ranks, accept his lifelong service to Ilm and Nadwatul Ulama, and grant patience to his family, students and all who loved him. May Allah continue to allow us to benefit from the legacy of our teachers. 

Aameen.

T.I. and Brian Steel, the lawyer who spent years on the Young Thug case, sat down and said the part the paperwork hides. 

The courts do not run on trials. They run on pleas. The Sixth Amendment promises a speedy, public trial by an impartial jury. The Fifth says no person shall be deprived of liberty without due process. 

In practice, poor defendants sit in jail, or burn through jobs while a case lingers, then get offered probation against the threat of years. The form says the plea was free and voluntary. 

About 97 percent of people sentenced in federal court last year never saw a jury. That is not a system testing its evidence. That is a settlement machine. 

The Constitution made the jury the check on the state. A right you are punished for using is a right in name only.

text:
A broke drifter walks into a bar looking for work.

Five minutes later, a stranger offers him $10,000 to kill his wife.

He accepts.

Except there’s one problem.

He’s NOT the hitman.

Michael Williams has just arrived in a small Wyoming town with almost no money and nowhere to go.

Then a wealthy man mistakes him for a professional killer.

Instead of correcting him, Michael decides to take the money.

Easy money.

Until the wife offers him even more to kill her husband instead.

Now Michael is stuck between two people who both want the other one dead.

And neither of them is telling the truth.

Then the REAL hitman arrives.

And suddenly Michael realizes he has walked into a game where absolutely nobody is playing fair.

Nicolas Cage is young, sweaty and wonderfully chaotic in Red Rock West (1993).

Dennis Hopper is completely unhinged.

Lara Flynn Boyle brings the perfect femme-fatale energy.

And the snowy Wyoming setting makes everything feel even more isolated.

One wrong decision.

One fake identity.

One town full of liars.

Red Rock West is the kind of forgotten thriller that makes you wonder how you missed it.

text:
Dhiwangkara Seta's "αLPα" opens on a body in revolt and closes on a body at rest, and the nineteen minutes in between chart the quiet, unnerving distance between the two. A punk vocalist is dragged from the stage mid-set and delivered into a regime built to sand him smooth. That the film registers this as loss rather than correction is its clearest statement of intent.

“Alpa” review is part of the Submit Your Film Initiative

The vocalist is Banyu (Elang El Gibran), twenty years old and all raw nerve, arrested during a gig and deposited in a moral rehabilitation centre that runs on repetition. Recruits chant their devotion to nation and discipline, drill their bodies through punishing routines, and learn above all that individuality is a defect to be corrected. Banyu will not be corrected. He needles the institution and defaces a poster of the man whose face presides over the place: Deri (Whani Darmawan), a revered cleric who proves far more tightly bound to Banyu than either can comfortably admit.

That bond is the film's engine, and Seta withholds it almost to the end. Where a broader drama would announce the connection between the rebel and the patriarch, αLPα lets it surface through suggestion, a glance held a beat too long, a familiarity neither man has earned in the present tense. When the two are finally alone together, the truth of what they are to one another lands not as plot but as collapse; the confrontation dissolves into tears and an embrace the whole film has been quietly bracing for.

What follows is stranger and more deliberately opaque. Deri, the very emblem of order, marks his eyes with black and sits in stillness while Banyu circles the office in something between a dance and an exorcism, the roles of the caged and the free briefly traded. The film ends elsewhere entirely, on a memory: a father and a much younger son at the edge of a lake in the dark, a before to everything that has curdled since. The image is offered without commentary, and the film trusts its audience to carry it.

Seta, who came to film from graphic design by way of the music community on the outskirts of Jakarta, is plainly drawn to the systems that shape young men, class, nation, faith and the narrow scripts of masculinity passed down between fathers and sons. αLPα reaches for all of this in the register of allegory rather than argument. It is sparing with dialogue and it declines the tidy, redemptive resolution a Western treatment might have chased. The effect is thoughtful and, at its best, genuinely haunting.

It is also where the film's brevity begins to tell. A short has only minutes to make its people legible and its feeling land, and "αLPα" asks for investment in a relationship it has largely kept offscreen. The confrontation is powerful, but much of the material around it stays at the level of the intellect rather than the gut, so that the embrace moves more than the film that leads to it. A little more room, a few more beats of Banyu and Deri as people rather than symbols, and the closing images might cut as deeply as they clearly intend to.

https://t.co/zuPKEdWoEV

Even so, "αLPα" is a confident, visually controlled piece of work with real ideas on its mind and the discipline to trust an image over a line of explanation. It marks Seta as a film-maker worth following, and after a premiere at JAFF and a place in the Wide Angle Asian Short Film Competition at Busan, it is meeting exactly the audiences it should. It reaches for more than it fully grasps, but the reach itself is the point.

Introduction

Celebrity Cruises occupies a unique position in the cruise industry. Neither a mass-market cruise line nor an ultra-luxury operator, Celebrity has developed what it calls a "premium cruise" experience, blending contemporary luxury, sophisticated dining, innovative ship design, and destination-focused itineraries.

By the 2028-2029 season, Celebrity Cruises is expected to operate one of the most modern premium fleets at sea, including its award-winning Edge Series vessels and an expanding portfolio of itineraries across all seven continents. History of Celebrity Cruises

text:
“But whoever drinks the water I give them will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give them will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life.” — John 4:14

Over Crater Lake, Cascade Range, Oregon, USA.

It was noon in Samaria, the hottest hour of the day, when a woman walked out alone to Jacob’s well. Most people drew water in the cool of the morning, together. She came when no one else would be there. But Someone was. A tired Jewish Rabbi sat by the well and asked her for a drink, crossing every line that was supposed to keep them apart.

Then He offered her something she had never been offered: living water. He knew her whole story, every disappointment and every closed door, and He did not turn away. He spoke to her with dignity and told her plainly who He was. She left her water jar right there by the well and ran back to the very town she had been avoiding. “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.” The people came, Jesus stayed two more days, and many believed. The woman who arrived at noon in hiding went home as the first messenger to her whole village.

Like this deep blue lake that fills from snow and rain, a heart can be filled from a source above it. Whatever dry place you are walking through, Jesus meets you there, not after you have it all together. Drink deeply from His kindness this morning. Let it settle the restless thirst for approval and carry it into ordinary moments: a warm greeting for the person who usually sits alone, patience with someone who is running on empty, a quiet word of hope. Grace that is received has a way of spilling over, and Thursday is a fine day for it.

text:
If you didn’t get a chance to watch tonight’s gubernatorial debate between @ChristineDrazan and @GovTinaKotek , you can watch it in the link:

My takeways of the topics addressed:

🔸Data Centers: Christine Drazan and Tina Kotek both spoke about a moratorium on data centers. Christine specifically said that each community should have the ability to decide whether data centers are something they want in their community or not.

🔸Affordability: Christine Drazan committed to lowering costs for Oregonians. Tina Kotek has been in office for the last four years while costs have continued to rise.

🔸Housing: Christine Drazan addressed lowering property taxes and making housing more affordable. Tina Kotek did not offer the same level of specificity, but rather focused more on government-subsidized housing, which ultimately costs taxpayers more.

🔸Wildfire Prevention: Christine Drazan and Tina Kotek both talked about resiliency and prevention. I especially appreciated Christine’s focus on proactive forest management and protecting Oregon’s long tradition and values of environmental stewardship.

🔸Oregon’s Business Climate: Christine Drazan has suggested that the Corporate Activity Tax needs to be modified or repealed, and that regulations that have become overbearing on businesses need to be pulled back. Tina Kotek has continued to support Oregon’s tax-and-spend approach during her time in office.

They also went into a host of different topics, usually the politically loaded ones. Tina continued to speak as though she were running against President Trump ( which is odd when there are many republicans who are not happy about some of the policies coming out of the White House), while Christine focused more on Oregon and the issues facing Oregonians.

My conclusion is simple: I like Christine’s vision, and we have felt the impacts of Tina Kotek’s governing style. The key is holding true to campaign promises once elected, we are at that moment and critical hour in Oregon.

Christine Drazan is a longtime Oregonian who has been living in a very liberal state. I don’t think the pendulum is necessarily going to swing the way Tina is suggesting if Christine wins.

I especially liked Christine’s plan and was happy that she addressed Oregon’s long tradition and values of protecting our environment. She talked about how clear-cutting is a thing of the past and that we have much more sustainable ways to selectively harvest timber and do preventative forest management. I couldn’t agree more!

All in all, we’ve lived under Tina Kotek’s plan for Oregon, and what we’ve seen is continued businesses leaving, increasingly extreme wildfires, heavy-handed government, and an unquenched thirst for more tax revenue; something that is simply becoming unaffordable for Oregon families and individuals.

It seems to me that Tina Kotek is more focused on government subsidies for housing, while Christine Drazan is talking more about empowering people, lowering the costs of building and homeownership, and making property taxes more manageable.

I believe that if we allocate the money we already have more fiscally responsibly, we can accomplish a lot more for Oregonians without continually reaching deeper into their pockets.

Personally, I think completely repealing the CAT tax would be a great way to jump-start businesses.

And sustainable forest management is a must. I think we should take it a step further and put our downed timber to good use instead of letting it go to waste. Leave the biologically necessary amount on the forest floor, but take the rest and repurpose it throughout all 36 counties.

That timber could be mulched and chipped and used for sustainable, low-water gardens in our communities. It could be used in highway medians, parks, playgrounds and other public spaces throughout the state.

We have our own resources sitting right there in our forests. Let’s manage them properly.

Army, I came across these two comments on tt, and I think they offer a perspective worth considering.
First, I want to make it clear that I’m absolutely not defending people gathering outside the members’ hotels or invading their privacy. I fully support respecting their boundaries, especially now that Namjoon himself has explained how much the situation is affecting them....But I do think we need to be mindful of how we approach these situations and how we react to people. Not everyone gathering in these areas is necessarily Army. Some may be fans who knowingly disregard boundaries, but others may simply be curious bystanders who have no idea about the expectations within our fandom. And unfortunately, there are also people who are deliberately looking to provoke Army because they know they’ll get a reaction.
I’ve seen some pretty aggressive responses from within the fandom, including comments about physically confronting people or even doxxing them. I understand the frustration, but those reactions can make things worse. People outside the fandom don’t necessarily understand the context. They just see fans threatening or attacking others, and that can create even more hostility. The first comment also raises an interesting point about how constantly amplifying these situations can unintentionally attract more attention, including from people who weren’t even interested in going there initially.
None of this means we should stay silent or stop advocating for the members’ privacy. It simply means we should be thoughtful about how we communicate, recognize that not every situation is black and white, and avoid giving people who are intentionally antagonizing us the reactions they’re looking for....and to be clear, anyone making threats or deliberately harassing Army is responsible for their own behavior. I’m not placing that responsibility on the fandom. I just think there’s value in taking a moment to assess the situation before reacting. We can be firm about boundaries without being aggressive, and we can educate people without immediately assuming everyone has bad intentions.
At the end of the day, our goal is to protect the members’ peace and safety, as well as the safety of Army. We should make sure our approach is actually helping accomplish that.

But inside this same Pakistan, a system full of weaknesses and flaws, there exists one institution so successful you probably couldn't find a more successful one anywhere in the whole world: the military establishment.

There's no field in Pakistan's whole system, from A to Z, where this institution doesn't have its hand in. There's no one in the entire country who can cross the set boundaries and criticize this military institution. Sure, there are plenty of people who criticize the army, but even they're only allowed to criticize up to the point this institution itself can tolerate, and even that's permitted only so no one can say criticism of the army is forbidden entirely.

Pakistan's history has made this plain: whenever anyone, from any field or profession, has criticized the military institution in a way that crossed its set limits, they've been silenced so thoroughly that not only do they never speak again, but people close and distant to them never again dare that kind of criticism, and don't even try to go near that line. That's exactly why this institution is such an extraordinarily successful one.

So if you look at it purely from the angle of holding onto power, influence, and dominance, this is an unmatched, successful institution. Some people might say, how can we accept this is a successful institution when its history of servility and subservience to the British is plain for everyone to see, and there's plenty of other criticism leveled at it too?

But these objections only deserve to be heard once someone first proves this institution is actually a Muslim institution, that Muslims built its foundation, or that it was created to protect and defend Muslims. In Parinda, he played the Mafia Don, whose eyes scared the hell out of you, he became the character, just like he did with most of the movies he acted in.

In Prahaar, he played the role of an Army Man, and he made you believe that he was a man in uniform all his life.

In Agnisakshi, the husband who controlled every moment of his scared wife, he gave you a character that you just could not get of your mind.

In Krantiveer, his iconic dialogue of "Hindu ka Khoon, Musalmaan ka Khoon" captured the national imagination like none other. 

In Ab Tak Chapan, he held your attention in every frame, and you were convinced that Nana Patekar was actually an Encounter Specialist all his life. 

But then he played Tabrez Alam in Apaharan and now you corrected yourself. He was actually one of Bihar's most notorious Mafia Don's, his Bihari accent, his ruthlessness for his quest for power, you were simply blown away by his potrayal of Mohammad Shahabuddin(Lalu Yadav's favourite Mafia Don turned politician)

In Welcome, he was a Don, who made you laugh, with his dead pan face expressions and the iconic "Aaloo le lo, kandha le lo" lines

In Rajneeti, you finally realized that in reality Nana Patekar was a brilliant Political advisor to a very powerful Political family. The multi-starrer had many brilliant actors and Nana there too stood out with his craft.

Actor par excellence, who became the character, who convinced you with each role that he was actually that character all his life.

In India, there are stars, superstars and then there are actors, who were treated as stars, and Nana Patekar belonged to that rare category.

At 75, you felt he still had a lot to offer to the World of Cinema, but God had other plans.

Thank you for such fine performances, thank you for such classy entertainment, where you connected with all types of Cinema lovers.

Privileged to be the part of generation, who saw most of your movies, while growing up.

Rest in Peace, Nana Patekar

text:
Why so SI-rious?
Artificial intelligence worries American voters. Donald Trump has found a more manageable problem: its name.
At the United Nations on September 22nd, he took issue with “Artificial Intelligence”. Artificial made it sound fake. He preferred “Super Intelligence”, or SI. A week later, the preference became an executive order. Federal agencies were instructed to use the new term in correspondence, websites, reports and policy documents. Existing laws, contracts and historical records could stay as they were. So could the legal definition, at least for now. The president’s science and technology adviser had roughly 60 days to propose legislative changes.
The name had been promoted. The definition would follow.
A Reuters–Ipsos poll published on October 7th supplied an unhelpful backdrop. Of 3,526 registered voters surveyed, 84% considered AI a threat to American workers. That was considerably more than the 60% who said the same of illegal immigration, and more than the proportions concerned about competition from foreign workers or the power of big corporations.
Some 57% thought the Trump administration was not taking AI’s risks seriously, including roughly a third of Republicans. Stronger regulation appealed to 80% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans. More than half supported limits on new data centres; 62% worried about the technology escaping human control.
With fewer than four weeks until the November 3rd midterm elections, these concerns were difficult to dismiss as somebody else’s partisan grievance. A June survey by the Pew Research Centre found that 56% of Democrats were more concerned than excited about AI’s growing presence in everyday life, compared with 49% of Republicans. Three years earlier, the order had been reversed. Anxiety had political leanings, but no permanent party membership.
Nor did voters need to imagine machines acquiring souls to find something worth worrying about. Jobs, electricity bills and a large, power-hungry building arriving in the neighbourhood would do.
The employment evidence remains unsettled. Tracking developments through June, researchers at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab had not found clear evidence of an economy-wide employment decline caused by AI. A more troubling pattern appeared among workers aged 22 to 25. In occupations highly exposed to AI, employment was about 19% below the level implied by the employment trend among similarly aged workers in less-exposed occupations. A year earlier, the gap had been 15%.
Much of the adjustment appeared to involve hiring fewer young workers rather than dismissing existing employees. The researchers cautioned, however, that these trends could not establish how much of the difference AI had caused.
A CESifo working paper, meanwhile, found no unusual rise in unemployment among recent university graduates that summer. The International Labour Organisation’s 2025 occupational index placed clerical work among the most exposed categories, while judging the transformation of jobs more likely than their wholesale disappearance.
These findings need not contradict one another. An economy can avoid a wave of redundancies while becoming harder for young people to enter. A firm does not have to sack ten experienced employees to change the labour market. It can simply stop hiring two beginners. Employment statistics distinguish between a job lost and a job never offered. For someone trying to pay the rent, the difference may be less reassuring.
Trump has a simpler account of technological progress: America must win, particularly against China. SI supplies a suitably impressive name for the prize.
“Artificial intelligence” can sound like a technology to be tested, used and regulated. “Super intelligence” lends itself to the language of national destiny. Attention shifts from what the systems can do, and who answers when they fail, to whether America will reach the finish line first.
There is a serious political calculation here. Governments seeking investment in research and infrastructure need a public argument for it. National competition supplies one. A project that benefits a technology company becomes easier to defend when it can also be presented as essential to the country’s future.
But a country winning a technological race does not ensure that every citizen shares the winnings. A data centre’s profits may belong to its operator while some of the costs of expanding the electricity network fall elsewhere. A company’s savings from automation need not reappear in its employees’ wages. National strength and household prosperity are related questions, not interchangeable answers.
On September 29th, leaders from six technology companies also signed a voluntary safety accord. They included Google’s Sundar Pichai, Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. Trump described the agreement as morally binding, but not legally so. The companies promised stronger safety measures; the accord supplied no clear legal penalty for failing to deliver them.
The instruction to federal agencies to change their terminology, by contrast, was an order. Safety commitments were voluntary. Vocabulary had firmer rules.
Outside the White House, Musk offered a small demonstration. Discussing the technology’s benefits, he said “AI”, then corrected himself: “SI, pardon me.” Trump thanked him and patted his arm. In the following days, Musk promoted SI on social media, while Huang described data centres as “SI factories”.
The terminology was still catching on. The etiquette had arrived.
Musk had no legal obligation to apologise. The order governed federal agencies, not his conversation. Nor does a single correction tell us whether he thought the new term technically sound. It does show that, in that setting, one expression had become more appropriate than another.
This could be dismissed as ordinary political flattery. But flattery is itself a useful reminder that power need not issue an instruction every time it gets its way.
In his inaugural lecture at the Collège de France on December 2nd 1970, Michel Foucault argued that discourse was not merely the expression of political struggle. It was also something people struggled over, and something they struggled with.
His interest went well beyond vocabulary. Why does one person’s statement count as knowledge while another’s is treated as an opinion? Whose definition reaches a textbook, a court judgment or a government report? Who acquires the authority to make such judgments, and how is that authority maintained?
Evidence matters. So do the institutions through which evidence becomes an accepted basis for action. Papers undergo peer review. Doctors require qualifications. Courts follow procedures for admitting evidence and reaching judgments. In his later discussions of a “regime of truth”, Foucault examined the arrangements through which societies produce, circulate and recognise statements as true, and the power attached to doing so.
This is not a claim that a ruler can make something true by announcing it. Calling today’s AI superintelligence will not improve a model’s reasoning. Trump can, however, make the federal government use the name.
The executive order exposes the distinction neatly. It requires SI while retaining AI’s existing legal definition. The president can choose what his government calls the technology, but must still borrow the old definition to specify what he is talking about. Renaming has not supplied new technical knowledge. It has established a rule for official usage.
That is less than control over truth, but more than a cosmetic alteration.
Government reports are quoted by journalists. Policy language finds its way into industry analysis and corporate compliance documents. Conference organisers borrow official terminology. A description can gain a considerable advantage in circulation without first winning an argument about its accuracy.
America also has a convenient distribution channel: English. AI is already a global abbreviation, used in research, software and everyday conversation. Washington cannot order the rest of the world to replace it. It can try to put SI into documents that others will cite.
Such advantages matter because an expression need not persuade every reader to influence a debate. It may be enough to establish the question everyone is expected to answer. Should the discussion move from “How should AI be governed?” towards “How can America win the SI race?”, critics could reject the administration’s policies while still accepting part of its account of what is at stake.
That remains a possibility, not an accomplished result. AI continues to appear in research, products and other governments’ language. An American executive order cannot make laboratories reach different conclusions or compel private speakers to adopt a preferred term.
Calling this Orwellian Newspeak therefore overstates the order’s reach. In the appendix to Nineteen Eighty-Four, the purpose of Newspeak is to strip away words and meanings until unorthodox thought becomes impossible to express. Americans remain free to say AI. An administrative style rule is some distance from ownership of the English language.
Orwell’s 1946 essay, Politics and the English Language, offers a closer comparison. Its concern is with language that obscures concrete actions, responsibilities and consequences. SI does not remove the risks associated with AI. It can help direct attention elsewhere: towards technological promise and national competition.
The difference has consequences for the argument over expansion. Someone questioning a project’s safety or electricity costs may now be asked to explain why America should risk falling behind. The proposed development has acquired a patriotic presumption in its favour. Critics must argue against that as well as against the project.
SI also borrows prestige from something that has not yet been delivered.
In AI research, superintelligence generally refers to systems whose cognitive abilities surpass those of humans across a very broad range of fields. It is not a standard description of every AI product now available. Trump has taken the name of an anticipated level of capability and applied it to the technology already in use.
Today’s systems get tomorrow’s title.
That might seem no more consequential than an extravagant advertising claim. But technology investment routinely depends on expectations. Companies anticipating more capable models buy chips and build data centres. Investors expecting growing demand supply capital. Governments fearing a rival’s breakthrough increase research spending.
These decisions happen before the predictions have been vindicated. Expectations help determine which projects receive money, which problems attract researchers and which risks governments are willing to tolerate. A description of the future can therefore help shape the conditions under which that future might emerge.
There is nothing inherently wrong with this. Important research often requires someone to finance an outcome that cannot be guaranteed. The difficulty comes when an expectation is quietly promoted into a premise.
Once “the age of superintelligence” is treated as an established fact, further expansion can begin to look self-evidently necessary. Whether a particular data centre is worth building, how its electricity costs should be allocated and what safeguards its customers should meet become subordinate questions. “We cannot afford to lose” is a powerful answer precisely because it leaves so much unspecified.
The prediction may still fail. The spending does not wait. Land is committed, electricity networks are expanded and public resources are allocated while the promised capabilities remain uncertain. Some people are already paying for a future nobody can yet describe with confidence.
Others would prefer that parts of it never arrive.
Bernie Sanders has been writing superintelligence into a different kind of document: a proposed ban.
On March 25th, he and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed legislation to halt the construction or upgrading of AI data centres until stronger protections were established for electricity consumers, the environment and affected communities. On September 23rd, Sanders and Representative Greg Casar proposed a ban on artificial superintelligence. It sought to prohibit the development and deployment of systems meeting specified capability or danger thresholds, and to pause advanced AI development until a new regulatory system was in place.
Trump wants SI to cover the AI already here. Sanders wants to draw a boundary around capabilities that should not be developed or deployed. For the White House, the term offers a banner under which to expand. For Sanders, it identifies something to restrict.
The policies are not equivalent. An executive instruction on terminology has already been issued; a proposed development ban must still pass through Congress. Nor does seeking a precise legal boundary mean Sanders has found a workable one. How should dangerous capabilities be measured? Who should judge them? Could a ban be enforced without also stopping useful research? A bill’s title cannot resolve those questions.
Still, the competing uses reveal a limit to Trump’s naming power. Promoting SI would not give him exclusive rights over its meaning. The White House sees a future America must win. Sanders sees capabilities that may be too dangerous to pursue. The same word can support demands for expansion and demands for restraint.
This is another part of Foucault’s account that the language of “controlling the narrative” tends to miss. A term can be borrowed, challenged and turned against those who use it. Official acceptance does not end the struggle over meaning. Trump can tell his agencies to write SI. He cannot require Sanders to admire it.
The larger imbalance lies elsewhere: those best placed to describe the future are often also best placed to commit resources to it.
Technology companies decide how much computing capacity to buy. Governments approve projects and allocate public money. Legislators debate the restrictions. People with little influence over these decisions must nevertheless live with their results: fewer vacancies in a particular occupation, a strained local electricity network, a changed bill.
They need not oppose technological progress to ask who has agreed to the terms on their behalf.
That is why the 84% deserves attention. It does not establish that AI has caused employment losses on anything like that scale. Nor does the Reuters–Ipsos survey show whether the rebranding has changed public opinion; it supplies no before-and-after test. It does record a large majority worried about a threat to workers while the administration and technology executives celebrate a new era.
Official compliance, technical credibility and public consent are different achievements. The White House has obtained some of the first. A change of name supplies neither of the other two.
Musk said AI, corrected himself and was thanked.
The president had secured the wording he wanted. Who gets to choose the future it promises—and who must pay for it—remains rather less settled.

text:
Elon Musk shared the full speech delivered by Secretary of State Marco Rubio from the historic Pnyx in Athens, bringing Rubio’s message regarding the future of the Western world to his massive audience on X. Musk reposted the speech without adding any specific commentary of his own.

Rubio’s appearance at the Pnyx—with the Acropolis and the Parthenon visible in the background—was deliberately symbolic. Speaking from the site associated with the democratic assembly of ancient Athens, the U.S. Secretary of State linked ancient Greece to Western civilization and the political traditions that ultimately shaped the modern West.

At the heart of Rubio’s address was a call for the United States and Europe to rediscover what he described as core Western values. He highlighted ideas associated with ancient Greece—including curiosity, courage, ambition, and a willingness to explore the unknown—while arguing that the West must regain confidence in itself.

Rubio presented the foundation of the West as a long continuum extending from ancient Greece and Rome, through Christianity and European civilization, to the present day. He argued that this location remains a singular place of significance as the Union and its European allies face a period of geopolitical competition.

The speech also conveyed a strong message regarding national identity and sovereignty. Rubio argued that Western nations must stand up for their interests, uphold their societies, and contribute to security, forging deep ties among themselves and with Europe.

The choice of venue lent special weight to the occasion. The Pnyx was the site where the citizens of ancient Athens gathered for political debate and decision-making, making it a fitting setting for a speech focused on democracy, Western political traditions, and the future of the transatlantic relationship.

Musk’s decision to share the full speech with a wide audience amplified the reach of Rubio’s address in Athens. With the Acropolis looming in the background, the video offered a highly symbolic illustration of Rubio’s argument: that the West must look back to the foundations of its civilization as it considers its future.

The speech comes as Washington and its European allies deliberate on issues of defense, energy, technology, and the shifting balance of power. During his time in Athens, Rubio also described Greece as a strong NATO ally and spoke of greater European engagement with visitors to the continent.

text:
“If a ‘large share’ of scientists are creationists then show me one published paper from a non creationist journal which rejects evolution and posits creationism as the explanation for how humans came to exist.”

Listen to the demand. A scientist counts only if he can publish the creationist conclusion in a secular journal that gatekeeps creationism and the data that indicate it. That is the gate announcing itself as the test. The journal will not print the conclusion, and the refusal is then offered as proof that no qualified person holds it.

The people are not missing. The demand is that a creationist conclusion appear in a journal that will not print a creationist conclusion. The training and the empirical papers are already in the secular record. The inference is the part the same record bars.

John Sanford took his PhD in plant breeding and genetics at the University of Wisconsin. He joined the faculty at Cornell in horticultural sciences and held that post for decades. With Edward Wolf and Theodore Klein he co-invented the biolistic gene gun, the particle-delivery method used to transform plant cells, and the patents and the transformation papers went through the secular plant literature. That work is not a church pamphlet. It is the method laboratories used. After that record he published the genetic-entropy argument: most mutations are deleterious or near-neutral, selection does not remove the subtle load, and a multicellular genome degrades under the measured clock rather than constructing new coordinated systems. The gene-gun papers were acceptable. The entropy conclusion was not going to be printed as the origin of humans in the journals that treat common descent as the frame. The man who built the tool did not lose the doctorate when he followed the load.

Nathaniel Jeanson took a PhD in cell and developmental biology at Harvard Medical School. The doctoral work was in the secular literature, under the ordinary committee and the ordinary journals of that field. He later published the creationist reading of the genetic data, including the argument that the mutation rate and the time depth cannot be run together without destroying the genome. Harvard did not grant the degree to a man who had never handled the data. The degree is the part your test counts. The conclusion drawn from the same data is the part your test excludes in advance.

Georgia Purdom took a PhD in molecular genetics at Ohio State. The training was cloning, expression, and the ordinary molecular toolkit, not a seminary track. She taught at the university level and then stated the creationist conclusion in public. A doctorate in molecular genetics is not erased by the conclusion. Your test erases it anyway, because the test is not the doctorate. The test is whether a secular journal will host the inference the journal has already ruled out.

Robert Carter took a PhD in cellular and molecular biology at the University of Miami. His empirical work included coral genetics, published in the secular marine and molecular journals. Population differences, variation inside a kind, and rearrangement of existing sequence are in that literature. Common descent of humans from an undirected mutational series is a further claim. He rejects the further claim. The coral papers passed. The rejection is what you are calling unpublished, because the venue you named will not carry it.

That is the gate, stated in the demand. Publish the transformation method, the developmental experiments, the molecular thesis, and the coral data, and the man counts. Publish the inference that the measured clock degrades code and does not write a human body plan, and the man ceases to count, because the journal will not print it. A large share does not need to be a majority inside the journals that police the conclusion. It needs to be real people with real degrees whose empirical work already went through, and whose excluded conclusion is the thing you asked to see inside the excluding venue. The degrees are public. The gene gun is public. The missing pathway from mutation to a new body plan is public. The rule that bars the inference is the indoctrination, not the absence of the geneticists.

Truth is still the data, not the gate. A blank does not write a code. The measured clock degrades code. A journal rule that excludes the inference does not make the clock run the other way. The demand is the indoctrination. The geneticists are the rebuttal to the claim that only nutjobs hold the other reading.

The U.S. Department of Transportation said late on Wednesday, October 7, that it has granted Aurora and other self-driving trucking companies a five-year exemption from rules requiring warning triangles to be placed around a stopped truck, Reuters reported — clearing a hurdle for trucks with no one on board.

Under the exemption, Level 4 autonomous trucks can instead use amber warning beacons mounted on the cab, which USDOT said offer an equivalent or greater level of safety. Companies must notify the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration before using it and disclose any crash that happens while the beacons are, or should have been, switched on; the agency says it will revoke exemptions that lower safety. The decision replaces a run of temporary three-month waivers issued since October 2025, the latest of which was due to expire on October 9. Aurora — which has around 20 driverless trucks in on-road operations and filed for a five-year waiver in April — said the decision "underscores the government's recognition of the immense economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking." Waymo and Aurora first sought the waiver in 2023, and Aurora sued FMCSA in early 2025 after it was denied.

Why it matters: a driverless truck can't climb out and set triangles, so this five-year rule change takes away one of the last practical blocks on running them at scale on U.S. highways.

Sources: Reuters; Pittsburgh Business Times, 7 Oct 2026.

text:
8 October 2026
Today in History

1652
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Foggy, cold weather during the morning. The wind blew moderately from the northwest.
Several men were sent to the salt pan to collect salt, as the supply already on hand was almost exhausted.
The men, however, returned empty-handed.
It was speculated that it would first have to become much warmer before the salt would crystallise and could be collected.

1653
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The entries for 8 and 9 October 1653 were recorded together under the same date in the diary.
The weather over the two days is described as pleasant.
A light north-westerly wind blew during the day.
Towards evening, the wind changed direction and blew from the west.
Five Saldanhars arrived at the fort with news that some of their people were on their way to the fort. According to the group, the purpose of their visit was, naturally, trade. Their spokesman said that the group would arrive in approximately three to four days.

1654
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
A lovely, warm, sunny day, with a light but constant westerly breeze.

1655
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The entries for 7 and 8 October were recorded together under the same date in the diary.
No mention is made of the weather conditions.

Sunday, 8 October 1656
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daglimier brought a warm, sunny day to the Cape. The wind blew moderately from the north.
The British officers enjoyed lunch at the fort and returned to their ships towards evening.
Everyone at the fort was treated to beer and tobacco for smoking that day. The treat was not given without reason, however, as the diary records that considerable effort had been devoted to the work being carried out at the jetty.

1657
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Morning at the Cape is described as cloudy, with intermittent rain. The wind blew moderately from the northwest.

1658
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The south-south-easterly wind had begun blowing the previous afternoon and was still raging at daybreak.
During the morning, Doman arrived at the fort together with some of the Chainouqya people. That day, 16 cattle and 48 sheep were exchanged, to everyone's satisfaction.
Eva was still with the Cochoquas.

1659
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The entries for 8 and 9 October were recorded together under the same date in the diary.
The weather over the two days is described as pleasant, with the wind constantly swirling.

1760
Jacobus Coetzee was baptised on this day.
He was the first European to officially describe and make known the existence of the Orange River.
In other words, this was 19 years before Colonel Robert Gordon did so.

1811 George
The town of George was established.
Thirty erven were sold by public auction on this day, 8 October 1811.
George was initially part of the Swellendam district.
The district was, however, very large, and for this reason the Earl of Caledon, Governor of the Cape, requested permission to increase the number of districts in the Colony.
On 23 April 1811, Caledon, as Governor, declared the area a separate drostdy.
During June 1811, work began on laying out the town, and on this day the first erven were sold.

1828 
Dr James Barry
Dr James Barry was transferred from the Cape to Mauritius.
Barry is remembered as the “man” who performed the first successful Caesarean section.

1835–1840
The recollections of the Voortrekker J. H. Hatting during the Great Trek.
Hatting wrote that, after some time, they arrived at the Buffalo River.
Two envoys were sent to Mpanda to bring news concerning the whereabouts of the commando and to find out whether Mpanda perhaps knew where Dingane was.
(The battle that was about to take place became known as the Battle of the Maqonqo Hills, which occurred on 29 January 1840.)

Saturday, 8 October 1836
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Louis wrote that they set out early that morning to go hunting.
They were unsuccessful, however.
Rossetoe—the Venda chief, whose name is actually spelled “Rasethau”—arrived at Tregardt's encampment and brought two dogs with him.
Adonis, one of Tregardt's workers, went together with another man to fetch his belongings. Unfortunately, Tregardt does not state where the man's belongings were or exactly what they intended to fetch.
Siliewiele—it is not known who the man was—came to Tregardt with a story that Rammaboya had taken 12 cattle, 14 goats and 6 sheep from Captain Serubele, in an attempt to provoke a dispute.

Sunday, 8 October 1837
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
The Tregardt party had been up and active for some time when Sekwati arrived.
Louis and the man held a conversation.
Louis wanted to hire four of Sekwati's followers until the party had passed through the Baloela gate/pass.
Louis offered to reward each of the four men with a hide and a quantity of fat.
Sekwati agreed.
Louis offered Sekwati a lame cow together with a calf for the use of the men.
Sekwati accepted the offer.

Sunday, 8 October 1837
From the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.
Reverend Smit wrote that he held a church service for those present in Piet Retief's tent.
The laager commandant, A. Greyling, moved the ox-wagons belonging to Retief's wife, as well as those belonging to the Reverend and his wife, into the middle of the laager.
The Voortrekker A. Joubert's wagon also arrived at the laager later and was drawn into the circle of the laager.

1838
There are no entries for this day in Reverend Erasmus Smit's diary.

1853 — Gold discovered
Pieter Jacob Marais discovered alluvial gold in the Jukskei River.

Monday, 8 October 1900
Anglo-Boer War — Day 363
A small Boer commando arrived at Ficksburg. After a short engagement, the town was taken.
Commandant Hans Botha, commander of a small Boer commando, attacked a train at Vlakfontein on the Natal railway line. The engagement was brief and the British forces surrendered.
Former General H. J. Schoeman, together with Captain Anderson, was captured by a burgher named Mostert. The two men were sent under armed escort to General Beyers, who was at Buyskop.

Monday, 8 October 1901
Anglo-Boer War — Day 728
General L. Botha crossed the Pongola River near Lüneburg.
Two Dutch prisoners of war, H. A. de Haas and H. Mulder, escaped from St Helena in a small boat. They were, however, spotted by the ship HMS Doris and returned to the island.
Commandant F. J. Wolmarans captured an ox-wagon convoy consisting of 40 wagons near Potchefstroom. Later that day, a group of Royal Engineers was captured by a section of Wolmarans's commando while they were building blockhouses near Ventersdorp. Twelve ox-wagons were seized.

When he made the taken out of context remarks in Nebraska, he was literally talking about gas prices and the Iran war, what he actually said was this:

“It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s this is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

Well known reporter and fact-checker Daniel Dale, agrees his remarks were decontextualized and he is not a Trump supporter.
He is CNN’s fact-checker. 

This is what he wrote “Let ’em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it’s a small price to pay” and wrote: “This isn’t a direct quote from Trump, and I very much don’t think it’s a correct paraphrase.” His point was the one Trump has made for months: higher gas prices are “a small price to pay” next to what an unchecked Iran could do to a city. He called the delivery “especially rambling and incomplete.” He wrote: “It’s Trump’s fault you kinda have to be steeped in TrumpRallySpeak to know what he was saying last night.” He also wrote that “you can say it’s inappropriate regardless for the president to casually float the possibility of a city being wiped out, but the context exists and is important.” That is the edge of an honest and intelligent opinion. But you intentionally distorted it and are floating the false narrative that Trump is calling for a real obliteration of LA and SD.

It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. I’m not only talking about Israel and big parts of the Middle East, but let them hit us with a nuclear weapon.” 

The White House said he “was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.” One reply under your post said it plain: “You deliberately ripped the quote out of context and pretend Trump was offering up LA and San Diego as collateral.” That is your whole dirty trick.

By the time Desire Luzinda took up a microphone at Dembe FM, she was already an established recording artist with several songs to her name. Her radio career, however, lasted only about eight months.

Born Racheal Desire Luzinda on August 15, 1980, at Mulago, Luzinda entered the media industry through television. She worked at WBS TV, although accounts differ on the timing of her stint, placing it between 2004 and 2007.

One biography says she later spent about two years at Radio Samba, although details of that period are limited.

Her most clearly documented radio job was at Dembe FM, where she joined in February 2011. She co-hosted the evening drive show, Dembe Taxi, alongside Kasuku, Mayende and John Ssozi, also known as Emperor Orlando.

Luzinda left the station in October 2011, bringing her documented stint to about eight months. After Dembe FM came under Nation Media Group, Walden — who had started at the station as a receptionist before hosting a Sunday teenagers’ programme — replaced her on Dembe Taxi.

Her short radio career came at a time when music was already her main professional focus. She had recorded Nakowa Emikwano in 2006, Mubiite in 2007 and Nyumirwa Nyo in 2008. The latter was produced by Benon Mugumbya of Swangz Avenue.

Radio was therefore a brief detour in a career that had already been built around music and television.

In February 2015, Capital FM reportedly offered Luzinda a role on its love show alongside Val for Shs2.5 million a month. She declined the offer.

The offer came months after a private-photo leak in November 2014 had drawn intense public attention to Luzinda and increased demand for her live performances.

Luzinda later moved from secular music into gospel and released a project titled Transition. In 2020, she qualified as a medical assistant at San Leandro Adult School in California.

In 2021, she established the Desire Luzinda Foundation. She has since been based in California.
