text:
India's Battery Energy Storage Push Hits a Viability Wall: Up to One-Third of Projects Bid Out So Far Could Be Unviable, With 24 GWh of BESS Projects Cancelled or Re-Tendered Amid Aggressive Bidding and Rising Battery Costs

The Core Problem
India's green energy transition faces headwinds as efforts to support wind and solar power with battery storage falter, driven by aggressive bidding, project unviability and widespread contract cancellations

Industry experts believe as much as one-third of the projects bid out so far could be unviable

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) store solar and wind energy for later use; the government has mandated BESS integration for all future solar and wind tenders

Data from the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA) shows a total of 24 GWh of BESS projects were cancelled or re-tendered during 2018-2026

The cancelled or re-tendered capacity comprises over 11% of the Central Electricity Authority's target of 208 GWh by the decade end

A year-wise breakup of scrapping or re-tendering was not available

Battery Setback: BESS Projects in India (GWh, as of 30 Sep)
Total: 167.5 GWh
Request for selection: 55.3
Under construction: 49.3
Cancelled: 24.0
Awarded: 22.6
Operational: 13.5
Bidding closed:* 2.4 (recently closed bids where winners are yet to be announced and awarded)
Notice inviting tender: 0.3
Source: IESA ESS Market Update September 2026

Aggressive Bidding and Viability Gap Funding
Another 22 GWh capacity awarded under the government's ₹5,400 crore viability gap funding (VGF) 2.0 plan is also under strain, as BESS developers got these contracts by bidding at unviable rates of below ₹2 per kWh, said three people in the know

As per current trends, BESS tariff must be at least ₹2.4 per unit to be viable

Under the VGF scheme, the government supports up to ₹18 lakh per MWh for battery storage of up to 30 GW

July power ministry data shows letters of award issued for 22.43 GWh, but financial closure achieved for only 5 GW

Alok Kumar, director general of the All India Discoms Association and a former power secretary: concerns persist over viability of about one-third of the projects bid out so far

"Companies are still figuring out the technology. It is estimated that around 30%, or up to one-third of the projects, may not be viable as developers are yet to complete financial closure"

"This is a learning stage, but norms should be in place to select efficient players, rather than focusing on the lowest tariff quoted"

Cancellations and Disputes
NTPC terminated the ₹413-crore contract awarded to Gurugram-based GR Infraprojects Ltd (GRIL) for a 400-MWh BESS project at the Mouda Super Thermal Power Station in Maharashtra, due to the contractor's failure to meet contractual obligations and achieve progress

NTPC said the project, awarded in March 2026, was scheduled for completion within 15 months

A contractual notice was issued to GRIL calling for immediate corrective action, but GRIL failed to undertake remedial measures, so NTPC scrapped the contract and encashed ₹91 crore of securities

In May, West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd annulled the tender for a 250MW/1,000MWh standalone BESS at Goaltore and withdrew the letter of award to PM Green Pvt. Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Power Mech Projects Ltd

In an exchange filing, Power Mech attributed the action to administrative and procedural exigencies "beyond the control of either party" and said it was not non-compliance

In June, the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity set aside Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission's nod to Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd's tender for procurement of 2,000MW/4,000MWh of BESS capacity, effectively cancelling one of India's largest standalone battery storage tenders

The tribunal said MSEDCL brought a new norm after the bidding process concluded, per a report by JMK Research & Analytics

Industry Voices
An NTPC official: "There is concern over the viability of several projects. Initially, several frivolous players came up and placed very low bids in order to win tenders"

Reji Kumar Pillai, president of the India Smart Grid Forum: many newcomers jumped into BESS projects and submitted bids aggressively, expecting the battery price trajectory to keep falling

But owing to policy changes in China last year, battery cell prices increased by 32% during January-July, making many projects unviable

He said the industry globally is at a nascent stage; none of the large megawatt hour-scale projects have crossed 10 years, and all gigawatt hour-scale ones started less than five years ago

Vikash Venkataramana, chief product officer, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies: the prospect of more cancellations is "a major concern" for the industry as it threatens to derail national clean energy targets and broader market confidence

A pattern of frequent cancellations creates regulatory uncertainty that deters major foreign and local institutional investors, making financing more expensive and fragile

Because India relies heavily on China for battery tech, local projects are uniquely vulnerable to volatile Chinese input costs and shifting export markets

Brighter Spots
The re-tendering for a couple of projects has seen a rise in tariff bids, showing a shift towards "realistic tariffs", said people in the know

Debmalya Sen, president, IESA: "We hope to see an upward correction in tariffs, going ahead"

By end-September, 13.47 GWh of BESS capacity was installed in India, while 153 GWh was in the pipeline

Core Theme 
India's rush to pair solar and wind with battery storage is colliding with reality, as reckless low bidding (below ₹2 per kWh against a viable level of about ₹2.4), a 32% jump in Chinese cell prices and procedural disputes have led to 24 GWh of cancellations or re-tenders and left up to one-third of awarded projects at risk of being unviable, with only 5 GW reaching financial closure out of 22.43 GWh awarded; while the 167.5 GWh pipeline and a shift toward more realistic tariffs in re-tenders offer some hope, industry leaders say selection norms must reward efficient players rather than the lowest bid to protect the 208 GWh national target and investor confidence.

Let’s talk about the same facts.

Starlink’s hardware kit — including the satellite dish, Wi-Fi router, and cables — costs around $395, followed by a monthly subscription of around $100.

First, the majority of Indians cannot afford this. Second, India already has fiber internet services that offer high-speed internet for around $4.13/month, along with additional benefits such as OTT subscriptions.

Starlink’s main purpose is to provide internet access in remote and underserved locations. At its current price, it is difficult for the average Indian user to justify the cost.

Starlink provides high-speed internet through satellites, but India already has companies working in the satellite-internet and space-tech sectors, including Jio Space Technology and Eutelsat OneWeb.

India also has several startups working on space technology and lower-cost rocket launches, including Astrome Technologies, Skyroot Aerospace, and Agnikul Cosmos.

And one more point: some people argue that Indians don’t really feel the need for high-speed internet. But India has rapidly adopted 5G. Within just two years of its launch, 5G had already covered around 86% of the population.

So, in my view, India doesn’t need Starlink

text:
India needs @Starlink 🇮🇳

• 11,256 of India’s listed villages still lacked 4G coverage as of May 2026.

• India had 1.093 billion internet subscriptions in March 2026, but only 440.87 million were rural. Rural subscription density was 48.31 per 100 people, compared with 126.80 in urban India.

• BharatNet had laid over 850,000 route-km of fibre and made about 221,000 Gram Panchayats service-ready. However, its Points of Presence were reported operational at only 80,472 Gram Panchayats in June 2026.

• Only 4.26% of India’s internet subscriptions were wired connections in March 2026. Starlink could give underserved communities another route to high-speed broadband.

• Starlink has already built 20 gateway sites in India, according to SpaceX Vice President of Starlink Business Operations Lauren Dreyer, speaking at India Mobile Congress today.

• Starlink says it has developed India-specific security controls designed to keep Indian user data within India.

• Its satellite network could bring high-speed internet to remote villages, mountains and islands where extending fibre or mobile networks is difficult.

• Better connectivity could help rural schools access online learning, clinics offer remote consultations and small businesses reach more customers. Starlink already supports education and healthcare in remote communities internationally.

• Portable Starlink terminals have supported disaster response around the world. They could give Indian emergency teams backup connectivity when floods, earthquakes or storms damage ground networks.

• Direct to Cell could also help ordinary 4G phones connect beyond tower coverage, subject to Indian approvals and mobile operator partnerships.

• The government itself identifies difficult terrain, low commercial viability and infrastructure constraints as reasons for remaining coverage gaps. This is exactly where Starlink could help India reach more people.

• India should complete the remaining clearances and spectrum allocation so Starlink can begin commercial service.

• SpaceX’s Vice President of Starlink Business Operations, Lauren Dreyer, said that Starlink is ready to help achieve Prime Minister Modi’s vision of 100% connectivity across India. She highlighted its potential to connect remote classrooms, support telemedicine and restore connectivity after disasters, adding, “With Starlink, people can get connected within minutes, not years.”

India’s hardest-to-reach communities deserve reliable internet too.

text:
Anderson: Cut From Its Christian Soil, Australia Is a Wilting Flower
by @Rod_Lampard [COMMENTARY]

John Anderson’s first Substack essay is too important to miss.

The piece introduced Anderson’s new Our Civilisational Moment (OCM) page in April.

Named after Os Guinness’s 2024 book, Anderson’s inaugural OCM essay asserted that the decline of the modern West connects to de-Christianisation.

Essentially, the unravelling of social cohesion is, in part, a consequence of external and internal forces driving Western culture away from the Western Christian tradition.

Saving Australia is spiritual. The mission, or task ahead, is more than just economics or the military.

According to Anderson, “We must identify the nutrient-rich soil in which our wilting flower once grew. I believe this soil was Christianity, which was once, believe it or not, even very powerful in Australia.”

He then clarified this by stating, “This doesn’t demand that my readers must believe in the truth-claims of Christianity, as I do.

“Perhaps, though, some will come to conclude that the reason Christianity had such a salutary influence on Western civilisation was not merely because it was good and beautiful, but also because it is true.”

Before talking about what I would call the salvific power of the cross behind Australia’s success, Anderson leaned on Guinness’s metaphor of a cut flower, warning that although the beauty and vitality of the flower remain, it’s “rapidly wilting.”

A British success story, Australia, he said, “is still one of the greatest countries in the world. But for how long?”

Proactive and pragmatic, the former deputy prime minister offered hope in the form of five nation-saving, future-defining proposals.

First on the list was wresting Australia’s foundational freedoms back from diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI).

Anderson said DEI is not about public safety.

He argued it’s a disguise for a “power-grab by ideological elites to shape a society in their own image, whether Australians want it or not.”

Preserving Australia’s social fabric was second.

“Australia was once a happy, unified, and peaceful nation,” he explained, “But lately Australians have watched their country change rapidly and become fragmented under a reckless immigration system.

“As former Prime Minister Tony Abbott has recently shown in his timely history of Australia, Australia’s cultural foundation and most powerful cultural force until very recently was Anglo-Celtic.

“Arguably, Australia, like Western civilisation in general, is a flower in the process of being cut from its own heritage.

“I submit that Australia needs a revival of interest in and appreciation of our Anglo-Celtic cultural heritage. Crucially, this should be accompanied by an immigration policy that complements Australia’s cultural heritage; not one that effectively undermines it.”

Third on Anderson’s future-defining list was getting the nation’s economy and housing right.

Read this way, home ownership and the realistic prospect of achieving it are foundational to the nation’s survival.

Crucial to this is lower inflation and better pay, which make cost-of-living pressures more manageable.

Resentment about generational wealth was also a problem the government needed to take seriously.

“Just as bad,” Anderson said, “is when they perceive that the older generation has borrowed against them to maintain their own high living standard and financial security, younger generations become resentful as victims of intergenerational theft.”

Fourth and fifth on his OCM list were energy and geopolitics.

As Anderson stated, “The simple fact is that our elites’ renewables obsession is driven by politics and greed, not science or care for the climate.

“Our elites know that they are putting Australians through much pain with this energy revolution, full well knowing that it will actually do nothing to reduce global warming.

“The question is whether Australia will wake up to this disastrous policy or continue down the path of energy and economic self-sabotage.”

The implication? A key part of stopping Australia’s decline is ditching net zero and moving the national economy away from Communist China.

This includes three security imperatives: improving the defence force, creating and securing better fuel reserves, and cultivating Australia’s longstanding relationship with the United States.

For example, Anderson correctly stated, “We must be realistic and understand that without a strong US alliance, Australia, with its great wealth, finds itself very vulnerable in an increasingly predatory international order in which raw power is increasingly becoming the measure of right.”

Holding fast, Anderson shared some of his April assertions with the Melbourne Catholic Lawyers Association (MCLA) on 8 September.

Melbourne Catholic said his speech was wide-ranging and included references to Os Guinness, Arnold Toynbee and Thomas Sowell.

The report also stated Anderson encouraged Australia’s young and old to work together.

MC reported the former Nationals leader as saying that Australia is a “good country that has lost its way,” at least in part, because the decline of faith had left people less able to acknowledge their limitations, seek forgiveness or draw on a moral framework.

Anderson said, “We are, in the end, spiritual beings. We have souls that need to be given meaning and purpose and direction.”

Speaking on the importance of Christian community to national security, identity and social cohesion, Anderson noted that churches had traditionally confronted people with the need for confession: the recognition that “we haven’t got it all right,” whereas modern culture increasingly encouraged people to see themselves as the final authority over their own lives.

He also reportedly told the MCLA that societal division and decline happened “on our watch” and “it happened because we’ve hollowed out our own culture.”

text:
I think the difficulty with discussions like this is that the answers are rarely simple enough to fit into a few paragraphs. 
Even a reasonably concise explanation of libertarianism requires a chapter in a book because there is a spectrum of libertarian thought and practice.
There are classical liberals, minarchists, anarcho-capitalists, constitutional libertarians, free-market liberals and more pragmatic libertarians who concentrate on reducing the size and reach of the state while recognising that some government functions remain necessary.
My own libertarianism is firmly in the latter camp.
It is not an argument for anarchy or “no government”. It is an argument for smaller government, greater individual freedom, personal responsibility and voluntary cooperation wherever possible.
That distinction matters enormously.
Argentina under Javier Milei provides a fascinating real-world example. 
As I argued in my recent Substack, Milei inherited an economy that had been distorted by decades of intervention, excessive government spending, monetary instability and regulation. His response has necessarily been transformative rather than marginal. The results so far are remarkable: Argentina has restored fiscal surpluses, achieved substantial disinflation, returned to economic growth and seen poverty fall dramatically from the extraordinary levels reached during the preceding crisis. The IMF now describes the economy as having regained stability and notes the return of growth, consecutive primary surpluses and improving investment conditions. International Monetary Fund

But Argentina is not Australia.

That is an important distinction in applying libertarian principles.
Australia does not need an Argentine-style economic rupture. We have a functioning constitutional democracy, established institutions, functioning markets, a substantial private sector and a civil society that already provides an enormous amount of social support.
My view is therefore that Australia is better suited to a marginal but persistent reduction in the size and reach of government.
Cut regulation.
Remove unnecessary programs.
Reduce taxation.
Return responsibilities to individuals, families and communities.
Expand competition.
Allow private enterprise and civil society to do more.
Then do it again.
And again.
Until government is doing the things only government really needs to do.

This is where I think the Australian experience is often misunderstood by socialists. Libertarianism does not mean abandoning people who need help.

Human beings have been caring for the disadvantaged for thousands of years — through families, churches, charities, community organisations, mutual societies and voluntary associations — long before the modern welfare state existed.

Socialists do not have a monopoly on compassion.

Nor should government have a monopoly on providing human services.

Look at health. Almost 46% of Australians now have private hospital cover, creating a substantial second pillar alongside the public system. 

Look at education. In 2025, more than 1.5 million Australian students were enrolled in non-government schools, and independent-school enrolments have grown substantially faster than government-school enrolments over recent years. 

Look at aged care. Australia has more than 3,100 providers, with private and not-for-profit organisations providing the overwhelming majority of services rather than government directly operating them. 

These aren't examples of a society abandoning people. They are examples of pluralism, competition, choice, charity and civil society operating alongside government.

And that is the important lesson.

Private health insurance creates an alternative source of funding and choice. Private and Catholic schools create alternatives that compete for families and students. Private and charitable aged-care providers offer different models, choices and forms of care.
Competition doesn't have to destroy the public system. It can force the public system to perform better.

That is a profoundly libertarian insight.

We don't need to believe that every government service must immediately disappear. We should ask a more useful question:
Why does government need to have a monopoly?

The same principle applies to taxation.
I believe the present level of taxation in Australia has crossed the line into something that can legitimately be described as theft from the fruits of people's labour. But that does not mean my argument is “no tax”.

Civil society needs some government. Government needs resources to perform its legitimate functions.
The libertarian argument is about limits.
How much can legitimately be taken?
For what purposes?
Who decides?
And how much freedom are we prepared to surrender in exchange?
That is very different from saying that government should disappear.
And this, ultimately, is why I find libertarianism so attractive.
It starts with the individual.
It trusts individuals to make decisions about their own lives. It trusts families to care for each other. It trusts communities to solve problems. It trusts entrepreneurs to discover opportunities. It trusts competition to reveal better ways of doing things.
And where government genuinely is required, it should be limited, accountable and proportionate.

So I don't see libertarianism as a utopian instruction to abolish the state.

I see it as a direction of travel:
less coercion, less central planning, less bureaucracy, less taxation and less government — and more freedom, responsibility, choice, enterprise, family and civil society.

Argentina demonstrates what can happen when a country makes a dramatic correction after decades of collectivist economic policy. Australia has the opportunity to make the same philosophical correction without requiring the same economic trauma.

That, to me, is the practical Australian form of libertarianism:
not no government — but government that knows its limits.
not abandonment — but freedom for society to care.
not anarchy — but liberty under law.
not revolution for its own sake — but a persistent return of power from the state to the individual.

The ultimate objective isn't to create a smaller state for the sake of having a smaller state. It is to create a larger space in which free people can live, create, care, prosper and determine their own futures.

The federal government's pursuit of a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is a digital shackles project, threatening your financial freedom and privacy. Resist this digital tyranny.

Executive Order 14178, 'Strengthening American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology,' issued January 23, 2025, states: 'Except to the extent required by law, agencies are hereby prohibited from undertaking any action to establish, issue, or promote CBDCs within the jurisdiction of the United States or abroad.' This temporary guardrail is insufficient.

The same order further declares: 'Except to the extent required by law, any ongoing plans or initiatives at any agency related to the creation of a CBDC within the jurisdiction of the United States shall be immediately terminated, and no further actions may be taken to develop or implement such plans or initiatives.' This executive action offers a momentary reprieve, but not a permanent barrier.

H.R. 1919, the 'Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act,' passed the House on July 17, 2025. This bill would prohibit a Federal Reserve bank from 'offering products or services directly to an individual,' or 'maintaining an account on behalf of an individual,' or issuing a CBDC. It is a necessary legislative step, but remains stalled.

Our Founders understood true money. Article I, Section 10, Clause 1 of the Constitution states: 'No State shall… make any Thing but gold and silver Coin a Tender in Payment of Debts.' While applying to states, it reveals a clear intent for tangible, decentralized currency beyond federal digital manipulation.

The Fourth Amendment guarantees: 'The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated.' A CBDC, tracking every transaction, would utterly demolish this fundamental security against government intrusion, creating an omnipresent financial surveillance state.

To preserve liberty, Congress must enact H.R. 1919 or S. 1124 into permanent law, prohibiting any federal CBDC. We must sunset all executive branch initiatives that even explore this path, and return monetary policy to sound, constitutional principles of limited government, protecting individual financial sovereignty.

Should the federal government persist in pursuing a CBDC, states must exercise their sovereign authority to refuse cooperation and nullify any federal mandate for such a system within their borders. Will you stand for financial freedom or accept digital servitude? #ReclaimSovereignty #FoundersVoice

The Real Constraint on the CPU Renaissance Isn't Demand. It's Supply.

Citi raised its 2030 CPU TAM estimate from $29 billion to $300 billion, a 60% CAGR, and lifted AMD's target price from $575 to $800. The demand-side logic holds: agentic AI runs continuously rather than idling between chat prompts, and the CPU-to-GPU ratio is shifting from 1:4–1:8 toward 1:1–1:2. We discussed Muse's architectural pull on CPU in our previous analysis of the agentic AI CPU bottleneck. This note focuses on a dimension that has not been fully examined: the supply-side constraints that determine how fast that TAM can actually be delivered, and how they change AMD's benefit path.

Citi's $300 billion is an upper-bound demand estimate, not a supply-side delivery path. Three constraints set the pace: leading-edge process capacity, ABF substrates, and DRAM supply. Demand growth is certain. Revenue recognition is slower than the demand curve.

Demand-side logic is validated and not repeated here

The mechanism by which agentic AI pulls CPU demand was detailed in our prior work: Muse's one-VM-per-user architecture assigns each user an independent virtual machine, CPU demand runs 4–8x GPU demand, Arm estimates CPU cores per GW rise from 30 million to 120 million, and TrendForce data show CPU can account for up to 90.6% of end-to-end latency in agent workflows. We do not repeat those figures.

One detail in Citi's framework deserves more attention: CPU consumption in agentic AI is not linear. Muse showed service degradation below one million DAU; a 120-subagent stress test created only 33. Altimeter estimates that in a scenario with 25 million active VMs, Meta may need 12.5 million physical CPU cores, not the 200 million vCPUs implied by nominal allocation (per Altimeter). The gap between nominal and actual resource consumption means unit CPU demand has large optimization headroom.

Supply constraint one: leading-edge process capacity

AMD EPYC Turin uses TSMC N3 and N4. TSMC's N3 capacity is booked through 2027 by Nvidia GPUs, Apple silicon, and Qualcomm mobile chips (per supply chain sources). CPU demand growth competes with GPU demand growth for the same process pool.

This is not a problem capital can solve quickly. N3 capacity expansion is limited by EUV tool delivery, cleanroom construction, and yield ramp. Nvidia's Rubin platform, AMD's MI400 series, and Apple's M5 series all compete for the same capacity. CPUs sit behind GPUs in TSMC's customer priority.

Supply constraint two: ABF substrates

Server CPUs use ABF substrates, sharing the same supply chain as AI GPU advanced packaging. ABF substrate lead times have reached 12–14 months, and the six major suppliers are sold out for 2026, with secondary suppliers auctioning capacity (per SemiAnalysis). CPU shipment growth is directly capped by substrate supply.

Ibiden raised its FY2026 capex to ¥210 billion and warned that ABF area needed by 2028 will be 10.7x 2024 levels (per Ibiden). New lines take 18–24 months to come online. Even if AMD secures wafer capacity from TSMC, without substrates, chips cannot be packaged and shipped.

Supply constraint three: DRAM supply

Each Muse user gets 8 GB of memory; 100 million users imply 800 PB of nominal demand. Even after adjusting for oversubscription and actual utilization, the structural increment to DRAM demand is significant. DRAM is already in structural shortage, with HBM taking priority on wafer capacity. Micron has said CPUs are becoming a constraint on DRAM (per Micron public statements). CPU shipment growth is therefore capped not only by its own capacity but by DRAM supply. CPU's high memory attach rate makes it an additional driver of DRAM demand. Rising DRAM prices feed into total CPU platform cost and influence cloud procurement decisions.

Competitive landscape: AMD's benefit path needs unbundling

Citi lists AMD as top pick, Intel as secondary beneficiary, and maintains Buy on Nvidia. The ranking logic is that core count has become the first variable in CPU selection, and AMD EPYC leads on core density. But the ranking overlooks an unfolding architectural split.

Arm entered with its first self-designed AGI CPU, 136 cores, TSMC 3nm, with Meta as first customer and co-development partner; ByteDance and Oracle have joined the customer list (per Arm). Meta is deploying Arm AGI CPU, Nvidia Grace, and AMD EPYC simultaneously — it has not locked CPU supply to a single architecture. Arm claims AGI CPU performance up to 2x x86.

Nvidia sells Vera CPU as a standalone product, 88 custom Olympus cores, 1.2 TB/s memory bandwidth, 50% single-core performance improvement (per Nvidia). Oracle Cloud Infrastructure plans to deploy hundreds of thousands of Vera CPUs from 2026. Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro will offer Vera standalone CPU server configurations.

CSP self-design is also advancing. AWS Graviton, Google Axion, and Microsoft Cobalt are already deployed. Meta added tens of millions of AWS Graviton cores to its compute portfolio in April 2026. The combined effect: AMD's x86 server CPU share gains are capped by Arm and CSP self-design diversion. AMD's net benefit equals "x86 share gain" minus "x86 overall share erosion to Arm." UBS data show AMD's server CPU unit share at about 33.2% in Q1 2026 (per UBS), while Arm's share rises in parallel.

Beneficiary re-rating

AMD's benefit is real, but the path is more complex than Citi's framework implies. AMD gains from EPYC demand and Intel share loss, but Arm AGI CPU and CSP self-design erode x86's overall share. AMD's benefit certainty must be unbundled into "architecture choice gain" and "supply bottleneck risk."

Memory makers may have higher benefit certainty than CPU makers. Agentic AI's pull on DRAM is architectural, while CPU demand can be partially offset by efficiency optimization and architecture migration. Mizuho has raised targets on Dell, SanDisk, and Super Micro on "strong agentic AI server and memory demand" (per Mizuho).

Intel's "secondary beneficiary" label may understate its rebound potential. Intel Xeon 6 lead times run up to six months (per supply chain sources), indicating strong demand. Intel is shifting some Core capacity to Xeon, improving supply. If Intel makes progress on 18A, Xeon 7 competitiveness could exceed expectations.

Three variables to verify

First, AMD EPYC actual shipments, not lead times. Lead times above 30 weeks mean demand exceeds supply, but revenue recognition depends on actual shipments. Track AMD data center CPU revenue quarter-over-quarter and management guidance on 2027 supply additions.

Second, Arm AGI CPU and Nvidia Vera customer adoption speed. If Meta migrates a meaningful share of agentic workloads to Arm or Vera in 2027, AMD's x86 share gain is compressed. Track Arm AGI CPU deployment scale and CSP allocation between x86 and Arm.

Third, CPU efficiency optimization in agentic AI. Muse's current one-VM-per-user architecture is resource-intensive. If Meta cuts per-user CPU demand by 50% through VM sharing, dynamic scheduling, and model caching, the CPU TAM growth curve shifts right. Track the ratio of Muse DAU growth to resource consumption.

Citi's $300 billion TAM is an upper-bound demand estimate, not a supply-side delivery path. AMD($AMD )'s benefit certainty must be unbundled into "architecture choice gain" and "supply bottleneck risk." Memory makers may have higher benefit certainty than CPU makers because agentic AI's pull on DRAM is architectural, while CPU demand can be partially offset by efficiency optimization and architecture migration.

text:
Yet, because India was the "Golden Bird"—immensely rich, peaceful, and content—it attracted every passing predator. For three thousand years, it was invaded by almost everyone who had a sword and the willingness to fight: the Mughals, the Greeks, the Turks, the Portuguese, the French, and the British. Anyone who was capable of fighting made their way here, because India offered almost no resistance.

Why was there no resistance?
Politicians will tell you it was weakness. I tell you, it was a completely different dimension of logic. The people of India were simply not interested in fighting. Their logic was clear: in a fight, you are going to lose your peace. And the people coming to invade had nothing to lose. When a man with everything fights a man with nothing, the rich man is always afraid. So, rather than destroying their inner peace in warfare, the people of India simply let the invaders control the outer boundaries of the country.

But we must look deeper. The true reason India remained enslaved for nearly a thousand years was not the strength of the external invaders. The British were a tiny island nation—the size of a single Indian district—yet they managed the greatest empire the world had ever seen. How? Because the Indian mind had been conditioned into a state of deep psychological dependency.

For centuries, false gurus and rigid traditions taught the people to look outward for authority, to rely on destiny, and to remain passive. When you are spiritually dependent on a guru or a dogma, you easily become politically dependent on a king or a foreign ruler. This inner slavery of the mind always precedes the outer slavery of the body.

The invaders, from the Mughals to the British, tried desperately to destroy the very spirit of this land. They wanted to turn this vast, colorful continent into a uniform, boring machine. They gave it names from the outside—like "Hindu" or "India"—derived simply from the mispronunciation of the Sindhu River. They tried to impose their languages, their manners, and their political structures.

And yet, look at the miracle. The empires have vanished. The British left, the Mughals crumbled into the pages of history textbooks, but the spiritual current of India flows on. They could conquer the land, they could tax the people, but they could never conquer the inner consciousness of this country.

True freedom—Purna Swaraj—does not mean just changing the color of the politicians sitting in the capital. True freedom means dropping the dependency of the mind. India will only regain its lost glory when it realizes that its strength does not lie in copying the violent, political ambitions of the West, but in reclaiming its unique identity: a land of meditation, a land of freedom, and a beautiful garden of individual consciousness.

"Osho"

text:
🇺🇸🇨🇦 David Eby’s post treats U.S. tariffs and this year’s wildfires as the reason small businesses in British Columbia are in trouble. Those shocks are real. Softwood still faces stacked U.S. duties, and fire losses are not imaginary. They are not the binding constraint either. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has been clear that the hurdles operators name first are tax and regulatory costs, wage costs, and fuel costs — the cost structure built under the government he leads, not a gap in Ottawa’s tariff programs. Federal liquidity support already exists, including PacifiCan’s Regional Tariff Response Initiative, with non-repayable help up to $3 million for eligible firms. Blaming Washington for a provincial cost problem is campaign framing, not a diagnosis.

The remedy on offer is not relief. It is a $500 million Small Business Tariff and Wildfire Relief Fund of interest-free loans of up to $1 million, repayable over as long as 72 months. A firm with tight margins does not get stronger by taking on more principal it still has to repay. “Interest-free” only means the borrower does not pay the interest. Taxpayers do, on top of a fiscal position that has already collapsed. British Columbia posted a multi-billion-dollar surplus in 2022–23, the year Eby became premier. The September 2026 update projects a $13.8 billion deficit this year, then $12.7 billion and $12.0 billion. Taxpayer-supported debt has roughly doubled on his watch, credit ratings have been cut repeatedly, and debt service is now one of the largest lines in the budget. A loan fund financed by a government that cannot balance its own books is a transfer of risk, not a rescue.

The $5,000 refundable credit for hiring someone aged 18 to 30 into a first full-time, 12-month job does not change that arithmetic. Five thousand dollars does not offset the employer health tax, payroll load, permitting delays, or the fuel and input costs that decide whether a hire is affordable. The diversification add-on is thinner still: about $6 million a year in market-research grants and advice. Geography has not moved. Canadian softwood exports in the first half of 2026 still went about 89 percent to the United States, and new overseas volumes covered only a sliver of the American shortfall. Forest products remain one of British Columbia’s largest goods exports, and most of that wood still goes south. A grant to “look for customers elsewhere” does not replace the customer that actually buys the product.

This is a snap-election promise, called with an October 24 vote already set, from a premier who turned a surplus into a structural deficit before the latest tariff round. Interest-free debt and a token hiring credit leave the constraints that were already driving closures in place: regulation, tax, energy and project delays, and a public balance sheet that now competes with business for capital. The useful test is simple. If the plan worked, firms would need less government paper, not more of it.

text:
Aloka is an Indian Pariah stray dog who became a global symbol of peace and loyalty after walking thousands of miles alongside Buddhist monks across India and the United States. The monks named him Aloka, which means "light" or "enlightenment" in Sanskrit. Aloka became a viral internet sensation, though he briefly needed veterinary care for an upset stomach after receiving too many treats from loving crowds along the American roads... 

A group of Buddhist monks completed a historic nearly 2,300-mile walk across the United States from Texas to Washington, D.C., ending in July 2022. They walked barefoot on hot pavement, through cold winds, and across long stretches of open highway. Their mission is simple and quiet. They hope to spread compassion, mindfulness, and non-violence to everyone they meet along the way.

In a world full of noise, arguments, and quick tempers, these men are choosing to move slowly and peacefully, one single step at a time.

Walking thousands of miles on foot is difficult for anyone, but the monks are not doing this alone.

Walking right beside them is a small rescue dog named Aloka.

Aloka was originally a stray dog living on the streets of India before she was rescued and brought into a safer environment. During an earlier peace walk organized by the monks, the tiny dog began following the group. She did not have a leash around her neck, nor did she have any formal training.

Nobody forced her to follow, and nobody gave her an official job to do. Yet day after day, Aloka kept moving forward alongside the monks.

For more than 100 days during that first long journey, Aloka walked mile after mile through intense heat, freezing temperatures, and total exhaustion. She never complained, and she never turned back. She did not know where they were going, and she did not know if there would be warm shelter or a guaranteed bowl of food waiting at the end of the day.

Despite all the uncertainty, she stayed close to the brown robes of the monks. Throughout that cross-country Walk for Peace, Aloka was right there, walking step by step with her chosen family.

The monks walk to remind humanity about the power of kindness and inner peace, but Aloka’s presence delivers a message that touches people just as deeply. Her journey has become a living symbol of devotion, loyalty, and strength. She is a tiny creature who had every reason to sit down, give up, or wander away, but she chooses to keep moving forward every morning.

People along the highway often pulled their cars over to watch the peaceful procession pass by.

Drivers rolled down their windows, and local residents stepped out onto their front porches to offer water, fruit, or quiet words of gratitude.

One local resident who stopped along the road to watch the group pass by looked at the small dog with tears in her eyes.

"Seeing this tiny dog walk so many miles without complaining changed how I look at my own life," she said softly.

"If she can carry on with so much love and no fear, maybe all of us can learn to be a little kinder to each other too."

When the sun began to set each evening, the group finally stopped to rest their tired feet. The monks settled down on the ground, and Aloka curled up quietly right at their feet, resting her dusty head on her paws.

In a world full of loud speeches and endless debates, true peace does not always need words to be understood.

Sometimes the deepest spiritual lesson comes without any noise at all, carried quietly across the earth on four tired paws that simply refuse to stop loving.

text:
IRAN WAR DAY 223 UTC

SITREP WATCH — U.S. moves toward strike-ready posture as tanker attack widens Gulf risk

Verdict: Reported completion of CENTCOM preparations moves Washington closer to decision-ready major combat operations, while a casualty-producing tanker attack north of Qatar shows that commercial-shipping exposure now extends well beyond the Hormuz transit corridor.

1. CENTCOM reportedly ordered to complete preparations for renewed major operations

* What changed: Axios reports that the Pentagon instructed CENTCOM “several days ago” to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations against Iran. The directive reportedly contained no strike date, and President Trump has made no final decision. The exact directive date and time were not disclosed. 
* Evidence status: REPORTED / NOT OFFICIALLY CONFIRMED. The Atlantic independently reports that the White House requested pre-midterm strike options. Pentagon and White House officials publicly offered only standard formulations: the department develops options, and the president retains all options. 
* Why it is material: This is more than routine contingency discussion if the reported instruction was to complete preparations. It indicates an effort to make a large strike package executable on presidential direction, reportedly including Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets.
* Operational clock changed: The U.S. decision clock advances from options development toward decision-ready force planning. It does not establish an execution order, a selected date or an imminent strike.
* Assessment: A renewed campaign would test whether episodic U.S. pressure can prevent Iran from regenerating between strike periods. Iran has used the extended conflict as a classroom for dispersal, adaptation and identifying weaknesses in U.S. and allied defenses; returning briefly to high-intensity strikes without sustained suppression would repeat that underlying strategic problem.
* Watch next: Bomber and tanker generation, carrier-position changes, regional air-defense dispersal, airspace restrictions, unusual strategic-airlift activity and evacuation or force-protection measures would provide stronger evidence that planning has crossed into execution.

2. Tanker struck deep inside the western Arabian Gulf

* Commercial-risk status — SITREP ASSESSMENT: Western Arabian Gulf risk worsened. No new publicly available independent underwriter or JMIC regional rating was located by the cutoff, but the physical attack materially expands the demonstrated danger beyond the Strait of Hormuz itself.
* What changed: At approximately October 7, 2026, 19:00 UTC / October 7, 2026, 2:00 p.m. CDT, a tanker reported being struck by multiple projectiles roughly 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar. UKMTO reported casualties; the vessel, casualty total, weapon and attacker remained unidentified at the cutoff. 
* Evidence status: CONFIRMED incident; UNVERIFIED attribution and casualty details. UKMTO is the originating authority. There is presently no basis to attribute the attack to Iran, the Houthis or another actor.
* Why it is material: The attack occurred hundreds of miles west of Hormuz, along approaches serving Qatari, Saudi, Bahraini, Kuwaiti and Iraqi energy traffic. Clearing the chokepoint therefore no longer ends a vessel’s kinetic-risk exposure. Specialist maritime reporting describes it as the first reported tanker attack in the western Gulf in weeks. 
* Standing judgment changed: The shipping-risk ledger expands from hazardous chokepoint transit to regional post-transit exposure. Escorting or monitoring a narrow Hormuz corridor cannot by itself establish commercial control over the wider Gulf.

text:
🇮🇷|The Iranian military recently released a pilot recruitment video requiring applicants to specify their Russian language proficiency and any prior training on Sukhoi fighter jets. This detail quickly drew significant attention, as it is viewed as a clear signal that Iran is preparing for the large-scale induction of Russian-made Sukhoi fighter aircraft.

📋 Recruitment Details: Russian Language Skills and Sukhoi Experience as Mandatory Requirements

According to recruitment forms disclosed by various media outlets, applicants must explicitly state their level of Russian proficiency and indicate whether they have previously undergone training on Russian-made Sukhoi fighter jets. This requirement is no coincidence; it points directly to the Iranian Air Force's ongoing, large-scale modernization drive centered on Russian-made combat aircraft.

Brigadier General Ali Shadmani, Deputy Coordinator of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters of the Iranian Armed Forces, had previously publicly confirmed the Su-35 procurement agreement, although Iranian officials subsequently attempted to downplay the statement.

✈️ Su-35 Procurement: An Order for 48 Aircraft with the First Batch of 20 Completed

Iran has ordered 48 Su-35 fighter jets, a figure revealed in Russian government documents. The Russian aviation plant in Komsomolsk-on-Amur has completed production of the first batch of 20 Su-35s; the Iranian Ministry of Defense is currently covering maintenance costs within Russia, and the aircraft are ready for handover once infrastructure upgrades at Hamadan Air Base are finalized.

Damage to infrastructure at Hamadan Air Base has been identified as the primary cause of the delivery delay, and engineering teams are currently carrying out reconstruction work.

🎓 Pilot Training: Yak-130s Serve as a Bridge; Training in Russia Has Already Begun

In preparation for the arrival of the Su-35s, Iran began receiving Yak-130 advanced jet trainers as early as September 2023. These aircraft used by the Russian Air Force to train pilots for the Sukhoi fighter series serve as a crucial platform for Iranian pilots to transition to the Su-35.

Iranian pilots and technicians have already completed the initial phases of flight and maintenance training in Russia. Reports indicate that approximately 30 Iranian pilots were sent to Russia last year to begin their training.  

📅 Delivery Schedule: Starting in 2026, with subsequent models to follow

Deliveries of the Su-35 to Iran are expected to begin in 2026. Additionally, Russian sources have confirmed that the Iranian Ministry of Defense has ordered 12 Su-30SM2 fighter jets; these are slated for delivery starting in mid-2027, sourced from the inventory of Russian frontline units. The Su-30SM2 shares the same engines and advanced avionics as the Su-35 but offers lower costs and easier maintenance; it is better suited for ground-attack missions and can serve as a training platform for Su-35 aircrews.

🌍 Strategic Significance: A Historic Upgrade for the Iranian Air Force

This marks Iran's first large-scale procurement of fighter jets since the 1990s, signaling a fundamental shift for its air force from reliance on aging Cold War-era models (such as the F-14, F-5, and F-4) toward a modernized force. The Su-35’s combat radius of nearly 2,000 kilometers and its ability to operate from short runways or improvised airfields will give Iran the potential to launch deep-penetration strikes across the Middle East, while simultaneously reducing its reliance on fixed airbases.

Recruitment requirements regarding Russian language proficiency alongside inquiries into prior Sukhoi training experience further confirm that Iran is systematically and extensively preparing pilots for this new fleet, rather than merely conducting a limited-scale trial.

text:
In an opinion piece published in the Times of Israel titled "Why Somaliland Should Be on the Global Investment Map," foreign policy specialist Mohamed Abdi asserts that a quiet economic transformation is unfolding across the Horn of Africa, positioning #Somaliland as an emerging destination for foreign direct investment, trade, and regional infrastructure development.

According to Mohamed, while international discourse surrounding Somaliland has long focused on political status and regional security, global investors are increasingly drawn to its strategic geography along the Gulf of Aden, proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and expanding maritime logistics capacity anchored by the modernized Port of Berbera and the Berbera Economic Zone.

The analyst highlights that the modernization of Berbera Port is evolving beyond a transit point into a broader economic ecosystem. Connected by logistics corridors to landlocked regional markets, the port and its surrounding economic zone offer commercial opportunities in warehousing, light manufacturing, food processing, packaging, and regional distribution.

Beyond logistics, Mohamed outlines untapped potential across traditional and emerging sectors, including value-added livestock processing, sustainable fisheries along its Red Sea coastline, solar and wind energy generation, and an expanding digital economy driven by mobile finance, e-commerce, and technology ventures.

Addressing commercial risks, the author notes that sustainable growth will depend on strengthening institutional frameworks, ensuring regulatory predictability, and enforcing transparent legal standards to build investor confidence. He emphasizes that capital investment must align with local capacity building, technical training, and supply chain integration.

The analysis specifically points to potential synergies with nations possessing advanced technological capabilities, such as Israel, in sectors like desert agriculture, water management, renewable energy, cybersecurity, and tech entrepreneurship. 

The author concludes that as global supply chains seek resilient new maritime corridors, Somaliland's combination of infrastructure, location, and private-sector dynamism warrants serious consideration on the international investment map.

text:
King Faisal Hospital Rwanda has completed 14 life-saving pediatric cardiac catheterization procedures for children with congenital heart disease, including babies as young as two days old.

The procedures were carried out last week under the leadership of Dr. Gerard Misago, who recently returned to Rwanda after completing his fellowship in Israel.

Dr. Misago led a multidisciplinary team supported by Dr. Abdul Jabbar, a senior Interventional Pediatric Cardiologist from Dhaka Shishu (Children’s) Hospital in Bangladesh, and Dr. Richard Hubbard of the University of Maryland and the Children’s Cardiac Care Foundation.

The procedures are part of efforts to strengthen Rwanda’s capacity to diagnose and treat complex congenital heart conditions locally, reducing the need for children to seek specialised cardiac care abroad.

For some of the youngest patients, including newborns only two days old, the intervention offered what the hospital describes as a new lease on life.

King Faisal Hospital Rwanda has expressed appreciation to the Children’s Cardiac Care Foundation, Dr. Richard Hubbard, Dr. Abdul Jabbar and programme coordinator Shamimur for supporting the team.

The milestone also highlights the growing importance of specialist training, international medical collaboration and local capacity-building in expanding access to advanced paediatric cardiac care in Rwanda.

text:
I went to a friend’s birthday dinner and only found out when the bill arrived that I was expected to pay for strangers’ drinks.

A few days earlier, he’d messaged our group chat:

“Birthday dinner on Saturday. Come along—we haven’t caught up in ages.”

There were six of us in the group, all old friends. I said yes and asked if he wanted anything.

“Don’t worry about a gift. Just come.”

I bought him one anyway.

When I arrived at the restaurant, there were already ten seats at the table. His girlfriend had brought a few friends I’d never met.

Fine by me. I said hello and sat down.

I’d been having stomach problems, so I mentioned straight away:

“I’m eating light tonight, and I can’t drink. I’m on medication.”

He nodded.

“Of course. No worries.”

I had some rice, a few pieces of meat, and water. Meanwhile, the other end of the table ordered seafood and two bottles of liquor.

Someone offered me a glass. I politely declined and reminded them about the medication.

Around nine, I said I needed to leave because I had an early start the next morning. I handed my friend his gift.

“Happy birthday, mate. Send me what I owe for dinner and I’ll transfer it.”

“Hang on. We’re getting the bill now.”

One of his girlfriend’s friends picked up the bill, tapped a few numbers into his phone, and announced:

“Ten people. That’s 1.2 million dong each.”

I asked:

“Does that include the alcohol? I didn’t have any.”

He shrugged.

“We’re splitting everything equally. We can’t count every bite everyone took.”

“I’m happy to split the food. But could the people who drank split the bottles?”

The table went quiet.

My friend had been sitting opposite me without saying anything. I looked over, expecting him to explain that I hadn’t been drinking.

Instead, he put his glass down.

“You’re really going to ruin my birthday over 1.2 million?”

Before I could answer, he added something that made me reach across the table and take my gift back

text:
Per @grok 

All 50 states and the District of Columbia allow people without a traditional street address to register to vote by describing a non-fixed location they consider their residence, such as a shelter, park, street corner, or the place they sleep or spend most of their time. A separate mailing address (shelter, general delivery, friend’s home, or P.O. box) is typically required so election mail can be delivered.
Several states use methods similar to Pennsylvania’s map:
•  Massachusetts instructs voters without a traditional address to draw the location of their primary residence on a map printed on the registration form; the local election office then assigns a precinct.
•  Georgia permits a map or diagram of the residence, or the address of the place the person usually stays.
•  Alabama accepts an address or a map/diagram of the place of residence.
•  Minnesota allows a written description of an outdoor sleeping location (for example, a park corner near named streets); such registrations may be marked “challenged” and require an oath at the polls.
•  Texas requires a concise description of the residence location when there is no street address, along with a mailing address.
•  New Jersey accepts a “contact point” or the location where the person spends most of their time.
•  Colorado allows the address of a location the person “regularly return[s] to.”
The National Conference of State Legislatures notes that identifying a sleeping location on a map is a recognized method used by multiple states to assign the correct precinct and ballot. The ability to request a mail or absentee ballot sent to an address other than the registration residence also exists in states that offer no-excuse or excuse-based mail voting, though the exact rules and verification steps vary. List-maintenance processes that rely on postal change-of-address data face the same limitation in other states for registrants who never had a conventional address.

text:
Εδώ η ιστορική πλήρης ομιλία του κ. Μarco Rubio σε κείμενο. Για όσους τους αρέσει να διαβάζουν.

Προσωπικά ένα μεγάλο Ευχαριστώ ! @SecRubio 

Secretary Rubio: There are great ruins all across the world. In many cases, they are places where history seems to have exhausted itself: remnants of distant cultures that have long passed beyond living memory.
But the Acropolis is different.

For thousands of years, the civilization that built what stands behind me has captivated the imagination of the Western world. Generations of our statesmen, artists, and philosophers have looked to it — they’ve looked to it with wonder and they’ve looked to it with awe.

Now time has a tendency to dull the senses: great victories and catastrophic defeats, they seem to shrink to becoming like a footnote in a textbook, another fact for our schoolchildren to memorize and forget. But the Greeks of antiquity, they seem to have an almost mystical hold on our memory. They call us back to them, again and again.

480 years before Christ, the armies of Xerxes arrived in this city and they put its sanctuaries to the torch. Most Athenians had by then evacuated by ship to a nearby island. But there was a handful of them that refused to leave their home. So instead, they barricaded themselves in the rocky fortress of the Acropolis to fight an extraordinary last stand, heaving massive stones down the cliffs onto the Persian invaders and holding the greatest empire of the age at bay for days. They were eventually overwhelmed. The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon.

For 25 centuries since, the Parthenon has stood. Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow. And the progeny of the men who built it — the sons of Athens and Rome — have carried their civilization with them to the ends of the Earth.

Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now — I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain — I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish.The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity. 

Greece is literally carved into the architecture of our government: in the towering columns, in the domes and the monuments across our capital city. The city where our Constitution was born — Philadelphia — is itself a Greek name.

The men who founded my country were fascinated by the heritage we inherited from yours. They were exceptionally well-read in history — they were vividly aware of their unique place in it — but no other age of the past held their attention or their imagination quite like that of antiquity. Many, many people are surprised to learn that the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was not an Enlightenment philosopher or political theorist. 

No, the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was Plutarch, the Greek biographer of Greece and Rome’s great men.

Now, much has been written and said about the influence of ancient Greece on the ideas of the American Founders — and, for that matter, on all of the Western philosophers and statesmen that preceded them. Most of us are familiar with the basic history. Athens gave us democracy. Plato and Aristotle gave us Western philosophy. Our ideas of law, of virtue, of citizenship, and republican government were shaped in the Greek city-states. Even much of our political vocabulary — words like democracy, tyranny, the word “politics” itself — found its origins here.

Now, all of that is true. But the things we owe to this place — as Americans, and as Westerners — are actually far far deeper. These institutions and ideas — these institutions and ideas were the outward expression of more fundamental qualities we see in the ancient Greeks — qualities that can’t be reduced to any particular political system or theory.

Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West: fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory. An insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates, a hunger to know the mysteries of nature and grasp the secrets of the cosmos. An impatience with the notion of impossibility, chafing at all boundaries and limits, straining to peer into the depths of the unknown.
These were not just the formulas or precepts of a particular school of philosophy. They were the characteristic of a people — expressed in their traditions, their stories, their imagination; in the qualities they demanded of their citizens; in the things they lived and fought and died for.

To know them is to know ourselves.

What blossomed here in this place was the Western desire to uncover all that ignorance, darkness, and distance had kept hidden from the mind of man. The Greeks did not just shape history; the Greeks gave us history itself. Much of what we know about many ancient civilizations comes almost entirely from the records of Greek explorers and historians, explorers and historians who didn’t just chronicle the histories of their own people, but ventured outwards to observe and record the sagas of foreign peoples and cultures all across the world.

Where others looked inward, the Greeks were the first to direct their focus outward, to chase the thrill and glory of seeing all that was strange and new. It was this trait — it was this trait that would push the West to create and build things that others could not, marking us out from so many other cultures and civilizations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life.

But it is not just the ambition to explore the unknown that we inherit from the Greeks; it is the conviction that the unknown can be known. The confidence that the world can be charted and measured and mapped and understood — and that there is a rational order to the cosmos, governed by certain fundamental laws, laws that men can observe and the mind can come to understand.

This was the foundation of the Western mind: our math, our science, our medicine. Our philosophy, ethics, and religion. It paved the way for the gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom. It was the foundation of the riches of Christian theology — of Augustine and Aquinas and the whole tradition of natural law.

It gave birth to a civilization marked not just by a common culture, it was marked by a common anthropology — a common view of man and his place in the universe. Its descendants would share not just the idea of a natural order, but a distinctive understanding of virtue; of destiny and fate; of truth, goodness, and beauty; of a code that dictates how men ought to live; of objective standards and ideals to strive towards.
For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence. They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft. The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle — to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.

Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel. The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat. Too often these days, we build downwards. We design our standards to ensure no one will lose; we preoccupy ourselves more with the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best. We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.

The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things. The ancient Greek city-states were filled. They were filled with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict. But from that constant struggle for distinction — from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.

The thumos, as the ancient Greeks called it — the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride — is the heart of great civilization. And without it? Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive.
Today, too much of the West has forgotten this quality. Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional. 

We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world. Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt. We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness.
The word “nationalism” became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments; we condemned our own history. And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit. In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay.

And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control.

But others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left — the vacuum left behind by our weakness. And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead.

And now, today, we find ourselves at a crossroads. Because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.
Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.

We choose to reach for new frontiers: in advanced manufacturing and super intelligence; in drones, weapons, and warfare; in chips, minerals, cyber, and every other domain of human possibility. To unleash our energy, to rebuild our factories, to return our astronauts to the moon and launch a new age of exploration in space.

Now for all their lofty ideals, the ancient Greeks were not naive. They understood that nations have interests. They understood that statecraft requires prudence and diplomacy, but they also understood that it requires the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail. They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.

This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim — reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization.
We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.

There are already signs.

Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift: skyrocketing defense spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programs, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defense commitments made last year in The Hague.

Greece has been at the center of this shift. The people of this nation have proved themselves once again to be an indispensable friend to Europe and to the United States alike, on everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally.
And it’s our sincerest hope that all of Europe will follow your example. Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them. Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age.

And we can. 

Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum. Quite the opposite: our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts. It is a vision we saw in action just last month, in an unprecedented new agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland — an agreement that will reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO. All three partners in that deal emerged victorious. All of Europe — and NATO and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.

We want to win together. We must win together.

Now it’s has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people. And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else.

They believed — fiercely — in the ideal of the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds. But they believed that glory and fame, those things were won through striving, sacrificing and achieving greatly for something larger than yourself. The recurring hero of the ancient Greek world was the man who was willing to pay any cost for a cause worthy of his loyalty.

We see this in Socrates, who refused to abandon the inquiry into truth even at the cost of his own life. We see it in the legendary stand of 300 Spartans — surrounded and hopelessly outnumbered by the vast armies of Persia — who refused the chance to save themselves, choosing to fight to the last man rather than abandon their post or abandon their duty. And we see it in the epic myth of Achilles, who is offered the choice to return home and live a long and peaceful life — but chooses instead to remain at Troy and perish in pursuit of eternal glory.

These — these are the qualities that would shape the Western moral imagination. From the Christian martyr who refused to betray his faith to the patriot who gave his life for his country; from Saint Thomas More to the Battle of the Alamo, running through the immortal closing words of the Declaration of Independence of the United States which says, “We mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty — an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country. Our heroes, the heroes of the West are those who choose to remain faithful to their duty precisely when it is most difficult and painful to do so: the man who is bound by his word, the soldier who will not abandon his post, the captain, the proverbial captain, who goes down with his ship.

This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.

Our heroes — our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but our heroes do not worship death. It is precisely because we value life that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles. Now, we take the West’s conception of these things — heroism, honor, duty — we take these things for granted. We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places. They are not. They are the product of a distinct character, a distinct character which arose here and shaped the whole story of the civilization that came after it. A civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.

The men who built the Parthenon were succeeded by the architects of European Christendom, who raised the cathedrals of Milan, Cologne, and Florence. The quest to perfect the human form that moved the ancient Greek sculptors found a new expression in Michelangelo. The Greek philosophers’ search for the structure of the universe was inherited by Copernicus, and then Galileo, then Kepler, and in Newton.

The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’ discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon. And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.
And in America, that same tradition rediscovered itself anew. An open and wild land became the site of a great revival of Western imagination and ambition. 

The Greek aspiration for new horizons became the American frontier spirit. The civilization of Athens and Rome transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire.

The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers — born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world.

Together, we must now rediscover that spirit. We are at an inflection point — an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization. The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity.

National interests did not vanish in the face of international institutions. War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace. Other states continued to arm, to seek influence, to compete for territory, and technology, and resources, and markets, and energy, and power.

And now, there is war again. There is new competition between great powers again. There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again.

And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together — understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them. And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.

We have built a model of that with our partners here in Greece. In our defense partnerships, in energy and technology, in our shared ambition to secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration. Our friendship dates back to the earliest years of my nation. 

When Greece rose in 1821 to recover its independence after centuries of Ottoman rule, Americans recognized something familiar in that struggle. Three years later, the great American statesman Daniel Webster, he delivered a famous address to Congress, helping bring the cause of the Greek Revolution before the representatives of the young American republic.

And he began by calling their attention to everything around them. This is what he said in his speech; he said: “This free form of government, this popular assembly… this practice of free debate, and public discussion, the contest of mind with mind… even the edifice in which we assemble, these proportioned columns, this ornamented architecture, all remind us that Greece has existed, and that we, like the rest of mankind, are greatly her debtors.”

Those words are as true today as they were when he said them. And all of us — not just Americans, but Europeans and our friends across the West — must relearn the lessons our forefathers took from this place and from its history.

The history of Greece — the history of Greece does not just offer us a glimpse — it does not offer a glimpse of our institutions in their earliest forms. The history of Greece shows us an image of ourselves.

It shows us that ours is the inheritance of great heroes, and that we should be proud — that we should be intensely proud — of where we come from. We should marvel at what our forefathers carved out of this countryside. The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man. And it began here, with the first men and women of the West. From them — from them — we can rediscover the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time.

Thank you.
