What makes us break other people's homes? Only demons can do it, isn't it? Then why are demons holding the power while we are so many in numbers?

🏚️ Rahim Nagar, Jammu: October 3, 2026

On Saturday, October 3, 2026, authorities in Jammu demolished nearly a dozen structures mostly huts occupied by Rohingya refugees on forest land in Rahim Nagar, within the Raika Forest on the outskirts of Jammu. This was the second major eviction drive targeting the community in Jammu within a month.

The anti-encroachment drive was carried out by the forest department in collaboration with the Forest Protection Force, revenue department, and police. Officials claimed the occupants had been warned twice within a fortnight before the demolition. They claimed residents were allowed to remove their belongings, and that women and children were moved outside with the assistance of women's police personnel.

But a native of Jammu named Stephen, whose structure was also demolished, alleged he was not served any prior notice. He said the demolition team arrived early in the morning and gave little time to remove belongings. He had been living there for 10-12 years, and after the demolition, he had nowhere to go with his children.

The Rohingya immigrants said they had been living in the area for nearly two decades after fleeing Myanmar. One man, Abdul Khaliq, said: "We escaped oppression in our country and took shelter here out of compulsion. We are not here to stay permanently. We hold identity cards issued by the United Nations." He added: "We have nowhere to go and are uncertain about the future of our children".

🪪 The UN Card That Means Nothing in India

This is the part that turns my stomach.

These people hold UNHCR identification cards. They are registered refugees. They fled genocide. They have papers.

But India does not recognize those papers.

India is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol. The Government of India has stated in the Supreme Court, in official advisories, in every forum that UNHCR cards offer no protection from detention. Rohingyas are treated as illegal migrants under the Foreigners Act and the new Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025.

The MHA issued an advisory in 2017 to states to identify and deport Rohingyas as illegal immigrants. Around 40,000 Rohingyas are living in India, with UNHCR registering about 22,500. Those cards help them access some basic services. They do not give legal right to stay.

So here is the reality: The international community gave these people a piece of paper that says "we see you, you are refugees." And the Indian government said, "We don't care. That paper means nothing here."

The UNHCR card is a promise. India treats it as trash.

Where do these people go? The UN gave them an ID and sent them to a country whose government is a puppet and now their homes are being dismantled. They don't go anywhere. They just stop existing in the official record. They become ghosts.

🏛️ What the Government Says

The official line is predictable. Forest officials said: "The action was not directed against any particular community or group, but was solely aimed at removing encroachment from forest land. The forest rules are the same for everyone. There is no question of targeting any particular group".

They suggested that those needing accommodation "should seek rented housing or acquire land through legal means".

Rented housing. With what money? With what documentation? With what legal standing in a country that has declared you illegal?

Acquire land through legal means. These are people who fled genocide. They have no land. They have no legal status. They have no rights. And now they are being told to buy property in a country that refuses to recognize their existence.

The eviction came after a High-Level Committee on Demographic Changes visited Jammu in August 2026. The committee was constituted on May 26 under Justice Prakash Prabhakar Navalkar (retired) to examine demographic changes and suggest administrative and legal measures. Government data presented to the committee showed 7,656 Rohingyas identified across Jammu and Kashmir 6,737 in the Jammu region alone.

This is not about forest land. This is about demographic engineering. This is about making a community disappear.

🧠 The Questions one must Ask

What makes us break other people's homes?

Power that has decided some people are not people.

As I stated in the beginning Only demons can do it, isn't it?

Yes. And the demon is not some supernatural entity. The demon is a system that has learned it can do anything to Kashmiris, to Muslims, to Rohingyas, to protesters in Delhi and nothing will happen. The demon is the confidence of impunity.

Then why are demons holding the power while we are so many in numbers?

Because numbers mean nothing without organization. Because we have been taught to see each other as separate. Because we have been trained to look away when it's someone else's home being bulldozed. Because the silence of the many is the permit of the few.

 If you remain silent watching atrocities with anyone, it will come to you.

I have shared this time and again, years after years. And it is coming, it is happening right in front of you

They started with Kashmir. You stayed silent. They moved to Delhi. You stayed silent. Now they are in Jammu, tearing down the homes of people who have already survived genocide.

The lesson is being written in real time. And we are still not reading it.

🕯️We must say clearly, without decoration:

This is not about forest land. This is about a state that has decided certain people do not deserve to exist in its sight.

This is not about law. This is about a legal system that has been weaponized to make refugees into criminals.

This is not about "encroachment." This is about the systematic dismantling of the most vulnerable people in the country, while the rest of us watch.

The Rohingya in Jammu have been there for nearly two decades. They fled genocide. They hold UN cards. They have nothing. And now they have even less.

Where will they go?

They will go nowhere. They will be pushed from one temporary shelter to another, from one eviction to the next, until they are gone from the official record. And then, when they are no longer visible, the state will say the problem has been solved.

The problem will not be solved. It will just be buried.

And one day, when the bulldozers come for your home, for my home, for the homes of everyone who stayed silent, we will remember that we had a chance to speak and we didn't.

We are speaking now. We must not stop.

🧵 Same register: methods and the religious variable, no accused.

**Part 1 — The fact**

For fifty years most rich countries went from having enough children to replace themselves to having far fewer. No single decree was required. A set of tools was enough: medical technique, legal change, the price of adult life, and a story that stopped treating a child as an obligation of continuity. Religion did not cause the fall by itself. It decided who slowed it and who went along with it.

Replacement needs about 2.1 children per woman. Italy is near 1.2. Spain, Germany and much of northern Europe sit between 1.2 and 1.6. South Korea fell below 1. China, after restricting the second child, fell below replacement and cannot climb back. The pattern is too wide for one law or one pill. It reads better as a toolbox used, with different force, in almost every country that urbanized.

**Part 2 — The technical tool**

The first tool was technical. The contraceptive pill, the IUD, the injectable, emergency contraception and legal abortion separated sex from birth. Before, avoiding a child required abstinence, withdrawal, or an unreliable method. After, the decision could be private and reversed late. No country that offered this at scale kept the fertility of 1960. The technique does not force anyone to use it. It makes use cheap.

**Part 3 — Law and school**

The second tool was legal and educational. Mass entry of women into university and paid work pushed the first birth later. Each year of study shortens the biological window. Divorce law, equal-pay rules and abortion law redefined marriage: it ceased to be the near-only frame of adult life and became one option among others. Where school presented career and autonomy as success, and a large family as a brake, the average number of children fell without a fine.

**Part 4 — Price**

The third tool was economic. Costly housing, unstable jobs, and a state that covers old age with taxes rather than with children change the family account. In a village a child is labor and insurance. In a city with a pension a child is a long cost and an uncertain benefit. Countries that tried to pay that cost with subsidies — birth grants, nurseries, leave — slowed the fall. They rarely reversed it. Money compensates. It does not manufacture the wish.

**Part 5 — Coercion, the limit case**

The fourth tool was coercive. From 1979 to 2015 China’s one-party state restricted the second child with fines, forced abortions and household registration. The public reason mixed scarcity and “population quality.” Some of the language came from the same 1970s international literature that spoke of stabilizing the global South through aid and contraception. The instrument was different: a state able to enter the house. So was the result. Fertility collapsed. When the same state later asked for more births, the population did not answer. A child can be forbidden. The desire to have one cannot be decreed
.

**Part 6 — Development policy**

In parallel, aid agencies and development ministries funded family planning for decades in Africa, Asia and Latin America. The public argument was maternal health and poverty reduction. Some European governments added, out loud, another: less migration pressure if the population at origin grows more slowly. Denmark said this without euphemism in 2016. It was not a back-room secret. It was development policy with a border calculation.

🇺🇸 General Dynamics Mission Systems partnered with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Aviation and Missile Center (AvMC) to complete a successful hypersonic flight demonstration of its GPS-denied, software-defined receiver, Multiple Orbit Navigation (MO-Nav). @GDMS @USArmy 

MO-Nav is a compact, single-board circuit card assembly capable of GPS-denied radio frequency navigation using multiple Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) signals of opportunity and commercially provided position, navigation and timing (PNT) signals.

The successful demonstration of MO-Nav on the reusable Talon-A hypersonic test aircraft, which can travel and maneuver at speeds of Mach 5 or higher, advances the technology readiness of a key GPS-denied navigation component for hypersonics and precision-guided munition programs.

MO-Nav was previously demonstrated in a cannon-fired artillery application, successfully surviving extreme launch loads and providing critical signal measurements to the munition mission computer.

General Dynamics Mission Systems continues to invest in Multiple Orbit Highly Assured Weapons Kit (MOHAWK), building upon the MO-Nav architecture to offer increased spectral diversity, expanded constellation diversity and scalable anti-jam protection. MOHAWK is also designed to support an optional integrated M-Code receiver capability, as well as federated external M-Code GPS receiver support with anti-jam and anti-spoof protected radio frequency output.

General Dynamics and DEVCOM AvMC are co-investing to demonstrate MOHAWK with integrated M-Code capability in a 2027 hypersonics demonstration, followed by additional MOHAWK demonstrations in precision-guided munition platforms in 2028.

🇺🇸 AMERICA, I NEED YOUR HELP. AND YES, I AM BEGGING!

The Bridge to Liberty is building an American Neighbor Network across the United States to help Afrikaner refugees who are arriving in our country and struggling to get established.

I am asking Americans to step forward. Not necessarily with money, but with their time, their connections, their communities, and their hearts.

I DO NOT HAVE AN AMERICAN TEAM, AND I DESPERATELY NEED ONE.

Most of my current team is working with Afrikaners who have been deemed ineligible for the refugee program. Meanwhile, we have refugees arriving in America who need housing, employment, furniture, transportation, and simply someone who cares enough to help them navigate their new lives.

We cannot do this alone.

You do NOT have to take responsibility for an entire state!

Start with ONE community. Your own hometown!

Go to your church and ask whether they would be willing to help a refugee family. Visit your local senior center and ask whether anyone would like to volunteer, donate household items, or simply become a friend to someone new to America. Talk to your friends, your family, your neighbors, local employers, landlords, and community organizations.

Find one person willing to help, then another. Build a small network in your community, and when that community is established, reach into the next town. One community at a time, one family at a time.

We already have an American volunteer in Michigan doing exactly this! He has helped refugees find apartments, assisted families with relocating, and is now working to gather furniture and household essentials. That is the kind of local leadership we desperately need throughout America.

Refugee resettlement agencies receive taxpayer funding to provide specific services to refugees. Those services come with responsibilities and obligations. We are receiving concerns that some refugees are not getting the assistance they need, and we intend to seek answers, document those concerns, and bring any substantiated failures to the attention of the appropriate oversight authorities.

But that process takes time.

IN THE MEANTIME, AFRIKANER REFUGEES ARE FALLING THROUGH THE CRACKS!

We cannot simply sit back and wait while families struggle to establish themselves.

That is why we are developing our REFUGEE WELCOME WAGON REGISTRY.

Every participating refugee will be able to register their essential household needs. Americans who want to help will have TWO options: purchase a needed item as a housewarming gift or offer useful items they already have in their homes and arrange to ship them directly to the refugee.

NO LUXURIES. JUST NECESSITIES.

Beds, bedding, towels, kitchen essentials, basic furniture, and the everyday items a family needs to make a house a home.

Because unrestricted wish lists have gotten out of hand in the past, The Bridge to Liberty will oversee the Welcome Wagon Registry to ensure requests are reasonable, necessary, and properly coordinated.

We are also building a Job Board, an American Neighbor Network, and individualized action plans to help refugees work toward stability and independence.

We recently received our Georgia state nonprofit status, and next week I will begin working on our federal tax-exempt application. Once approved, we hope to pursue grants to help fund these programs. But right now, WE HAVE NO FUNDING FOR DIRECT FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE.

What we do have is determination, a growing network, and a tremendous amount of work ahead of us.

You don't have to open your home. You don't have to write a check. You don't have to run an organization. You can simply be the person in your community who says, "I know someone who can help."

GET BACK TO US AND GET REGISTERED! EASY BREEZY! ❤️

🇺🇸 JOIN THE AMERICAN NEIGHBOR NETWORK HERE:

https://t.co/BlV9NlSbwG

Tell us your city, state, and how you would like to help. We will work together from there!

I AM NOT ASKING ONE PERSON TO DO EVERYTHING. I AM ASKING MANY PEOPLE TO DO SOMETHING.

God bless America, and God bless every person willing to extend a hand to someone starting over. 🇺🇸❤️

ONE NEIGHBOR. ONE COMMUNITY. ONE BRIDGE TO LIBERTY.

text:
Here's Marco Rubio’s full speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens, Greece:

There are great ruins all across the world. In many cases, they are places where history seems to have exhausted itself: remnants of distant cultures that have long passed beyond living memory.

But the Acropolis is different.

For thousands of years, the civilization that built what stands behind me has captivated the imagination of the Western world. Generations of our statesmen, artists, and philosophers have looked to it – they’ve looked to it with wonder and they’ve looked to it with awe.

Now time has a tendency to dull the senses: great victories and catastrophic defeats, they seem to shrink to becoming like a footnote in a textbook, another fact for our schoolchildren to memorize and forget. But the Greeks of antiquity, they seem to have an almost mystical hold on our memory. They call us back to them, again and again.

480 years before Christ, the armies of Xerxes arrived in this city and they put its sanctuaries to the torch. Most Athenians had by then evacuated by ship to a nearby island. But there was a handful of them that refused to leave their home. So instead, they barricaded themselves in the rocky fortress of the Acropolis to fight an extraordinary last stand, heaving massive stones down the cliffs onto the Persian invaders and holding the greatest empire of the age at bay for days. They were eventually overwhelmed. The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon.

For 25 centuries since, the Parthenon has stood. Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow. And the progeny of the men who built it – the sons of Athens and Rome – have carried their civilization with them to the ends of the Earth.

Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish.

The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity. Greece is literally carved into the architecture of our government: in the towering columns, in the domes and the monuments across our capital city. The city where our Constitution was born – Philadelphia – is itself a Greek name.

The men who founded my country were fascinated by the heritage we inherited from yours. They were exceptionally well-read in history – they were vividly aware of their unique place in it – but no other age of the past held their attention or their imagination quite like that of antiquity. Many, many people are surprised to learn that the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was not an Enlightenment philosopher or political theorist. No, the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was Plutarch, the Greek biographer of Greece and Rome’s great men.

Now, much has been written and said about the influence of ancient Greece on the ideas of the American Founders – and, for that matter, on all of the Western philosophers and statesmen that preceded them. Most of us are familiar with the basic history. Athens gave us democracy. Plato and Aristotle gave us Western philosophy. Our ideas of law, of virtue, of citizenship, and republican government were shaped in the Greek city-states. Even much of our political vocabulary – words like democracy, tyranny, the word “politics” itself – found its origins here.

Now, all of that is true. But the things we owe to this place – as Americans, and as Westerners – are actually far far deeper. These institutions and ideas – these institutions and ideas were the outward expression of more fundamental qualities we see in the ancient Greeks – qualities that can’t be reduced to any particular political system or theory.

Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West: fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory. An insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates, a hunger to know the mysteries of nature and grasp the secrets of the cosmos. An impatience with the notion of impossibility, chafing at all boundaries and limits, straining to peer into the depths of the unknown.

These were not just the formulas or precepts of a particular school of philosophy. They were the characteristic of a people – expressed in their traditions, their stories, their imagination; in the qualities they demanded of their citizens; in the things they lived and fought and died for.

To know them is to know ourselves.

What blossomed here in this place was the Western desire to uncover all that ignorance, darkness, and distance had kept hidden from the mind of man. The Greeks did not just shape history; the Greeks gave us history itself. Much about – much of what we know about many ancient civilizations comes almost entirely from the records of Greek explorers and historians, explorers and historians who didn’t just chronicle the histories of their own people, but ventured outwards to observe and record the sagas of foreign peoples and cultures all across the world.

Where others looked inward, the Greeks were the first to direct their focus outward, to chase the thrill and glory of seeing all that was strange and new. It was this trait – it was this trait that would push the West to create and build things that others could not, marking us out from so many other cultures and civilizations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life.

But it is not just the ambition to explore the unknown that we inherit from the Greeks; it is the conviction that the unknown can be known. The confidence that the world can be charted and measured and mapped and understood – and that there is a rational order to the cosmos, governed by certain fundamental laws, laws that men can observe and the mind can come to understand.

This was the foundation of the Western mind: our math, our science, our medicine. Our philosophy, ethics, and religion. It paved the way for the gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom. It was the foundation of the riches of Christian theology – of Augustine and Aquinas and the whole tradition of natural law.

It gave birth to a civilization marked not just by a common culture, it was marked by a common anthropology – a common view of man and his place in the universe. Its descendants would share not just the idea of a natural order, but a distinctive understanding of virtue; of destiny and fate; of truth, goodness, and beauty; of a code that dictates how men ought to live; of objective standards and ideals to strive towards.

For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence. They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft. The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle – to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.

Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel. The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat. Too often these days, we build downwards. We design our standards to ensure no one will lose; we preoccupy ourselves more with the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best. We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.

The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things. The ancient Greek city-states were filled. They were filled with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict. But from that constant struggle for distinction – from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.

The thumos, as the ancient Greeks called it – the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride – is the heart of great civilization. And without it? Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive.

Today, too much of the West has forgotten this quality. Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional. We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world. Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt. We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness.

The word “nationalism” became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments; we condemned our own history. And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit. In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay.

And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control.

But others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left – the vacuum left behind by our weakness. And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead.

And now, today, we find ourselves at a crossroads. Because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.

Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.

We choose to reach for new frontiers: in advanced manufacturing and super intelligence; in drones, weapons, and warfare; in chips, minerals, cyber, and every other domain of human possibility. To unleash our energy, to rebuild our factories, to return our astronauts to the moon and launch a new age of exploration in space.

Now for all their lofty ideals, the ancient Greeks were not naive. They understood that nations have interests. They understood that statecraft requires prudence and diplomacy, but they also understood that it requires the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail. They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.

This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim – reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization.

We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.

There are already signs.

Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift: skyrocketing defense spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programs, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defense commitments made last year in The Hague.

Greece has been at the center of this shift. The people of this nation have proved themselves once again to be an indispensable friend to Europe and to the United States alike, on everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally.

And it’s our sincerest hope that all of Europe will follow your example.

Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them. Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age.

And we can. Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum. Quite the opposite: our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts. It is a vision we saw in action just last month, in an unprecedented new agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland – an agreement that will reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO. All three partners in that deal emerged victorious. All of Europe – and NATO and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.

We want to win together. We must win together.

Now it’s has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people. And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else.

They believed – fiercely – in the ideal of the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds. But they believed that glory and fame, those things were won through striving, sacrificing and achieving greatly for something larger than yourself. The recurring hero of the ancient Greek world was the man who was willing to pay any cost for a cause worthy of his loyalty.

We see this in Socrates, who refused to abandon the inquiry into truth even at the cost of his own life. We see it in the legendary stand of 300 Spartans – surrounded and hopelessly outnumbered by the vast armies of Persia – who refused the chance to save themselves, choosing to fight to the last man rather than abandon their post or abandon their duty. And we see it in the epic myth of Achilles, who is offered the choice to return home and live a long and peaceful life – but chooses instead to remain at Troy and perish in pursuit of eternal glory.

These – these are the qualities that would shape the Western moral imagination. From the Christian martyr who refused to betray his faith to the patriot who gave his life for his country; from Saint Thomas More to the Battle of the Alamo, running through the immortal closing words of the Declaration of Independence of the United States which says, “We mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country. Our heroes, the heroes of the West are those who choose to remain faithful to their duty precisely when it is most difficult and painful to do so: the man who is bound by his word, the soldier who will not abandon his post, the captain, the proverbial captain, who goes down with his ship.

This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.

Our heroes – our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but our heroes do not worship death. It is precisely because we value life that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles. Now, we take the West’s conception of these things – heroism, honor, duty – we take these things for granted. We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places. They are not. They are the product of a distinct character, a distinct character which arose here and shaped the whole story of the civilization that came after it. A civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.

The men who built the Parthenon were succeeded by the architects of European Christendom, who raised the cathedrals of Milan, Cologne, and Florence. The quest to perfect the human form that moved the ancient Greek sculptors found a new expression in Michelangelo. The Greek philosophers’ search for the structure of the universe was inherited by Copernicus, and then Galileo, then Kepler, and in Newton.

The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’ discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon. And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.

And in America, that same tradition rediscovered itself anew. An open and wild land became the site of a great revival of Western imagination and ambition. The Greek aspiration for new horizons became the American frontier spirit. The civilization of Athens and Rome transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire.

The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world.

Together, we must now rediscover that spirit. We are at an inflection point – an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization.

The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity.

National interests did not vanish in the face of international institutions. War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace. Other states continued to arm, to seek influence, to compete for territory, and technology, and resources, and markets, and energy, and power.

And now, there is war again. There is new competition between great powers again. There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again.

And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together – understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them. And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.

We have built a model of that with our partners here in Greece. In our defense partnerships, in energy and technology, in our shared ambition to secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration.

Our friendship dates back to the earliest years of my nation. When Greece rose in 1821 to recover its independence after centuries of Ottoman rule, Americans recognized something familiar in that struggle. Three years later, the great American statesman Daniel Webster, he delivered a famous address to Congress, helping bring the cause of the Greek Revolution before the representatives of the young American republic.

And he began by calling their attention to everything around them. This is what he said in his speech; he said: “This free form of government, this popular assembly… this practice of free debate, and public discussion, the contest of mind with mind… even the edifice in which we assemble, these proportioned columns, this ornamented architecture, all remind us that Greece has existed, and that we, like the rest of mankind, are greatly her debtors.”

Those words are as true today as they were when he said them. And all of us – not just Americans, but Europeans and our friends across the West – must relearn the lessons our forefathers took from this place and from its history.

The history of Greece – the history of Greece does not just offer us a glimpse – it does not offer a glimpse of our institutions in their earliest forms. The history of Greece shows us an image of ourselves.

It shows us that ours is the inheritance of great heroes, and that we should be proud – that we should be intensely proud – of where we come from. We should marvel at what our forefathers carved out of this countryside. The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man. And it began here, with the first men and women of the West. From them – from them – we can rediscover the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time.

Thank you.

Iran’s false alternative—and why Tehran benefits
For Europe, the debate about Iran cannot be reduced to a choice between clerical dictatorship and Reza Pahlavi. The son of the shah deposed in 1979 enjoys international visibility, but the monarchy overthrown that year has no demonstrated serious prospect of restoration. His campaign offers what amounts to a fake opposition alternative: publicity and personal allegiance presented as substitutes for organised democratic change. By diverting attention from forces challenging the mullahs’ regime, it benefits Tehran, writes Firouz Mahvi.

Visibility does not establish a national mandate. A Reuters investigation found no apparent mass organised movement inside Iran ready to bring Pahlavi to power, an assessment he disputed. That organisational weakness helps explain his reliance on publicity and foreign military intervention.
In January 2026, Pahlavi told CNN that his platform had received more than 100,000 new applications, including from military and government personnel. Registrations do not establish verified defections. His separate claim of 1.5 million website views within twenty-four hours measures attention, rather than representative authority.
Treadstone 71 attributes some ostensibly pro-Pahlavi accounts to regime-linked operators working from Iran, describing how Tehran can pose as his supporters and attack other opponents. A separate European broadcasters’ investigation identified coordinated pro-Pahlavi amplification without establishing who controlled the accounts. Online activity requires scrutiny, rather than automatic acceptance as grassroots support.
The treatment of dissent within the diaspora raises more immediate concerns. In Canada, police recovered the remains of Iranian academic and activist Masood Masjoody on 6 March 2026. A week later, Mehdi Ahmadzadeh Razavi and Arezou Soltani were arrested and charged with first-degree murder. Reuters identified both as Pahlavi supporters. Masjoody had criticised Pahlavi and previously accused the pair of plotting to kill him. Their guilt and the motive remain matters for the courts; the case does not establish Pahlavi’s involvement.
Other incidents target journalists and political opponents. Kurdistan24 reported that its correspondent Dilovan Emadaldin was assaulted in London on 9 March while covering an attack on a restaurant. It attributed the assault to Pahlavi supporters through eyewitness accounts. Reuters also reported a Vienna conviction for threats and coercion following demands that an Iranian restaurant display the pre-revolutionary flag.
In July, Workers’ Liberty reported that Pahlavi supporters disrupted a London protest for an imprisoned Iranian oil worker and physically attacked a participant. This is the organisers’ account, rather than a judicial finding.
Dutch broadcaster Nieuwsuur documented a Telegram channel exposing personal details of more than 170 Iranians in the Netherlands and Belgium, including lawyers, academics and journalists. At least twenty people reported threats to police. A lawyer described a critic’s home being vandalised and her subsequent need to hide. Intimidation discourages democratic participation.
Pahlavi has condemned intimidation. Yet adviser Saeed Ghasseminejad has framed the political choice as loyalty to Pahlavi or alignment with the regime. Republicans, labour activists and rights defenders should not have to accept a hereditary claimant’s leadership to establish their opposition to Tehran.
Foreign intervention exposes the weakness of this project. In February 2026, Pahlavi argued on ABC that military action could be a “humanitarian intervention” to protect lives and accelerate the regime’s collapse. Reuters later questioned him about welcoming the war as a “game changer”. Without a demonstrated organisation capable of securing change inside Iran, he relies heavily on foreign military power, with himself envisaged as the subsequent leader. For supporters seeking a crown for him, outside force becomes the imagined means of handing him one. Bombardment cannot create democratic institutions.
The contrast with January’s prominence is striking. By July, Reuters reported a faltering campaign and disillusionment among some financial backers, including over his muted response to extreme wartime threats against Iran. This documents damage to his credibility abroad; inside Iran, presenting bombardment as liberation undermines his claim to represent those enduring it.
The Guardian reported supporters displaying SAVAK emblems, from which Pahlavi subsequently distanced himself. SAVAK was the shah’s security service, whose torture and repression Amnesty International documented. Celebrating it undermines the credibility of any democratic promise.
Institutional safeguards matter as much as rhetoric. Pahlavi’s revised February 2026 Emergency Phase Booklet promises referendums and elections but initially gives him extensive authority over transitional appointments and the armed forces. Promises of a later vote do not resolve concerns about concentrating power in an unelected individual during the transition itself.
This is how Tehran benefits. Pahlavi’s campaign obscures organised democratic opposition and shifts debate towards a hereditary claimant and foreign intervention. Tehran has political reasons to welcome that confusion, while reported infiltration of pro-Pahlavi networks offers a means of cultivating it. Support for foreign attacks also feeds the regime’s portrayal of dissent as foreign interference. European governments should scrutinise these consequences before mistaking international prominence for democratic legitimacy. Iran’s future depends on its citizens’ ability to organise, choose their government and hold it accountable.

text:
Η ιστορική ομιλία του Υπουργού Εξωτερικών των ΗΠΑ, Marco Rubio, στην Πνύκα στις 7 Οκτωβρίου 2026, στα αγγλικά.

There are great ruins all across the world. In many cases, they are places where history seems to have exhausted itself: remnants of distant cultures that have long passed beyond living memory.

But the Acropolis is different. 

For thousands of years, the civilization that built what stands behind me has captivated the imagination of the Western world. Generations of our statesmen, artists, and philosophers have looked to it – they’ve looked to it with wonder and they’ve looked to it with awe.

Now time has a tendency to dull the senses: great victories and catastrophic defeats, they seem to shrink to becoming like a footnote in a textbook, another fact for our schoolchildren to memorize and forget. But the Greeks of antiquity, they seem to have an almost mystical hold on our memory. They call us back to them, again and again. 

480 years before Christ, the armies of Xerxes arrived in this city and they put its sanctuaries to the torch. Most Athenians had by then evacuated by ship to a nearby island. But there was a handful of them that refused to leave their home. So instead, they barricaded themselves in the rocky fortress of the Acropolis to fight an extraordinary last stand, heaving massive stones down the cliffs onto the Persian invaders and holding the greatest empire of the age at bay for days. They were eventually overwhelmed. The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon.

For 25 centuries since, the Parthenon has stood. Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow. And the progeny of the men who built it – the sons of Athens and Rome – have carried their civilization with them to the ends of the Earth.

Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish. 

The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity. Greece is literally carved into the architecture of our government: in the towering columns, in the domes and the monuments across our capital city. The city where our Constitution was born – Philadelphia – is itself a Greek name.

The men who founded my country were fascinated by the heritage we inherited from yours. They were exceptionally well-read in history – they were vividly aware of their unique place in it – but no other age of the past held their attention or their imagination quite like that of antiquity. Many, many people are surprised to learn that the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was not an Enlightenment philosopher or political theorist. No, the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was Plutarch, the Greek biographer of Greece and Rome’s great men.

Now, much has been written and said about the influence of ancient Greece on the ideas of the American Founders – and, for that matter, on all of the Western philosophers and statesmen that preceded them. Most of us are familiar with the basic history. Athens gave us democracy. Plato and Aristotle gave us Western philosophy. Our ideas of law, of virtue, of citizenship, and republican government were shaped in the Greek city-states. Even much of our political vocabulary – words like democracy, tyranny, the word “politics” itself – found its origins here.

Now, all of that is true. But the things we owe to this place – as Americans, and as Westerners – are actually far far deeper. These institutions and ideas – these institutions and ideas were the outward expression of more fundamental qualities we see in the ancient Greeks – qualities that can’t be reduced to any particular political system or theory.

Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West: fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory. An insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates, a hunger to know the mysteries of nature and grasp the secrets of the cosmos. An impatience with the notion of impossibility, chafing at all boundaries and limits, straining to peer into the depths of the unknown.

These were not just the formulas or precepts of a particular school of philosophy. They were the characteristic of a people – expressed in their traditions, their stories, their imagination; in the qualities they demanded of their citizens; in the things they lived and fought and died for.

To know them is to know ourselves.

What blossomed here in this place was the Western desire to uncover all that ignorance, darkness, and distance had kept hidden from the mind of man. The Greeks did not just shape history; the Greeks gave us history itself.  Much about – much of what we know about many ancient civilizations comes almost entirely from the records of Greek explorers and historians, explorers and historians who didn’t just chronicle the histories of their own people, but ventured outwards to observe and record the sagas of foreign peoples and cultures all across the world.

Where others looked inward, the Greeks were the first to direct their focus outward, to chase the thrill and glory of seeing all that was strange and new. It was this trait – it was this trait that would push the West to create and build things that others could not, marking us out from so many other cultures and civilizations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life.

But it is not just the ambition to explore the unknown that we inherit from the Greeks; it is the conviction that the unknown can be known. The confidence that the world can be charted and measured and mapped and understood – and that there is a rational order to the cosmos, governed by certain fundamental laws, laws that men can observe and the mind can come to understand.

This was the foundation of the Western mind: our math, our science, our medicine. Our philosophy, ethics, and religion. It paved the way for the gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom. It was the foundation of the riches of Christian theology – of Augustine and Aquinas and the whole tradition of natural law.

It gave birth to a civilization marked not just by a common culture, it was marked by a common anthropology – a common view of man and his place in the universe. Its descendants would share not just the idea of a natural order, but a distinctive understanding of virtue; of destiny and fate; of truth, goodness, and beauty; of a code that dictates how men ought to live; of objective standards and ideals to strive towards.

For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence. They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft. The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle – to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.

Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel. The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat. Too often these days, we build downwards. We design our standards to ensure no one will lose; we preoccupy ourselves more with the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best. We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.

The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards.  They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things. The ancient Greek city-states were filled. They were filled with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict. But from that constant struggle for distinction – from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.

The thumos, as the ancient Greeks called it – the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride – is the heart of great civilization. And without it? Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive. 

Today, too much of the West has forgotten this quality. Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional. We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world. Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt. We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness. 

The word “nationalism” became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments; we condemned our own history. And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit. In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay. 

And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control.

But others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left – the vacuum left behind by our weakness. And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead.

And now, today, we find ourselves at a crossroads. Because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.

Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future. 

We choose to reach for new frontiers: in advanced manufacturing and super intelligence; in drones, weapons, and warfare; in chips, minerals, cyber, and every other domain of human possibility. To unleash our energy, to rebuild our factories, to return our astronauts to the moon and launch a new age of exploration in space.

Now for all their lofty ideals, the ancient Greeks were not naive. They understood that nations have interests. They understood that statecraft requires prudence and diplomacy, but they also understood that it requires the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail. They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.

This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim – reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization.

We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.

There are already signs.

Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift: skyrocketing defense spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programs, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defense commitments made last year in The Hague. 

Greece has been at the center of this shift. The people of this nation have proved themselves once again to be an indispensable friend to Europe and to the United States alike, on everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally.

And it’s our sincerest hope that all of Europe will follow your example.

Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them. Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age.

And we can. Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum. Quite the opposite: our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts. It is a vision we saw in action just last month, in an unprecedented new agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland – an agreement that will reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO. All three partners in that deal emerged victorious. All of Europe – and NATO and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.

We want to win together. We must win together.

Now it’s has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people. And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else. 

They believed – fiercely – in the ideal of the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds. But they believed that glory and fame, those things were won through striving, sacrificing and achieving greatly for something larger than yourself. The recurring hero of the ancient Greek world was the man who was willing to pay any cost for a cause worthy of his loyalty.

We see this in Socrates, who refused to abandon the inquiry into truth even at the cost of his own life. We see it in the legendary stand of 300 Spartans – surrounded and hopelessly outnumbered by the vast armies of Persia – who refused the chance to save themselves, choosing to fight to the last man rather than abandon their post or abandon their duty. And we see it in the epic myth of Achilles, who is offered the choice to return home and live a long and peaceful life – but chooses instead to remain at Troy and perish in pursuit of eternal glory.

These – these are the qualities that would shape the Western moral imagination. From the Christian martyr who refused to betray his faith to the patriot who gave his life for his country; from Saint Thomas More to the Battle of the Alamo, running through the immortal closing words of the Declaration of Independence of the United States which says, “We mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country. Our heroes, the heroes of the West are those who choose to remain faithful to their duty precisely when it is most difficult and painful to do so: the man who is bound by his word, the soldier who will not abandon his post, the captain, the proverbial captain, who goes down with his ship.

This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.

Our heroes – our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but our heroes do not worship death. It is precisely because we value life that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles. Now, we take the West’s conception of these things – heroism, honor, duty – we take these things for granted. We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places. They are not. They are the product of a distinct character, a distinct character which arose here and shaped the whole story of the civilization that came after it. A civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.

The men who built the Parthenon were succeeded by the architects of European Christendom, who raised the cathedrals of Milan, Cologne, and Florence. The quest to perfect the human form that moved the ancient Greek sculptors found a new expression in Michelangelo. The Greek philosophers’ search for the structure of the universe was inherited by Copernicus, and then Galileo, then Kepler, and in Newton.

The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’ discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon. And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.

And in America, that same tradition rediscovered itself anew. An open and wild land became the site of a great revival of Western imagination and ambition. The Greek aspiration for new horizons became the American frontier spirit. The civilization of Athens and Rome transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire.

The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world. 

Together, we must now rediscover that spirit. We are at an inflection point – an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization. 

The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity.

National interests did not vanish in the face of international institutions. War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace. Other states continued to arm, to seek influence, to compete for territory, and technology, and resources, and markets, and energy, and power.

And now, there is war again. There is new competition between great powers again. There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again. 

And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together – understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them. And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.

We have built a model of that with our partners here in Greece. In our defense partnerships, in energy and technology, in our shared ambition to secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration.

Our friendship dates back to the earliest years of my nation. When Greece rose in 1821 to recover its independence after centuries of Ottoman rule, Americans recognized something familiar in that struggle. Three years later, the great American statesman Daniel Webster, he delivered a famous address to Congress, helping bring the cause of the Greek Revolution before the representatives of the young American republic.

And he began by calling their attention to everything around them. This is what he said in his speech; he said: “This free form of government, this popular assembly… this practice of free debate, and public discussion, the contest of mind with mind… even the edifice in which we assemble, these proportioned columns, this ornamented architecture, all remind us that Greece has existed, and that we, like the rest of mankind, are greatly her debtors.”

Those words are as true today as they were when he said them. And all of us – not just Americans, but Europeans and our friends across the West – must relearn the lessons our forefathers took from this place and from its history.

The history of Greece – the history of Greece does not just offer us a glimpse – it does not offer a glimpse of our institutions in their earliest forms. The history of Greece shows us an image of ourselves.

It shows us that ours is the inheritance of great heroes, and that we should be proud – that we should be intensely proud – of where we come from. We should marvel at what our forefathers carved out of this countryside. The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man. And it began here, with the first men and women of the West. From them – from them – we can rediscover the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time.

Thank you.

In the occult system of Aleister Crowley, moving "forward in reverse" refers to the mandatory training of the magician to think, speak, write, and act backwards. Detailed in his work Liber ThIShARB (Liber 913) and later collected in Magick: Book 4, this process is designed to break down conventional frameworks of time and perception. 

The Law of Reversal
Crowley posited that to perceive the past, understand karma, or discover one's "True Will," an adept must master the Occult Law of Reversal. By forcing the mind to process reality in reverse, the practitioner aims to unlock hidden layers of memory and subconscious power. [1, 2]
According to Crowley’s specific instructions, an adept must train using the following methods:
Writing Backwards: Learning to write text in reverse, using either hand. 
Walking Backwards: Moving physically in reverse to disrupt muscle memory and spatial habit. 
Listening Backwards: Listening to phonograph records or audio clips played in reverse (a practice that later heavily influenced the concept of "backmasking" in music).
Speaking Backwards: Reversing phonetics out loud (e.g., transforming the phrase "I am He" into "Eh ma I"). [1]
Reversed Thinking: Seating oneself in meditation and mentally tracing the day's events perfectly backward, from the current moment down to the exact second of waking up.

Purpose and Cultural Legacy
Magical Aim: Crowley designed these techniques to shatter the psychological illusion of linear time and habitual ego-thought, assisting the magician in cultivating the "Magical Memory" (including past-life recall) and surviving profound spiritual states.
Backmasking Influence: Crowley’s recommendation to listen to reversed audio records later became a foundational reference point for the 20th-century concept of backmasking in rock and heavy metal music (such as allegations involving Led Zeppelin or the Beatles).

The three stages of alchemy
The Nigredo is the first of the three main stages the alchemical work must pass through to achieve what’s known as the philosopher’s stone. At the practical level, the philosopher’s stone is represented by gold, the purest of metals; psychologically, the stone is akin to the birth of the true, authentic self; and spiritually, we’re basically talking about enlightenment.

In brief, the three stages go like this (please don’t worry about retaining everything here because I’ll return to the parts you need to know):

First, the Nigredo, or blackening, in which the base matter is heated to burn away the unnecessary and bring impurities to light. Nigredo symbolism includes the Black Dragon, ravens or crows, bones and decaying bodies, and the Black Sun (or sol niger).

Next, the Albedo, or whitening, in which the matter is separated, distilled, and purified; its essence extracted and released. Albedo symbols include the white swan or dove, the moon, clear water, and the White Queen.

There is a transitional stage next, known as the Citrinitas or the yellowing, which involves the infusion of warmth and spiritual insight, symbolised by honey, ripening wheat, and the sun rising on the new day.

The Rubedo, or the reddening – the final stage of the work – involves the integration of opposites and the experience of the true self, culminating in the Philosopher’s Stone, the perfected work across all three planes: material gold, psychological wholeness, and spiritual enlightenment.

The symbols for this stage include the phoenix, the full sun, the Red King, and the hermaphrodite (or rebis) – which represents the integrated whole, where masculine and feminine are united.

The word rubio comes from the Latin word rubeus, which means "red". [1]

Etymology and Meaning Evolution
Latin Origin: It derives from rubeus (red or reddish, like a blackberry before it ripens).
Shift in Spanish: Over time in Spanish, the meaning shifted from "red" to describe golden, yellowish, or fair hair and complexions (blond). It historically started as a nickname for someone with red hair, a red beard, or a ruddy complexion before generalizing to fair-haired individuals.
Catalan Variant: In Catalan (Rubió), it can also function as a habitational name taken from places named Rubió in Catalonia.

Red giants are evolved from main-sequence stars with masses in the range from about 0.3 M☉ to around 8 M☉.[13] When a star initially forms from a collapsing molecular cloud in the interstellar medium, it contains primarily hydrogen and helium, with trace amounts of "metals" (in astrophysics, this refers to all elements other than hydrogen and helium). These elements are all uniformly mixed throughout the star. The star "enters" the main sequence when its core reaches a temperature (several million kelvins) high enough to begin fusing hydrogen-1 (the predominant isotope), and establishes hydrostatic equilibrium. (In astrophysics, stellar fusion is often referred to as "burning", with hydrogen fusion sometimes termed "hydrogen burning".) Over its main sequence life, the star slowly fuses the hydrogen in the core into helium; its main-sequence life ends when nearly all the hydrogen in the core has been fused. For the Sun, the main-sequence lifetime is approximately 10 billion years. More massive stars burn their fuel disproportionately faster and so have a shorter lifetime than less massive stars.

清 金鑲松石塔頂

金鑲松石塔頂是一件精美的清代金屬工藝品，典藏於國立故宮博物院。該作品以三件金屬部件層疊組合而成，整體高度為12.8公分。從形制上看，最下方和中間兩層皆呈須彌座形的蓮座，二者造型相似但尺寸略有差異，造型細膩而端莊，蓮座通常象徵神聖或莊嚴，突顯其宗教或祭祀用途。最上層為一瓶形器皿，造型如無流的奔巴壺，線條流暢柔和，顯示精湛的金屬工藝技藝。

器物外壁飾以綠松石鑲嵌，形成清晰鮮豔的色彩對比，使得整件作品在金色的襯托下更顯華貴。同時，塔頂最頂端鑲嵌一塊紅寶石，紅寶石的鮮艷色澤和松石的青綠色彩構成鮮明的視覺焦點，強調了物件的尊貴與神秘感。

附屬的木座為器物提供穩固的支撐，並使其展示更為端正。木座上置有一張黃色標籤，記載有重要的文獻資料：“乾隆五十八年(1793)八月二十六日收造辦處呈”，以及對材質與重量的說明：“覽金鑲松石塔頂一件，八成金嵌紅寶石一塊，連鑲嵌共重三兩”，這些紀錄不僅佐證了作品的清晰製作年代，亦為研究其製作技術和金屬成分提供可靠依據。

從這些文獻中，我們得知該塔頂由八成金製成，意指純金含量約80%，並嵌有一顆紅寶石，總重量約三兩（約37.5克），這段紀錄明確反映了該件金屬工藝品在清代皇室製作機構的製作背景。

觀者細看這件作品，應特別留意其疊合的三層結構，每一層的工藝細節與形制變化；其次是外壁松石的鑲嵌工藝，如何精確嵌入金面，且保持色澤鮮明；最後則是頂部紅寶石的鑲嵌手法與光澤效果。此外，黃色標籤的文字清晰記錄了歷史時間與材料成分，是理解本件物品文化歷史背景的關鍵。

綜合以上，此金鑲松石塔頂不僅展現了清代工匠高超的鑲嵌和金屬燒鑄技術，也反映了當時宮廷對於宗教與藝術器物的精緻要求。它是研究晚清金屬工藝及寶石鑲嵌藝術的珍貴實物，提供了理解清代宮廷文化和工藝水準的重要視角。

The Gold Stupa with Turquoise Inlay is a refined metalwork artifact from the Qing dynasty, housed in the National Palace Museum. This piece stands at 12.8 centimeters tall and is constructed by stacking three separate gold metal components. The two bottom segments each resemble a lotus-shaped pedestal, styled akin to Sumeru thrones—sacred, stylized bases featuring lotus motifs common in Buddhist art. Though similar in form, the two layers differ slightly in size, lending a sense of proportion and hierarchy to the assembly. The topmost element takes the form of a vase without a spout, specifically resembling a Bumpa vase, known for its smooth and rounded shape, which demonstrates the sophisticated craftsmanship of the era.

The outer surface of the artifact is decorated with turquoise stones inlaid neatly into the gold, creating a striking contrast between the vibrant green-blue hues of the turquoise and the warm luster of the gold beneath. This decorative technique enhances both the visual appeal and the perceived sacredness of the object. At the very apex of the stupa sits a ruby, whose deep red coloration provides a vivid and captivating focal point, reinforcing the object's significance and preciousness.

The stupa rests on a wooden base that provides stable support and an elegant presentation. Affixed to the base is a yellow paper tag bearing an inscription: "Received by the Zao Ban Office on the 26th day of August, 1793 (Qianlong 58). Viewing one piece of gold stupa inlaid with turquoise, made from 80% pure gold and set with one ruby, total weight including inlay three taels." This historical record confirms the object's Qing dynasty origin and provides crucial documented details on its material composition and date of manufacturing.

From this inscription, we learn that the metal comprises 80% pure gold, an alloy figure familiar in fine Qing metalwork, and that the total weight including the stone inlays amounts to approximately three taels—about 37.5 grams. These details situate the item firmly within the official crafts managed by the imperial manufacturing office, reflecting the quality control and recording standards of the period.

Viewers examining the stupa should pay special attention to the layered composition of the three gold sections, noting the subtle differences in size and form between the lotus-shaped bases and the vase-shaped top. Furthermore, one should closely observe how the turquoise has been meticulously embedded, fitting seamlessly into the gold outer wall while retaining brilliant coloration. Finally, the ruby inset at the pinnacle deserves focus, displaying refined mounting techniques that both secure the gemstone and optimize its brilliance. The yellow paper tag’s inscription provides an invaluable link to the object's historical provenance and material authenticity.

Overall, this Gold Stupa with Turquoise Inlay not only exemplifies the Qing dynasty’s high-level jewelry and metalwork skills but also embodies the era’s temple and ritual aesthetic. The piece offers significant insights into late Qing craftsmanship, gemstone inlay artistry, and the cultural context of religious artifacts commissioned by the imperial court. It remains an important object for the study of Qing metalwork and serves as a tangible connection to the artistic and spiritual values of its time.

text:
Camp David 2000 is the centrepiece of the rejection narrative. Ahron Bregman’s account, drawing on transcripts and participant records, shows that Ehud Barak moved further than any previous Israeli prime minister – on territory, on Jerusalem, on the willingness to countenance Palestinian sovereignty in parts of the Old City. However, the process was closer to forcing a reckoning than making peace. Patrick Tyler documents Barak’s strategy as an attempt to push Arafat into a final negotiation and, if he did not accept, declare that Israel had no partner. However, Arafat was not in a position to provide a definitive response either way. The Palestinians had wanted more months of preparatory talks, but Barak had not allowed it and had not implemented confidence-building commitments before the summit convened.

Early in the proceedings Barak killed the American written text, telling Bill Clinton “the paper no longer exists”, after which all discussions were oral with total deniability on anything proposed. Barak largely avoided substantive face-to-face negotiation with Arafat, saying he did not want Arafat to have a record, and thus preferred indirect channels through which positions could be floated and disowned. The summit then collapsed over Israeli sovereignty on the Haram al-Sharif, the Temple Mount compound containing the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa mosque. Barak would not relinquish it and Arafat could not concede it without Arab backing that had not been secured in advance, partly because Barak’s secrecy meant Arab leaders could not be briefed.

When Arafat asked for time to consult his leadership, Clinton treated the request less as a normal diplomatic step than as evasion, and the pressure shifted rapidly toward a yes-or-no reckoning that undermined the process.

Robert Malley co-authored with Hussein Agha a detailed rebuttal in the New York Review of Books arguing that the ‘generous offer’ framing was a post-hoc political construction. Malley was Clinton’s special assistant, directly involved in the talks, and Agha was a Palestinian academic with close ties to the Palestinian leadership and long involvement in back-channel diplomacy. Shlomo Ben-Ami, who was Israel’s chief negotiator, said in a 2006 Haaretz interview: “If I were a Palestinian, I would have rejected Camp David as well”. When the Israeli chief negotiator contradicts the rejection narrative, the narrative has a problem that more vivid memoir accounts cannot resolve.

The Clinton Parameters of December 2000 went further than Camp David on every core issue – including Palestinian sovereignty over the Haram – and represent the closest thing to an authoritative statehood framework. They were read orally rather than provided as a written document, because Barak feared Arafat would pocket any written text as an opening position, and Clinton wanted deniability should the proposals fail. On Bregman’s reading, Arafat’s failure to give the unambiguous ‘yes’ that Clinton demanded was a genuine missed opportunity, and Rashid later called it a strategic mistake. Shlaim’s interpretation complicates that verdict, observing that both sides responded with reservations. Israel’s own acceptance was heavily qualified by a twenty-page document, while Arafat’s qualified response was subsequently recast as outright rejection – partly, Clinton later told Saeb Erekat, the chief Palestinian negotiator, to preserve Barak’s domestic position. The failure was genuine, but the “Arafat rejected statehood” version of it is too simple.

Taba in January 2001 appears as another Palestinian rejection. Miguel Moratinos, the EU’s special envoy to the Middle East, produced a summary of where the parties stood at Taba, an unofficial document that became the main public record of the talks. The Clinton Parameters fed directly into Taba, hence why Taba was closer to agreement than at any previous point, with the parties’ own closing statement saying they had never been closer. Taba collapsed under a dying mandate: Barak was days from an election he was expected to lose, the talks had no durable political backing, and any understanding reached there would almost certainly have depended on a Barak Government that was about to disappear. Taba ended on 27 January, nine days before Sharon won the election on 6 February. There would be no serious negotiations for another seven years.

The Ehud Olmert entry requires the most imaginative reading of the word ‘rejection’. Months of talks culminated in a September 2008 meeting at which Olmert showed Mahmoud Abbas a map but would not leave it with him. Abbas asked to study it and consult his team – the response any negotiator would give before formally responding to a complex territorial proposal – and Olmert refused. Abbas said he would return with his negotiators for formal talks, but Olmert resigned weeks later under corruption investigations and the Netanyahu Government that followed repudiated the Olmert framework. Olmert himself has said publicly that Abbas did not reject the proposal but asked for time to consult.

The fair criticism of Abbas is that he neither responded with a counter-proposal nor made any effort to put Olmert’s offer on the record before the Olmert Government collapsed, thus leaving the most serious proposal he had received to disappear with the administration that made it. Although that is a legitimate failure of Palestinian diplomacy, it is not the same as rejecting a signed, written, implementable statehood agreement.

So, at the decisive moments in 2000, 2001, and 2008, there was no formal written Israeli proposal with agreed maps that Palestinians could have signed or refused. Positions were advanced orally, incrementally, and with deniability built in. The ‘generous offer’ narrative depends on that absence of a written record, so that subsequent recharacterisation of what was actually proposed could not be checked.
