text:
October 9, 1913: Judge Roan Grants Dorsey More Time to Answer Frank's New-Trial Motion

The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, October 9, 1913, page 5, column 4

Dorsey Asks for More Time

On Thursday, October 9, 1913, The Atlanta Constitution reported that Judge Leonard S. Roan was willing to postpone Leo M. Frank's new-trial hearing, scheduled for Saturday, October 11. Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey had been working in Valdosta, Georgia, with his assistant, E. A. Stephens, preparing the State's answer to the 115 grounds raised by Frank's attorneys.

Frank had been convicted of murdering thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan on Monday, August 25, 1913, and sentenced to death the following day. His attorneys, Luther Z. Rosser and Reuben R. Arnold, were now seeking another trial.

The Constitution reported that Judge Roan would grant Dorsey's request without requiring him to travel from Valdosta to Atlanta simply to appear in court on Saturday.

Roan explained that the State had already been allowed a reasonable amount of time to prepare its answer when the hearing was postponed on Saturday, October 4. He saw no reason to deny Dorsey's request for additional time (The Atlanta Constitution, 1).

October 8: Dorsey and Stephens Working in Valdosta

The Constitution included a special dispatch from Valdosta dated Wednesday, October 8. Dorsey and Stephens had been using the offices of Judge W. E. Thomas at the Lowndes County courthouse while Thomas was away.

They had access to his law library and were spending long hours reviewing the trial testimony and the defense's amended motion. Despite their efforts, they had examined only a small portion of the record.

The two men had traveled to Valdosta to avoid interruptions from their regular courthouse duties in Atlanta. Dorsey informed Judge Roan that he could not finish his preparations by Saturday and intended to remain in Valdosta until the State's answer was ready.

Dorsey declined to discuss the case beyond explaining his preparations. The newspaper reported that his absence was delaying other criminal business in Fulton County Superior Court, including a grand jury session expected that week.

Rosser Expresses Confidence

Luther Rosser told the Constitution that he would probably agree to give Dorsey additional time if the solicitor needed it.

When questioned about reports that the defense intended to file more affidavits, Rosser declined to provide details. He acknowledged that additional statements might be submitted if the attorneys obtained them.

The newspaper described Rosser as confident that Judge Roan would grant Frank another trial without requiring an appeal to the Georgia Supreme Court.

That confidence was Rosser's position in October 1913. The defense still had to prove its objections, and Judge Roan had not decided the motion.

The Accusations Against Henslee and Johenning

The October 9 article also reported that Frank's attorneys were continuing their attacks against jurors A. H. Henslee and Marcus Johenning.

Both men had served on the twelve-man jury that convicted Frank on August 25. The defense accused them of expressing opinions about Frank's guilt prior to the trial.

According to the Constitution, three people had submitted affidavits accusing Johenning of prejudice, while a larger number had made accusations against Henslee.

Henslee denied having expressed a fixed opinion of Frank's guilt prior to serving. Johenning likewise denied entering the trial with his mind already made up.

Their replies were important because the defense's accusations depended on proving prejudice at the time of jury service. Statements made after the verdict did not establish that either man had been unfair during the trial.

The Sparta Witnesses Receive Additional Support

The defense was also gathering affidavits supporting three men from Sparta, Georgia, who had accused Henslee of expressing an opinion about Frank's guilt prior to the trial.

The men were John M. Holmes, S. M. Johnson, and Shi Gray.

They claimed Henslee made the statements during a conversation in Holmes's office. Henslee denied their account of the date. He acknowledged visiting Holmes's office but maintained that the conversation about Frank occurred on September 2, 1913, eight days after the verdict.

The defense responded by obtaining affidavits from Hancock County residents who vouched for the honesty and character of the Sparta witnesses.

The Constitution reported that these statements were intended to strengthen the accusations against Henslee.

The new affidavits addressed the reputations of the accusers. They did not independently establish when the disputed conversation occurred. Henslee's account and the Sparta men's account still disagreed on the central question of timing.

A Third Juror May Be Accused

The Constitution also reported that the defense might file additional affidavits accusing a third member of the Frank jury of prejudice.

The newspaper did not identify the juror or name the people expected to make the accusations.

Rosser refused to confirm whether new affidavits would actually be submitted.

At the time of the October 9 report, Henslee and Johenning were the only jurors publicly identified in the article as facing such accusations. The report concerning a third juror remained unconfirmed.

October 31, 1913: Roan Denies the Motion

The new-trial proceedings continued through October. The defense presented its objections to the verdict, while Dorsey answered the accusations and defended the conduct of the jury.

On Friday, October 31, Judge Roan denied Frank's motion for a new trial.

Frank's attorneys appealed the decision to the Georgia Supreme Court.

On Tuesday, February 17, 1914, the Supreme Court affirmed Roan's ruling by a vote of four to two.

The court considered the accusations against Henslee and Johenning and recognized that the affidavits presented conflicting accounts. The jurors had denied the allegations under oath, and the trial judge had considered the evidence offered by both sides.

The Supreme Court held that Judge Roan had the authority to decide which account he believed. It found no abuse of that authority in his treatment of the two jurors (Frank v. State, 2).

Conclusion

The October 9, 1913, Constitution article documents Dorsey's request for additional time and the continuing effort by Frank's attorneys to challenge the jury.

Dorsey and Stephens were working in Valdosta, reviewing the trial record and preparing the State's response. Judge Roan was willing to postpone the hearing, and Rosser indicated that he would probably not object.

At the same time, the defense was still collecting affidavits against Henslee and Johenning. Additional statements had been obtained supporting the reputations of the Sparta witnesses, and there were reports of a possible accusation against a third juror.

The accusations against Henslee and Johenning remained disputed. Both jurors denied entering the trial with a fixed opinion of Frank's guilt. The defense continued to challenge their accounts, while the State gathered evidence in their support.

Judge Roan ultimately refused to overturn the verdict. The Georgia Supreme Court later upheld his ruling, finding no abuse of discretion in his handling of the conflicting affidavits.

References

The Atlanta Constitution. (Thursday, October 9, 1913). "Judge to Grant Dorsey's Request." Page 5, column 4. Conservatives’ more rigid thinking styles don’t seem to make them likelier than liberals to toe the party line | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

People who identify as liberal or conservative often appear worlds apart in how they think, but new research suggests they respond to political endorsements in much the same way. Although conservatives in the study tended to report more rigid thinking styles, liberals and conservatives were largely equally likely to shift their policy views to match the stated positions of their own party. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, indicate that at least one key psychological process behind partisan opinion operates similarly across the ideological spectrum.

The research was conducted at Michigan State University by Aymin Triki, then an undergraduate research assistant; Abigail L. Cassario, then a PhD candidate; and Mark J. Brandt, then an associate professor who ran the lab where Triki worked. Triki, the study’s lead author, is now a lab manager at the We-Search Lab at Harvard University, Cassario is a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Illinois Chicago, and Brandt is a professor of political psychology at Tilburg University.

“I’m proud of Aymin for leading this project and writing an excellent paper describing our work together,” Brandt told PsyPost.

The team aimed to explore the psychological mechanisms behind “party cues.” A party cue is a piece of information indicating whether a political party or its leaders support or oppose a specific policy. Learning that your own party supports a proposal generally makes you more likely to support it, while learning that the opposing party supports it makes you less likely to agree.

Psychologists have offered two main explanations for why party cues work. The first is that they act as a mental shortcut, allowing voters to skip the hard work of analyzing complex policies by simply trusting a group that generally shares their interests. The second explanation is that people are motivated to be good group members, and following a party endorsement is a way to express loyalty and protect their social identity.

“There is a long-running argument in political psychology about whether liberals and conservatives are characterized by different psychological processes,” Brandt explained. “That is, rather than just being different in terms of their values and policy positions, also being different in the psychological processes that drive their decisions and attitudes.”

The “asymmetry perspective” proposes that liberals and conservatives differ in deep-seated psychological ways, not just in their values. According to this view, conservative ideology tends to attract people with more rigid thinking styles, such as a stronger desire for firm, definite answers and less inclination to second-guess their first instincts. Some psychologists have argued that this profile, along with a greater emphasis on group loyalty and authority, should make conservatives more likely to rely on party cues.

Whether that rigidity shows up in how people actually handle political information is less settled. A study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that more conservative people updated their beliefs slightly less in response to new factual evidence, though the difference was very small.

An opposing “symmetry perspective” argues that liberals and conservatives process political information using the same basic psychological tools, even if they apply them toward different goals. A 2018 meta-analysis, which pooled the results of 51 experiments, concluded that liberals and conservatives were equally likely to judge identical information more favorably when it supported their side. But the authors of a 2019 commentary argued that the experiments in that analysis often relied on a narrow, unrepresentative set of policy issues, which may have hidden real differences between the two groups.

Triki, Cassario, and Brandt set out to address that criticism by testing party cue effects across a wide range of contemporary issues while also measuring participants’ thinking styles. “Prior work has examined ideological differences in party cues, but we wanted to do a more comprehensive study,” Brandt said. “In particular, we wanted to test these effects across a wide range of issues currently important in American politics. This way we can be sure that our results are not due to the specifics of a given policy and instead we can be confident in understanding how ideology and party cues intersect across a wide range of policies.”

The researchers first re-analyzed data from two earlier experiments, conducted in 2018 and 2020, that together included more than 4,300 participants and more than 80 policy issues. Both samples were recruited with the aim of resembling the U.S. population demographically. Participants rated their support for policies such as raising the minimum wage or privatizing veterans’ health care on a 1-to-7 scale. For randomly selected issues, they first learned where the two parties, or Barack Obama and Donald Trump, stood.

These analyses pointed toward symmetry. Democrats and Republicans shifted toward their own party’s position and away from the opposing party’s to essentially the same degree. On individual issues, conservatives sometimes responded more strongly and liberals sometimes did, in roughly equal numbers. A measure of liberal-conservative self-identification in one dataset also showed no difference between the groups, though that result was less conclusive.

“The overall party cue effect was reliable, but small,” Brandt noted. “It was the equivalent to .3 scale points on a 1-7 scale. However, this is just the average.”

“For some policies, the effect is much smaller (nearer to zero) and for others the effect is much larger (an effect larger than 1 scale point on a 1-7 scale),” he continued. “These larger effects would represent very large effects in the experimental literature on attitude change.”

To test whether particular thinking styles might still make a difference, the researchers ran a third experiment in August 2024 with 1,659 participants recruited through Prolific, an online research platform. This was a convenience sample, meaning participants were not selected to mirror the national population, though the researchers recruited roughly equal numbers of Republicans and Democrats. The experiment used 37 real policy issues on which Joe Biden and Donald Trump took opposing positions. For some issues, participants were told where “Democratic leaders” and “Republican leaders” stood.

The researchers measured ideology in four ways: party identification, self-placement on a liberal-to-conservative scale, right-wing authoritarianism, and progressive values. Right-wing authoritarianism reflects a tendency to defer to established authorities, value tradition, and favor harsh treatment of people who break social norms, while the progressive values scale captures an identity-focused form of left-wing ideology.

To assess thinking styles, participants completed a short reasoning test built around questions where the intuitive answer is wrong. They also completed questionnaires measuring need for closure, which is a desire for firm answers and a dislike of ambiguity, and dogmatism, which is the tendency to treat one’s own beliefs as unquestionably true.

In this sample, conservatives showed the profile that the asymmetry perspective predicts. Compared with liberals, they did worse on the reasoning test and reported a higher need for closure and more dogmatism. Conservatives, whether identified by party or self-placement, were also more responsive to party cues than liberals, as were people high in right-wing authoritarianism, while the progressive values measure showed no difference. Participants with a higher need for closure or more dogmatism also followed cues more closely, though results for the reasoning test were inconclusive.

This result conflicted with the first two analyses. When the researchers limited the analysis to nine issues that also appeared in the 2020 experiment, the difference persisted, suggesting the choice of issues did not explain it. Instead, they suspected the online convenience sample might not reflect the broader population, or that conservatives had become more responsive to party cues since the earlier data were collected.

To find out, the team ran a fourth experiment with 1,389 participants recruited using quotas to match the U.S. population on age, gender, race and ethnicity, and region. It used the same 37 issues and the same psychological measures as the third experiment, with additional attention checks.

Once again, conservatives did worse on the reasoning test and reported a higher need for closure and more dogmatism than liberals. However, the difference in how the two groups responded to party cues disappeared: whether ideology was measured by party or by liberal-conservative self-placement, liberals and conservatives were equally swayed by party endorsements. Reasoning test scores showed no link to how strongly people followed cues, and there was no evidence that need for closure or dogmatism made a difference, although those estimates were less precise. The progressive values measure gave inconclusive results.

“Notably, our core finding is that liberals and conservatives do not differ substantially,” Brandt emphasized. “In other words, the strength of party cue effects does not differ between liberals and conservatives. We do not think there is a practical difference in the size of the effect of party cues between liberals and conservatives.”

The finding that conservatives reported more rigid thinking styles is in line with a study covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found greater cognitive rigidity among Trump supporters than among supporters of liberal candidates, though that study looked at support for specific 2020 presidential candidates rather than general ideology. The overall symmetry in responses to party cues is also in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, in which liberals and conservatives alike rated political opponents as less moral than members of their own party, even after being treated fairly by them in an economic game. That study examined moral judgments rather than responses to party endorsements.

“We found ideological similarities in a specific psychological process. This is not an argument that all ideologies are the same,” Brandt cautioned.

“The liberals and conservatives in our samples differ from each other in other ways,” he said. “They support different policies. They follow different political leaders. And they cared more about different types of policies.”

The exception was right-wing authoritarianism. In both the third and fourth experiments, people scoring high on this measure followed party cues more strongly than those scoring low. The researchers considered whether this reflects a tendency to obey authority figures, but the part of the scale measuring submission to authority did not stand out from the others.

“This measure captures a type of conservatism that is particularly obedient to conservative authorities and aggressive in response to people who violate conservative norms,” Brandt observed. “Although we do not have an explanation for why this measure differed from the other measures of conservative ideology, it may be the case that there are particular types of conservatism that are more susceptible to party cues than others.”

Because the study covered so many issues, the researchers could also explore why differences between liberals and conservatives showed up on some topics but not others. “An advantage to looking at many different issues is that we can see if there are some issues with ideological differences and others without such differences,” Brandt said.

In these exploratory analyses, differences tended to emerge on issues where one group already held stronger views before seeing any cue. On those issues, the group with stronger initial views shifted less, either because they were more committed to their position or because they had little room left to move. In one dataset that also measured how aware people were of each policy, the group that was more aware of a given policy tended to shift less. The authors note that these analyses were not planned in advance and need to be replicated.

“One thing we found is that when an ideological group has a strong opinion on the issue, then they are less likely to be affected by party cues,” Brandt added. “This gives us insight into where we might expect people to be more or less likely to be affected by party cues.”

There are a few other things to keep in mind. The experiments measured how people’s stated attitudes shifted in response to party cues, but not whether those shifts translate into behaviors such as voting or protesting, where liberals and conservatives could still differ. The researchers also used accurate, real-world party positions, so the cues may often have matched what participants already believed. Future studies might examine how people respond to cues that run against their prior views, or to false information about where their party stands.

The conclusions also rest most heavily on three of the four experiments. The authors gave less weight to the third experiment because further analyses suggested that conservatives recruited through Prolific responded unusually strongly to party cues compared with liberals in that sample and with both groups in the other samples. The study also did not include every possible measure of ideology, such as left-wing authoritarianism, and all of the samples were from the United States.

“The goal of my lab is to understand how belief systems work,” said Brandt, who directs The Belief System Lab. “Major ongoing projects in the lab aim to map the structure of belief systems and to use that information to predict and understand the dynamics of political attitudes.”

U of Michigan: University of Michigan Hillel is ending its formal affiliations with student groups and national organizations engaged in Israel advocacy, lobbying or political organizing, while insisting that the policy does not represent a retreat from its support for Israel. The policy, announced by interim Executive Director Cindy Hughey in a message to students at the start of the academic year last month, is part of what Michigan Hillel described as a renewed focus on Jewish life, learning and community. University of Michigan Hillel said it will “no longer formally affiliate with national organizations or student groups whose primary work involves Israel-related advocacy, lobbying, or political organizing,” but it will continue to offer Israel education, cultural programming and discussions about Israel. Those programs, it said, should center “a range of student voices and perspectives” rather than advocacy. The change leaves Israel-related programming to Hillel staff or student clubs, rather than formal affiliations with outside advocacy groups. At the time of the decision, JStreet was the only advocacy group impacted. The decision will apply to all groups affiliated with national advocacy organizations, if they wish to affiliate with Michigan Hillel going forward, according to the group. The announcement comes weeks after Michigan Hillel pushedthe University of Michigan chapter of J Street U out of its umbrella, telling the student group that it could remain affiliated with Hillel only if it disassociated from the national organization. J Street U, the student organizing arm of the progressive Israel advocacy group J Street, has said the decision was effectively aimed at closing its chapter because of its political advocacy on Israel. The move has fueled competing interpretations of Hillel’s direction — some on campus see the new policy as an effort to further distance the organization from J Street and other progressive groups, while others argue that Michigan Hillel has already moved too far to the left by giving space to groups and perspectives they view as hostile to Israel.

text:
Happy birthday to former Booker T. Washington, Oklahoma State and NFL linebacker Jordan Brailford, born on this day in 1995 in Tulsa.

Brailford attended Tulsa's Booker T. Washington High School, where he was a first-team All-State selection as a senior in 2013 after making 105 tackles and nine sacks. He was also selected for the Semper Fidelis All-American Bowl, helping the West team win 31-24.

Brailford chose Oklahoma State over offers that included Baylor, Kansas State, Texas Tech, Tulsa and Washington State.

With the Cowboys, Brailford played in ten games as a redshirt freshman in 2015, making 23 tackles, 3.5 for loss and one sack.

A stress fracture in his leg suffered during the preseason caused him to miss the entire 2016 season. He bounced back in 2017, making 57 tackles, 11 for loss, five sacks and intercepting a pass, earning second-team All-Big 12 honors.

He followed it up by earning First-Team All-Big 12 a year later and was selected as a team captain. He made 54 tackles and had 16 tackles for loss and nine sacks, both of which led the Cowboys.

His play earned him the Cowboys' Leslie O'Neal Award, which goes to the team's outstanding defensive player.

In 2019, the Washington Redskins selected Brailford in the seventh round of the NFL Draft, but never played for Washington after being placed on injured reserve before the season's start.

In 2020, Brailford signed with the Minnesota Vikings and played in five games. In his first NFL game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, he had two tackles, forced and recovered a fumble as the Vikings won 27-24 in overtime.

He later signed with the Atlanta Falcons and the New Orleans Breakers and Memphis Showboats of the UFL.

text:
Nine formerly enslaved students refused to sing the spirituals your church still sings on Sunday morning. Those songs belonged to their mothers, they carried slavery inside them, and putting them on a stage for white audiences felt like selling the worst thing that ever happened to their family.

Then their school in Nashville ran out of money, and those songs were the only thing they owned that anybody would pay for. Every note of gospel you have ever loved came out of the yes they finally gave.

Behind a freedmen's school in Nashville, students turning over the dirt struck iron. What came up were chains and manacles, buried on the ground where Porter's Slave Yard had done its business, where people had been priced and handed across like livestock.

The students did not put the iron back.

They hauled it to a scrap dealer, sold it by weight, and spent every cent on Bibles and spelling books. That was the arithmetic they had learned to live by, that a thing used against you could still be turned into something else, provided you were willing to put your hands on it.

Five years later, nine of them were asked to do the same thing again, and not with iron.

Fisk opened on January 9, 1866, in a cluster of Union Army hospital barracks the government handed over to Northern missionaries, set in the middle of a camp of people who had walked off plantations toward the occupying army. It taught freedmen to read a ballot, write the names they had chosen for themselves, and count what they were owed.

Booker T. Washington said afterward that nobody outside those years could grasp what it looked like, that it was a whole race trying to go to school. Grown men came in from the fields at night and sat down in the same room as their own children.

By 1871 the school was five years old and nearly finished, because tuition could not be collected from families who had nothing and the American Missionary Association that sponsored it was preparing to write the place off. The barracks leaked, the floors were going, and the teachers were being paid late or not at all.

The treasurer was a white Gettysburg veteran named George Leonard White, a band sergeant on the Union march and a choirmaster before the war. He had an ear, and he had been listening to his students.

What he kept overhearing was not the parlor music he had been drilling into them.

It was the other songs, the ones they sang only among themselves, in the barracks, after dark, with the door shut. Nobody called them spirituals yet, and they were not meant for white ears.

Ella Sheppard, who would become the group's pianist and its spine, explained it later without any decoration on it. Those songs belonged to their parents, they were bound up with slavery and the dark past, and they stood for exactly the things a person was trying to leave behind.

She said they never dreamed of using them in public.

Sit with that for a second. These were young people who had spent five years learning Handel and parlor ballads for the specific purpose of proving that a Black mind could hold European music, because that was the argument being had about whether they deserved to exist in a classroom at all.

White wanted them to stop making that argument. He wanted them to take the sound of their own bondage, arrange it in four-part harmony, and sell tickets to it.

They said no for a long time.

What finally moved them was not White's persuasion. It was that the school was going under, and those songs were the only thing they owned that anybody was willing to pay money for.

On October 6, 1871, White took the last of what the treasury could spare, everything in his own pockets, and everything he could borrow, and boarded a train north with nine students. The Association had refused to fund it, his fellow teachers expected a public humiliation, and the parents did not want to let their children go.

When the missionaries told him he would shame the school, White gave them a farmer's answer, that it was root, hog, or die, and that he was depending on God and not on them. Sheppard remembered that not one of the singers owned an overcoat, and that White had an old gray shawl.

Look at who was on that train.

Ella Sheppard was twenty. Her father had bought his own freedom and then bought hers, but the owner would not sell her mother, and the two of them were kept apart for years.

Before that, when Ella was small, her mother learned that the mistress of the house had been training the child to spy on her. She carried Ella down to the river meaning to end both their lives rather than let her daughter be raised into that, and somebody caught them and stopped it.

Her father died when she was fifteen and left her with nothing, so she went out to Gallatin to teach freedmen and understood quickly that she was not qualified to be teaching anyone. She spent the next five months saving six dollars, walked into Fisk in the fall of 1868 with it in her hand, and within a year she was the school's first Black instructor.

Benjamin Holmes had taught himself to write while apprenticed to a tailor in Charleston, working out the letters off the signs and papers around the shop. He was locked in a slave pen waiting to be sold when he got hold of a newspaper and read the Emancipation Proclamation out loud to the men in there with him.

He said afterward that he had never in his life heard rejoicing like it. Holmes went on to teach freedmen in the Tennessee countryside, where one day somebody put a bullet through the window of the room he was teaching in, and he kept teaching anyway.

Maggie Porter was eighteen, and she had already lost a schoolhouse.

As a small girl in Nashville she used to sit on the curb outside a church with her feet down in the gutter, listening to the choir through the wall. Eventually she worked up the nerve to sit on the bottom step, and the choir leader came out and asked if she wanted to come inside and hear it properly.

She started school at twelve, was admitted to Fisk the year it opened, and came out of the Normal Department two years later. Her first teaching post was seventeen miles outside Nashville, and white men burned that schoolhouse to the ground over Christmas break.

She went and taught at another one.

Jennie Jackson was a washerwoman's daughter, born free and nearly dragged back into slavery by the man appointed to look after her mother's property. Isaac Dickerson had taught in country schools where threats were painted on the trees and the fence posts along the road he walked to work.

Minnie Tate was fourteen years old. These were the people being sent north to charm money out of white congregations.

They opened in Cincinnati, and the audiences were polite, and the receipts barely covered what it cost to feed and house them. Then Chicago burned.

The fire ran through that city for three days in October and the papers carried nothing else for weeks afterward. The Jubilees had just come off a concert holding real money for the first time since they left Nashville.

They had thirty dollars.

Maggie Porter's account of what happened next is one sentence long and it does not ask anybody for credit. They had thirty dollars, they sent every penny of it to Chicago, and they kept nothing at all for themselves.

Understand their exact position when they made that call. No overcoats going into an Ohio winter, no guarantee of a bed the following week, a school behind them that was days from shutting its doors, and nine people who had been somebody's property inside of a decade.

They gave it to strangers who had lost their houses.

The mayor of Chillicothe put out a public thank-you to the young colored people who had handed over an evening's proceeds to the relief fund. Two weeks after that, the same young people were in Columbus being turned out of decent rooms and made sport of in the local press.

The audiences did not come. The singers were sick, hungry and finished, and they sat down with their pastor to pray over whether to give it up and go home.

Sheppard was ill enough that a doctor told her to return to Nashville, and White would not release her. He was still writing letters promising that the most hopeful expectations would be exceeded.

By then even his own singers had stopped believing him.

On the fifteenth of November they limped into Oberlin, Ohio. The National Congregational Council was holding its annual conference there, several hundred ministers in one hall, the exact room full of the exact men whose churches could save Fisk with a single decision.

Oberlin was the first racially integrated college in the country and had trained a good share of Fisk's own faculty, so White expected a welcome. The council's answer was that his colored songsters could perform during the intermission.

Not on the program, during the break.

So the nine of them stood at the front of that hall and waited while several hundred ministers got up out of the pews, stretched their backs, and started talking among themselves about lunch. Nobody had asked for this and nobody was listening.

White got down on his hands and knees and crawled along the pew in front of them. He went singer to singer, giving each one a starting pitch under the noise of the room, quietly enough that the men standing six feet away never noticed him doing it.

Then he stood up and signaled, and they began "Steal Away."

Those were their mothers' words, used in the fields and in the woods and in the dark, where a person caught singing them could be badly hurt for it. Now nine of their children were putting them into a hall of white strangers who had turned their backs to talk about a meal.

The room stopped.

The talking died out row by row until nothing in the building was moving. The local paper wrote afterward that the singing was really fine, and that the collection basket came back full of scrip and greenbacks.

A few days later White sat down to write his brother-in-law that he had finally settled on a name for them. The Jewish year of Jubilee, when debts were canceled and the enslaved went free, was the only phrase he could find that fit what he had watched happen.

The Jubilee Singers.

On December 27 they reached Plymouth Church in Brooklyn, where Henry Ward Beecher was the most famous preacher in America. Somebody in the room that night described the girls standing in a row in waterproofs with long woolen comforters wound around their necks to protect their throats, and wrote that when the young men's voices came in underneath, he scarcely knew whether he was in his body or out of it.

Beecher instructed his wealthy congregation to give, and give generously.

After that the doors did not close again, and churches and theaters that had ignored them for two solid months suddenly wanted dates.

They sang "Go Down, Moses" for President Grant, who had no ear for music whatsoever. They sang for Mark Twain, who wrote to friends in England that nothing had moved him like it in thirty years, and that a man had to have been a slave himself to put that kind of life into a song.

At the World Peace Jubilee in Boston on July 4, 1872, they took a verse of "The Battle Hymn of the Republic" at a punishing high pitch in front of a crowd that had greeted them with hissing. By the end of the verse that same crowd was on its feet shouting for them.

Sheppard wrote that their sheet music was sold at intermission, and that before long the whole country was singing their slave songs in its own parlors. Within three months of leaving Nashville they had cleared nearly fifteen hundred dollars of the school's debts and carried home twenty thousand more, enough to buy the land the campus still sits on.

The praise came wrapped in insult the entire way.

A New York paper reviewed them by saying they carried themselves like trained animals when they performed European music and only loosened up on the plantation songs. A Baltimore ticket seller refused to sell Black customers reserved seats to their own concert.

America Robinson, who joined the company later, wrote home from a Brooklyn boarding house about a Southerner who lost his temper because the proprietor had let them stay. A Northern guest took their side, the argument ended with a chair swung at somebody's mouth, and half the boarders threatened to walk out.

That counted as a good night, because they got to keep the rooms.

In the spring of 1873 they sailed for England under the sponsorship of the Earl of Shaftesbury, and on May 6 they performed at Willis's Rooms in London. An observer wrote that they had the room won before the program was half finished.

The next morning they were taken to the Duke of Argyll's house. White was so frightened of protocol that he drilled them on curtsies on the way, convinced that one wrong form of address would cost them the patronage of half of England.

Then they were told who was coming.

Maggie Porter had spent the entire Atlantic crossing turning this over in her mind. She had grown up hearing that thousands of Black people had found liberty under that flag, and she had built the woman up in her head into something more than human.

Victoria walked in, and Porter's first reaction was disappointment.

There was no crown and there were no robes of state. The Queen was a small widow in a widow's cap, and she looked like plenty of Englishwomen Porter had already passed on the street.

Then Porter heard her speak in that deep low voice, and the disappointment turned into something else entirely. Victoria said she was delighted with their songs, and she asked them to sing "John Brown."

Think about what was standing in that room.

Nine people who had been the legal property of other people ten years earlier were being asked by the Queen of England to sing the marching song about the white man who died trying to end American slavery. Two days later the Dean of Westminster Abbey offered to pay for Isaac Dickerson's education, and Prime Minister Gladstone, himself the son of a slaveholder, had them to his house to sing for the Prince of Wales.

That is the true story, and it is better than the one you have been handed.

The version attached to nearly every Fisk Jubilee Singers post claims Victoria declared they must come from a city of music, and that this is how Nashville became Music City. There is no contemporary record of her saying any such thing, and the nickname actually traces to a radio announcer at WSM decades later.

The invented line is prettier and it costs the singers everything. It turns nine formerly enslaved young people into background scenery in a story about a city's nickname, when what actually happened is that they made a queen ask them for John Brown.

They stayed on the road for seven years.

The second tour came with a salary of five hundred dollars a year each, which was the singers' own condition for continuing, because they had worked out by then that they were professionals and had stopped agreeing to be a charity exhibit. The money did not shorten the schedule by a single night.

An advance man had a nervous breakdown. White's wife died of typhoid in Britain, and White himself collapsed with bleeding in his lungs and had to hand the choir over to Ella Sheppard.

Minnie Tate, who had left Nashville at fourteen, sang until her voice was gone, and it never came back to her. Benjamin Holmes, who had read the Proclamation out loud in a slave pen, had a cough that turned out to be tuberculosis, and he had to leave the company too.

Rival groups started touring under names like the Original Nashville Students and the Canaan Jubilee Singers, using up the audience the Jubilees had built with their own lungs. Fisk's president Erastus Cravath took over the scheduling, pushed the sick ones through Germany, and began planning the next tour after that.

Sheppard's doctor told her that if she stayed with the Jubilees, it would kill her.

She took the directorship anyway, on the single condition that the exhausted singers be allowed to go home when the bookings ran out. Cravath's response was to accuse her of desertion.

She wrote it down that night. Seven years of work, late and early, and the scar of that one word would stay on her heart as long as she lived.

At the last concert, on July 1, 1878, in Switzerland, Thomas Rutling refused to sing at all.

Five days later they sailed for home. On the ship, in a crowded cabin, they sang together one final time, and afterward a white woman followed Sheppard back to her room, threw her arms around her neck and wept that she had never imagined she could embrace a Negro before.

Sheppard wrote the whole scene into her diary, and then wrote one more line under it. She asked God to forgive them.

That is the last entry.

They had raised roughly a hundred and fifty thousand dollars for a school that had been days from closing. Jubilee Hall went up on the land they bought, six stories of Victorian Gothic brick, the first permanent building for Black higher education in the United States, and it is standing on that campus right now.

Inside it hangs the enormous painting Queen Victoria commissioned of them. Of the whole company that toured those seven years, exactly one member ever finished a Fisk degree.

Not one of them came home to live in the building they bought.

Rutling and Isaac Dickerson stayed in England for the rest of their lives rather than come back to American segregation. Maggie Porter went to Detroit, built a career of her own, and turned down every invitation Fisk sent her for more than fifty years.

She finally set foot on that campus again in 1931, an old woman near eighty, walking past the hall her voice had paid for. George White had died of consumption in 1895, and at his memorial the surviving Jubilees stood up and sang "Steal Away" one last time.

The songs went out into the world for free, and the people did not.

Every note of gospel, blues, jazz and soul that came afterward stands on nine young people who were talked into selling the only thing that had ever been theirs alone. They were charged their health, their voices, their friendships and their place at the school for doing it.

Every October sixth, Fisk students still walk out to two Nashville cemeteries and lay magnolia leaves from the campus on the graves of four of those singers. Four out of nine, one day a year.

The chains behind the barracks got weighed and sold and turned into spelling books, and nobody at the time thought twice about them. Nobody has thought much about the nine who did the same thing with their own throats, either.

Somebody should.

The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried songs that were born from suffering and transformed them into a sound that changed America forever. I share stories like theirs because the people who built our culture deserve to be remembered beyond the music they left behind.

text:
🚨💀 RFK JR: NOT A DOCTOR. THE GRAVES DO NOT REQUIRE A LICENSE. 💀🚨

Lights up on a too-expensive suit and a voice already broken by spasmodic dysphonia, the vocal cords clamping like a bad alibi. On the table: a bottle of cod liver oil, a laminated food pyramid held upside down, a 2012 deposition, a letter on Children's Health Defense letterhead addressed to a prime minister, and a brain scan nobody in the room is qualified to read. He is not a physician. He has never been a physician. The worm that once lived in his skull was not a physician either. Between them they still got the seal of the Department of Health and Human Services.

NON-DR.

Start with the diploma, since the letterhead keeps lying by omission. Juris doctor. Law school. Not medical school, not a residency, not a license to touch a patient or a population. The closest I came to a clinical note was a divorce deposition in 2012, where I explained that a doctor had looked at my scan and told me a worm got into my brain, ate a portion of it, and died. Same era: mercury poisoning. Tuna. Perch. I said the levels came back about ten times what the EPA calls safe. Memory loss. Brain fog. I offered it as evidence that my earning power was damaged. Then the earning power recovered the moment the checks needed a spokesman. Atrial fibrillation. Hepatitis C from the youthful needles. A voice that sounds like a fax machine drowning in beef tallow. None of that is training. It is a chart. The chart is not a white coat.

He taps the letter.

Samoa, 2019. Write it bigger than the American obituaries, because the American ones came later and the island ones came first. Two infants died in 2018 after nurses prepared MMR with a muscle relaxant instead of diluent. Manslaughter. The government suspended the program for months. Coverage collapsed. Into that pause walked a man with a famous last name and an anti-vaccine shop. June 2019. Independence celebrations. Photographs with the prime minister. Meetings with health officials and with local figures already casting doubt on the shots. Children's Health Defense had been on the story since the nurse error, questioning the vaccine rather than the preparation. A colleague's emails later described the trip as a mission tied to the discontinuity in vaccinations. I told the United States Senate that the visit had nothing to do with vaccines. The paper trail does not agree. Samoan officials later said the trip bolstered the credibility of the anti-vaccine voices. A nurse who worked the campaign said those voices got louder after I left.

September. The outbreak. By the end of the year: 5,707 reported cases, 1,867 hospitalizations, 83 dead. Mostly children under five. During the dying I wrote the prime minister on CHD letterhead and told him to investigate whether the outbreak was inadequate coverage or, alternatively, a defective vaccine, and I defended the so-called anti-vaccine movement. It was not a vaccine-derived strain. It was measles, in a population whose protection had been knocked down by a fatal preparation error, a government pause, and a chorus that treated the pause as proof. I did not mix the vials. I did not infect the infants. I arrived while the shield was down, lent the last name to the people telling parents the shield was the threat, and mailed a letter asking whether the vaccine might be the villain while the children were already in the ground.

He sets the letter down and picks up the bottle.

Texas, 2025. The sequel, now with federal stationery. Measles had been declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. It came back through undervaccinated pockets. I called the outbreak nothing unusual. It was the first measles deaths in the country in a decade. Unvaccinated. I went on television and talked up vitamin A and cod liver oil as if they were a side door around the shot. The department shipped vitamin A into the outbreak zone. Parents did what parents do when the man with the seal sounds sure. Covenant Children's in Lubbock started seeing the unvaccinated measles patients with the extra diagnosis: abnormal liver enzymes, yellow skin, vitamin A toxicity. High-dose vitamin A is a hospital tool for a deficient child who already has severe measles, measured by someone licensed, not a kitchen prophylactic and not a substitute for MMR. It is fat-soluble. It stays. It poisons the liver. Pediatric vitamin A exposure reports to poison centers rose. Two dead of the virus. A ward full of kids whose measles was complicated by the remedy I had just endorsed. I am not the syringe and I am not the virus. I am the lawyer who spent a decade telling people the syringe was the plot, then stood at the podium while the plot failed to show and the virus did.

He flips the pyramid so the steak drawings sit where the bread used to be.

And the poster. We took the old food pyramid and turned it over, then applauded like discovery. Protein, red meat, full-fat dairy, butter, piled at the wide end. Grains shoved to the point. Eat real food. Lovely guidance if you are twenty-four, carb-cycling, and someone else is weighing your chicken. A bad default for the country the guidelines are supposed to serve: the sixty-year-old on two jobs, the kid whose lunch is institutional, the diabetic without a private chef. Athletes already had this chart. They also had coaches. Average Americans do not get heart disease from a national shortage of ribeye. A flipped graphic does not become medicine because a man with a dead parasite in his resume prefers carnivore talking points. The people who cannot hire a dietitian inherit the poster.

Money, since none of this was a hobby. Children's Health Defense, the shop I chaired and lawyered: my compensation in the hundreds of thousands, half a million in a fat year, another three hundred thousand and change for a partial year on the way to the Cabinet. Skyhorse for the books, advances in the millions. Law firms for the contingency and referral work, including the Gardasil suits. A licensing fee for the slogan. Fear scaled. The upside-down pyramid scales. You do not need to be right. You need the last name, the nonprofit, the case list, and eventually the seal.

He lines the objects up: deposition, Samoa letter, cod liver oil, pyramid.

So the inventory. Not a doctor. A brain parasite I said ate a portion of me and died, plus mercury poisoning I blamed on fish, both offered in a divorce when a cognitive discount was useful. A nonprofit that paid me to professionalize vaccine panic. A 2019 trip to Samoa in the middle of a vaccination collapse, meetings with the doubters, a letter during the outbreak floating a defective vaccine, 83 dead, mostly small children, and a later claim to Congress that the trip had nothing to do with vaccines. An American measles outbreak in 2025 with the first deaths in ten years, unvaccinated, while I promoted vitamin A and cod liver oil and doctors logged liver toxicity in the kids whose parents listened. A national food graphic flipped toward the athlete's plate and handed to everyone else. Book deals. Legal fees. Salary. The worm finished its meal years ago. I kept the job, the voice, and the podium.

He raises the bottle. It catches the light. It does not prevent measles. It never did.

To the unsettled science. The kind that invoices.

Blackout.

text:
Thanks to SUSAN LINDAUER

I am well aware of Susan's story. She's a true American hero, and her endorsement means a lot to me. I summarized her experience with the CIA on pages 438-440 of my book, saying this:

"In 2011, a CIA asset of some nine years’ experience named Susan Lindauer came forward with insider information which clearly demonstrates the disturbing level of egregious duplicity with which the Bush White House lied the country into the war in Iraq. During the course of her duties, she also learned that there was a clear warning of the 9/11 attacks that was known to the Bush administration for at least five months. But it was ignored, presumably out of a desire to go to war.

A native of Alaska, Lindauer was from a politically prominent family; her father was once the Republican nominee for governor. She graduated from Smith College with a degree in public policy, and later attended the prestigious London School of Economics.The relevant part of her story with the CIA began in the summer of 2000. That was when she was sent by her agency handler, Richard Fuisz, to New York City to secretly contact the Iraqi delegation to the United Nations (UN). At the time, Saddam Hussein’s government was still under economic sanctions that had been imposed after the first Gulf War, because he had refused to disclose his weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) and prove that he was destroying them. Saddam said he had none and offered to let the US into Iraq to inspect. After a series of back and forth messages relayed by Lindauer to each party, a November 2000 agreement on that was in place with the administration of President Bill Clinton.

By the time the Bush administration came into office in January 2001, Lindauer was the chief back-channel CIA asset dealing with the Iraqi UN delegation. But the new administration ignored Saddam’s offer of inspections on WMD and began cranking up the pressure. In reaction, Saddam gave a little more. In February 2001, Lindauer reported to Fuisz that Saddam had further agreed to allow an FBI task force into Baghdad to investigate terrorism and arrest suspects. But again, Bush balked.

According to Lindauer, by April 2001, the CIA had learned that there was going to be an attack by Osama bin Laden on the WTC using hijacked planes. And she was instructed by Fuisz to warn the Iraqis delegation in the strongest terms possible that, if Iraq has any information about it, they had better tell her or, if there was an attack, the result would be war. She was also told to tell the Iraqis that this threat came from the highest level of the US government; the insinuation being that it came from the White House. The Iraqis told Lindauer that they had no information on that, at all.

Subsequently, by July of 2001, Saddam had weakened further. Lindauer reported to Fuisz that he had suddenly offered to sweeten the deal; he was now offering many business concessions in return for lifting the sanctions, which were crushing Iraq’s economy. He had offered to buy one million US automobiles a year for ten years and give American corporations lucrative contracts on many aspects of the Iraqi economy, like for example, telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, hospitals, etc. This could have averted war and been very beneficial to both countries, but again Bush refused the offer.

Lindauer also confirmed that in August 2001, the CIA delivered the Presidential Daily Brief (PDB) warning to Bush that bin Laden was “Determined to Strike in the US,” a report that, she said, was partially written by her handler, Richard Fuisz. A month later, the 9/11 attacks occurred exactly as had been described to her by Fuisz, five months earlier.

As the invasion of Iraq loomed clearly on the horizon, Lindauer says that she felt a personal responsibility to tell what she knew about Saddam’s peace offer in order to possibly avert that second war. To that end, she attempted to tell what she knew to several officials in Congress, including Senator John McCain and President Bush’s chief of staff, Andy Card, who happened to be her second cousin. But this resulted in quite the opposite outcome as intended. Within thirty days, she was arrested at her home by the FBI under the Patriot Act and charged with acting as an 'unregistered Iraqi agent,' for initiating those contacts ordered by Fuisz. She was also accused of 'misappropriation of government funds,' because, as the FBI indictment accused, she had spent an unauthorized $92.90 on three lunches she had with the Iraqis UN Delegation.

After her arrest, Lindauer ended up spending eight months in a military prison at Carswell Airforce Base in Fort Worth, Texas. Later, she was transferred to the Metropolitan Correctional Facility in New York, where she spent another four months. Her lawyer was finally able to convince Judge Michael Mukasey to drop all the charges against her, and she was released.

Lindauer has since intimated that her CIA contact, Fuisz, was paid $13 million out of Pentagon funds meant for Iraq to keep quiet about the July 2001 Iraqi peace offer and the April 2001 bin Laden threat against the WTC. She also says that, at one point after her detention, she was offered $10 million to keep quiet. But, standing on principal, she instead wrote a book about her experiences entitled EXTREME PREJUDICE."

Einstein's Equivalence Principle Passes a Quantum Test at Ben-Gurion University

A century after Einstein, scientists are still exploring how gravity and quantum mechanics fit together.

Now, an international study led by Prof. Ron Folman at @bengurionu has demonstrated that Einstein's equivalence principle remains consistent with quantum behavior under the conditions tested.

The experiment was conducted entirely at BGU's Atom Chip Laboratory, where Prof. Folman, doctoral student Or Dubkovsky, and the research team used an innovative quantum Galileo interferometer to observe how gravity affects atoms in quantum superposition.

The study brought together leading scientists, including Nobel laureate Sir Roger Penrose, Prof. Vlatko Vedral (University of Oxford), and Prof. Wolfgang Schleich (Ulm University), alongside collaborators from the University of Southampton, the German Aerospace Center, and the University of Texas.

Published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances, the findings offer new insights into one of physics' greatest challenges: reconciling gravity with quantum mechanics.

text:
Armenia Forms Task Force to Keep Plague Out as Russia Insists There Is No Outbreak 🇦🇲🇷🇺
➖➖➖
Armenia has created a government task force to prevent plague from entering the country from Russia, 2 days after Moscow told the World Health Organization that no plague had been found in the Irkutsk laboratory worker whose death prompted the alarm.

Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan ordered the creation of the task force, which Health Minister Anahit Avanesyan will chair. The body is advisory and coordinates preventive measures across government agencies, and Avanesyan will submit proposals to the Prime Minister on matters requiring interagency coordination. The decision was published on the https://t.co/ZpCgSMjtsd platform.

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old researcher at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died on October 2. Russia says she died of pneumonia of undetermined origin, while 197 of her contacts were placed under observation and quarantine.

Avanesyan told parliament on Wednesday that checks and temperature screening are being carried out at the border, and that Armenia is prepared to tighten controls on arriving travelers if the risk increases. "All the necessary tools are ready to be deployed depending on the level of risk," she said.

The task force will assess risks, coordinate preventive measures, verify the preparedness of relevant agencies, exchange information rapidly and prepare expert assessments. Its first meeting must take place within 10 working days of the decision entering force, and the National Center for Disease Control and Prevention provides its technical servicing.

Avanesyan said the situation is under the control of Armenian authorities. The Health Ministry's operational working group is monitoring reports from Russia, and the ministry is working with the WHO and other partners to assess whether additional precautions are needed.

"We are paying very close attention to this issue, remain vigilant and are carrying out all necessary work in a coordinated manner," she said. Armenian health authorities are also following reports of Ebola outbreaks in several African countries.

Armenia has suspended its participation in a plague conference at the Irkutsk research institute. "We are following the situation and developments, and at this moment the question of participation is suspended," ministry spokesperson Mariam Tsatryan said.

What Happened in Irkutsk
Shipilova was admitted to Shelekhov District Hospital in late September. Local outlets reported she told medical staff she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria while collecting samples.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, says extensive testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any pathogen she worked with, and that there were no incidents involving pathogens at the institute. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to rely solely on Rospotrebnadzor's statements and not to listen to rumors of an outbreak.

The 197 figure includes more than 100 people in hospital wards, with figures cited by regional and independent media ranging from 189 to 197. The Shelekhov district hospital was placed under quarantine, and restrictions were imposed on hospitals in Irkutsk including a maternity ward. More than 60 institute staff were confined inside the facility. Workers at the aluminium plant in Shelekhov were ordered to wear medical masks.

Alexei Tsydenov, head of neighboring Buryatia, said after Shipilova's death that she had died of plague, then amended it to possibly plague.

The WHO Asked Russia What Killed Her
WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said the agency picked up media reports of a suspected pneumonic plague death on October 2 and began monitoring. "A woman who worked at the laboratory in Irkutsk oblast has died, and the authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death," he said in Geneva.

The WHO asked Russia which pneumonia-causing pathogen killed her. Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Russian authorities had indicated no plague case had recently been reported in the region and that around 200 contacts had been quarantined.

Lindmeier said no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts and that none had shown symptoms. The WHO's initial risk assessment estimates the risk as moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia as a whole and very low for the WHO European region, and will be updated as more information arrives. The agency said on October 6 that it saw no signs the disease was spreading.

Russia told the WHO that day, under the International Health Regulations, that no case of plague had been recorded in Shipilova or anyone else, that around 200 contacts tested negative, and that medical monitoring of all contacts had concluded. It has not published laboratory results or named the pathogen.

Washington Offered Help and Asked for Answers
Trump said on October 5 that the United States was ready to assist Russia. "It's a rough disease. You know, that's a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army," he told reporters at the White House. "We'll help anybody that has that kind of a problem."

The following day he said a call with Putin was scheduled and would happen very soon, and that American intelligence agencies were in very deep discussions about the case. On October 7 he told reporters in the Oval Office that he does not think the plague is a bioweapon, and that Russia has said the situation is under control.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the White House had received limited information and called on Moscow for greater transparency. "Maybe there's nothing there, maybe it's bigger than we thought, we don't know," Rubio said in Iceland. A State Department official said the United States had been in touch with Russia about the incident since October 2.

Peskov said Russia welcomed the offer of assistance. Rospotrebnadzor replied that Russia was ready to assist the United States in tackling outbreaks of infectious diseases, citing measles outbreaks in 3 American states.

The US Embassy in Moscow issued a health alert on October 6 noting reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case that led to a death, along with quarantine measures and hospital closures. "U.S. citizens in the area should follow the advice of local health authorities, avoid visiting affected facilities, and seek medical attention immediately if they have fever or respiratory symptoms," it said. The alert repeated the State Department's standing instruction for Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it is closely monitoring reports of the suspected case and sees no indication of a broader threat to the United States.

What Plague Is
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals and their fleas. Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria infect the lungs and can spread between people through respiratory droplets.

The WHO says pneumonic plague can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours of onset if untreated, though common antibiotics for enterobacteria cure it when given early. The agency calls the pneumonic form of particular concern because of the high risk of triggering epidemics. Avanesyan said the risk of death is high when patients do not receive appropriate antibiotic treatment in time.

Pneumonic plague usually appears within 1 to 3 days of exposure, and contacts are monitored for 7 days.

Vasily Vlassov, a professor at the Higher School of Economics in Russia, said the measures taken appeared sensible, focusing on treating the sick, isolating them and their contacts, searching for new cases and carrying out final disinfection.
