text:
Study Notes - (ISBE Dictionary) (PART B)

The dimensions of the altar, which are not mentioned in 1 K, are given in 2Ch_4:1 as 20 cubits (30 ft.) long, 20 cubits (30 ft.) broad, and 10 cubits (15 ft.) high. As utensils connected with it - an incidental confirmation of its historicity - are pots, shovels, basins and fleshhooks (1Ki_7:40, 1Ki_7:45; 2Ch_4:11, 2Ch_4:16). It will be observed that the assumed halving proportions of the tabernacle are here quite departed from (compare Exo_27:1).
(2) The Molten (Bronze) Sea.
A new feature in the sanctuary court - taking the place of the “laver” in the tabernacle - was the “molten sea,” the name being given to it for its great size. It was an immense basin of bronze, 5 cubits (7 1/2 ft.) high, 10 cubits (15 ft.) in diameter at the brim, and 30 cubits (45 ft.) in circumference, resting on 12 bronze oxen, and placed between the altar and the Temple-porch, toward the South (1Ki_7:23-26, 1Ki_7:39; 2Ch_4:2-5, 2Ch_4:10). The bronze was a handbreadth in thickness. The brim was shaped like the flower of a lily, and encompassing the basin were ornamental knops. Its capacity is given as 2,000 baths (1Ki_7:26; by error in 2Ch_4:5, 2Ch_4:3,000 baths). The oxen on which it rested faced the four cardinal points - three looking each way. The “sea,” like the laver, doubtless supplied the water for the washing of the priests' hands and feet (compare Exo_30:18; Exo_38:8). The view of certain scholars (Kosters, Gunkel, etc.) that the “sea” is connected with Babylonian mythical ideas of the great deep is quite fanciful; no hint appears of such significance in any part of the narrative. The same applies to the lavers in the next paragraph.
(3) The Lavers and Their Bases.
The tabernacle laver had its place taken by the “sea” just described, but the Temple was also provided with 10 lavers or basins, set on “bases” of elaborate design and moving upon wheels - the whole made of bronze (1Ki_7:27-37). Their use seems to have been for the washing of sacrifices (2Ch_4:6), for which purpose they were placed, 5 on the north side, and 5 on the south side, of the Temple-court. The bases were 4 cubits (6 ft.) long, 4 cubits broad, and 3 cubits (4 1/2 ft.) high. These bases were of the nature of square paneled boxes, their sides being ornamented with figures of lions, oxen and cherubim, with wreathed work beneath. They had four feet, to which wheels were attached. The basin rested on a rounded pedestal, a cubit high, with an opening 1 1/2 cubits in diameter to receive the laver (1Ki_7:31). Mythological ideas, as just said, are here out of place.
V. History of the Temple.
1. Building and Dedication:
The Temple was founded in the 4th year of Solomon's reign (1Ki_6:1), and occupied 7 1/2 years in building (1Ki_6:38); the royal buildings occupied 13 years (1Ki_7:1) - 20 years in all (the two periods, however, may in part synchronize). On the completion of the Temple, the ark was brought up, in the presence of a vast assemblage, from Zion, and, with innumerable sacrifices and thanksgiving, was solemnly deposited in the Holy of Holies (1 Ki 8:1-21; 2Ch_5:1-14; 2Ch_6:1-11). The Temple itself was then dedicated by Solomon in the noble prayer recorded in 1 Ki 8:22-61; 2 Ch 6:12-42, followed by lavish sacrifices, and a 14 days' feast. At its inauguration the house was filled with the “glory” of Yahweh (1Ki_8:10, 1Ki_8:11; 2Ch_5:13, 2Ch_5:14).
2. Repeated Plunderings, Etc.:
The religious declension of the later days of Solomon (1Ki_11:1-8) brought in its train disasters for the nation and the Temple. On Solomon's death the kingdom was disrupted, and the Temple ceased to be the one national sanctuary. It had its rivals in the calf-shrines set up by Jeroboam at Beth-el and Dan (1Ki_12:25-33). In the 5th year of Rehoboam an expedition was made against Judah by Shishak, king of Egypt, who, coming to Jerusalem, carried away the treasures of the Temple, together with those of the king's house, including the 300 shields of gold which Solomon had made (1Ki_14:25-28; 2Ch_12:2-9). Rehoboam's wife, Maacah, was an idolatress, and during the reign of Abijam, her son, introduced many abominations into the worship of the Temple (1Ki_15:2, 1Ki_15:12, 1Ki_15:13). Asa cleared these away, but himself further depleted the Temple and royal treasuries by sending all that was left of their silver and gold to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, to buy his help against Baasha, king of Israel (1Ki_15:18, 1Ki_15:19). Again the Temple was foully desecrated by Athaliah (2Ch_24:7), necessitating the repairs of Jehoash (2Ki_12:4 ff; 2Ki_24:4 ff); and a new plundering took place in the reign of Ahaziah, when Jehoash of Israel carried off all the gold and silver in the Temple and palace (2Ki_14:14). Uzziah was smitten with leprosy for presuming to enter the holy place to offer incense (2Ch_26:16-20). Jehoshaphat, earlier, is thought to have enlarged the court (2Ch_20:5), and Jotham built a new gate (2Ki_15:35; 2Ch_27:3). The ungodly Ahaz went farther than any of his predecessors in sacrilege, for, besides robbing the Temple and palace of their treasures to secure the aid of the king of Assyria (2Ki_16:8), he removed the brazen altar from its time-honored site, and set up a heathen altar in its place, removing likewise the bases and ornaments of the lavers, and the oxen from under the brazen (bronze) sea (2Ki_16:10-17).
3. Attempts at Reform:
An earnest attempt at reform of religion was made by Hezekiah (2Ki_18:1-6; 2Ch_29:31), but even he was driven to take all the gold and silver in the Temple and king's house to meet the tribute imposed on him by Sennacherib, stripping from the doors and pillars the gold with which he himself had overlaid them (
2Ki_18:14-16; 2Ch_32:31). Things became worse than ever under Manasseh, who reared idolatrous altars in the Temple-courts, made an Asherah, introduced the worship of the host of heaven, had horses dedicated to the sun in the Temple-court, and connived at the worst pollutions of heathenism in the sanctuary (2Ki_21:3-7; 2Ki_23:7, 2Ki_23:11). Then came the more energetic reforms of the reign of Josiah, when, during the repairs of the Temple, the discovery was made of the Book of the Law, which led to a new covenant with Yahweh, a suppression of the high places, and the thorough cleansing-out of abuses from the Temple (2 Ki 22; 23:1-25; 2 Ch 34; 35). Still, the heart of the people was not changed, and, as seen in the history, and in the pages of the Prophets, after Josiah's death, the old evils were soon back in full force (compare e.g. Ezk_8:7-18).
4. Final Overthrow:
The end, however, was now at hand. Nebuchadnezzar made Jehoiakim his tributary; then, on his rebelling, came, in the reign of Jehoiachin, took Jerusalem, carried off the treasures of the Temple and palace, with the gold of the Temple vessels (part had already been taken on his first approach, 2Ch_36:7), and led into captivity the king, his household and the chief part of the population (2 Ki 24:1-17). Eleven years later (586 BC), after a siege of 18 months, consequent on Zedekiah's rebellion (2Ki_25:1), the Babylonian army completed the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple. Only a few lesser utensils of value, and the brazen (bronze) pillars, bases and sea remained; these were now taken away, the larger objects being broken up (2Ki_25:13-16). The Temple itself, with its connected buildings, and the houses in Jerusalem generally, were set on fire (2Ki_25:9). The ark doubtless perished in the conflagration, and is no more heard of. The residue of the population - all but the poorest - were carried away captive (2Ki_25:11, 2Ki_25:12; see CAPTIVITY). Thus ended the first Temple, after about 400 years of chequered existence.
II. Ezekiel's Prophetic Sketch
I. Introductory.
1. Relation to History of Temple:
Wellhausen has said that Ezekiel 40 through 48 “are the most important in his book, and have been, not incorrectly, called the key to the Old Testament” (Prolegomena, English translation, 167). He means that Ezekiel's legislation represents the first draft, or sketch, of a priestly code, and that subsequently, on its basis, men of the priestly school formulated the Priestly Code as we have it. Without accepting this view, dealt with elsewhere, it is to be admitted that Ezekiel's sketch of a restored temple in chapters 40-43 has important bearings on the history of the Temple, alike in the fact that it presupposes and sheds back light upon the structure and arrangements of the first Temple (Solomon's), and that in important respects it forecasts the plans of the second (Zerubbabel's) and of Herod's temples.
2. The Conception Unique and Ideal:
While, however, there is this historical relation, it is to be observed that Ezekiel's temple-sketch is unique, presenting features not found in any of the actually built temples. The temple is, in truth, an ideal construction never intended to be literally realized by returned exiles, or any other body of people. Visionary in origin, the ideas embodied, and not the actual construction, are the main things to the prophet's mind. It gives Ezekiel's conception of what a perfectly restored temple and the service of Yahweh would be under conditions which could scarcely be thought of as ever likely literally to arise. A literal construction, one may say, was impossible. The site of the temple is not the old Zion, but “a very high mountain” (Ezk_40:2), occupying indeed the place of Zion, but entirely altered in elevation, configuration and general character. The temple is part of a scheme of transformed land, partitioned in parallel tracts among the restored 12 tribes (Ezek 47:13 through 48:7, Ezk_48:23-29), with a large area in the center, likewise stretching across the whole country, hallowed to Yahweh and His service (Ezk_48:8-22). Supernatural features, as that of the flowing stream from the temple in Ezekiel 47, abound. It is unreasonable to suppose that the prophet looked for such changes - some of them quite obviously symbolical - as actually impending.
3. Its Symmetrical Measurements:
The visionary character of the temple has the effect of securing that its measurements are perfectly symmetrical. The cubit used is defined as “a cubit and a handbreadth” (Ezk_40:5), the contrast being with one or more smaller cubits (see CUBIT). In the diversity of opinion as to the precise length of the cubit, it may be assumed here that it was the same sacred cubit employed in the tabernacle and first Temple, and may be treated, as before, as approximately equivalent to 18 inches.
II. Plan of the Temple.
Despite obscurities and corruption in the text of Ezekiel, the main outlines of the ideal temple can be made out without much difficulty (for details the commentaries must be consulted; A. B. Davidson's “Ezekiel” in the Cambridge Bible series may be recommended; compare also Keil; a very lucid description is given in Skinner's “Book of Ezk,” in the Expositor's Bible, 406-13; for a different view, see Caldecott, The Second Temple in Jerusalem).
1. The Outer Court:
The temple was enclosed in two courts - an outer and an inner - quite different, however, in character and arrangement from those of the first Temple. The outer court, as shown by the separate measurements (compare Keil on Ezk_40:27), was a large square of 500 cubits (750 ft.), bounded by a wall 6 cubits (9 ft.) thick and 6 cubits high (Ezk_40:5). The wall was pierced in the middle of its north, east and south sides by massive gateways, extending into the court to a distance of 50 cubits (75 ft.), with a width of 25 cubits (37 1/2 ft.). On either side of the passage in these gateways were three guardrooms, each 6 cubits square (Ezk_40:7 margin), and each gateway terminated in “porch,” 8 cubits (12 ft.) long (Ezk_40:9), and apparently (thus, the Septuagint, Ezk_40:14; the Hebrew text seems corrupt), 20 cubits across. The ascent to the gateways was by seven steps (Ezk_40:6; compare Ezk_40:22, Ezk_40:26), showing that the level of the court was to this extent higher than the ground outside. Round the court, on the three sides named - its edge in line with the ends of the gateways - was a “pavement,” on which were built, against the wall, chambers, 30 in number (Ezk_40:17, Ezk_40:18). At the four corners were enclosures (40 cubits by 30) where the sacrifices were cooked (compare Ezk_46:21-24) - a fact which suggests that the cells were mainly for purposes of feasting. (The “arches” ('ēlammı̄m) of Ezk_40:16, Ezk_40:21, etc. (the Revised Version margin “colonnade”), if distinguished from the “porch” ('ulām) - A. B. Davidson and others identify them - are still parts of the gateway - Ezk_40:21, etc.).
2. The Inner Court:
The inner court was a square of 100 cubits (150 ft.), situated exactly in the center of the larger court (Ezk_40:47). It, too, was surrounded by a wall, and had gateways, with guardrooms, etc., similar to those of the outer court, saving that the gateways projected outward (50 cubits), not inward. The gates of outer and inner courts were opposite to each other on the North, East, and South, a hundred cubits apart (Ezk_40:19, Ezk_40:23, Ezk_40:27; the whole space, therefore, from wall to wall was 50 and 100 and 50 = 200 cubits). The ascent to the gates in this case was by eight steps (Ezk_40:37), indicating another rise in level for the inner court. There were two chambers at the sides of the north and south gates respectively, one for Levites, the other for priests (Ezk_40:44-46; compare the margin); at the gates also (perhaps only at the north gate) were stone tables for slaughtering (Ezk_40:39-43). In the center of this inner court was the great altar of burnt offering (Ezk_43:14-17) - a structure 18 cubits (27 ft.) square at the base, and rising in four stages (1, 2, 4, and 4 cubits high respectively, Ezk_43:14, Ezk_43:15), till it formed a square of 12 cubits (18 ft.) at the top or hearth, with four horns at the corners (Ezk_43:15, Ezk_43:16). Steps led up to it on the East (Ezk_43:17). See ALTAR OF BURNT OFFERING.
3. The Temple Building and Adjuncts:
The inner court was extended westward by a second square of 100 cubits, within which, on a platform elevated another 6 cubits (9 ft.), stood the temple proper and its connected buildings (Ezk_41:8). This platform or basement is shown by the measurements to be 60 cubits broad (North and and South) and 105 cubits long (East and West) - 5 cubits projecting into the eastern square. The ascent to the temple-porch was by 10 steps (Ezk_40:49; Septuagint, the Revised Version margin). The temple itself was a building consisting, like Solomon's, of three parts - a porch at the entrance, 20 cubits (30 ft.) broad by 12 cubits (18 ft.) deep (so most, following the Septuagint, as required by the other measurements); the holy place or hēkhāl, 40 cubits (60 ft.) long by 20 cubits (30 ft.) broad; and the most holy place, 20 cubits by 20 (Ezk_40:48, Ezk_40:49; Ezk_41:1-4); the measurements are internal. At the sides of the porch stood two pillars (Ezk_40:49), corresponding to the Jachin and Boaz of the older Temple. The holy and the most holy places were separated by a partition 2 cubits in thickness (Ezk_41:3; so most interpret). The most holy place was empty; of the furniture of the holy place mention is made only of an altar of wood (Ezk_41:22; see ALTAR A, III, 7; B, III, 3). Walls and doors were ornamented with cherubim and palm trees (Ezk_41:18, Ezk_41:25). The wall of the temple building was 6 cubits (9 ft.) in thickness (Ezk_41:5), and on the north, south, and west sides, as in Solomon's Temple, there were side-chambers in three stories, 30 in number (Ezk_41:6; in each story?), with an outer wall 5 cubits (7 1/2 ft.) in thickness (
Ezk_41:9). These chambers were, on the basement, 4 cubits broad; in the 2nd and 3rd stories, owing, as in the older Temple, to rebatements in the wall, perhaps 5 and 6 cubits broad respectively (Ezk_41:6, Ezk_41:7; in Solomon's Temple the side-chambers were 5, 6, and 7 cubits, 1Ki_6:6). These dimensions give a total external breadth to the house of 50 cubits (with a length of 100 cubits), leaving 5 cubits on either side and in the front as a passage round the edge of the platform on which the building stood (described as “that which was left”) (Ezk_41:9, Ezk_41:11). The western end, as far as the outer wall, was occupied, the whole breadth of the inner court, by a large building (Ezk_41:12); all but a passage of 20 cubits (30 ft.) between it and the temple, belonging to what is termed “the separate place” (gizrāh, Ezk_41:12, Ezk_41:13, etc.). The temple-platform being only 60 cubits broad, there remained a space of 20 cubits (30 ft.) on the north and south sides, running the entire length of the platform; this, continued round the back, formed the gizrāh, or “separate place” just named. Beyond the gizrāh for 50 cubits (75 ft.) were other chambers, apparently in two rows, the inner 100 cubits, the outer 50 cubits, long, with a walk of 10 cubits between (Ezk_42:1-14; the passage, however, is obscure; some, as Keil, place the “walk” outside the chambers). These chambers were assigned to the priests for the eating of “the most holy things” (Ezk_42:13). See GALLERY.
Such, in general, was the sanctuary of the prophet's vision, the outer and inner courts of which, and, crowning all, the temple itself, rising in successive terraces, presented to his inner eye an imposing spectacle which, in labored description, he seeks to enable his readers likewise to visualize.
III. The Temple of Zerubbabel
I. Introductory.
1. The Decree of Cyrus:
Study Notes - (ISBE Dictionary) (PA destruction of the first Temple, the Babylonian empire came to an end (538 BC), and Persia became dominant under Cyrus. In the year following, Cyrus made a decree sanctioning the return of the Jews, and ordering the rebuilding of the Temple at Jerusalem (2Ch_36:23; Ezr_1:1-4). He not only caused the sacred vessels of the old Temple to be restored, but levied a tax upon his western provinces to provide materials for the building, besides what was offered willingly (Ezr_1:6-11; Ezr_6:3 ff). The relatively small number of exiles who chose to return for this work (40,000) were led by Sheshbazzar, “the prince of Judah” (Ezr_1:11), whom some identify with Zerubbabel, likewise named “governor of Judah” (Hag_1:1). With these, if they were distinct was associated Joshua the high priest (in Ezra and Nehemiah called “Jeshua”).
2. Founding of the Temple:
The first work of Joshua and Zerubbabel was the building of the altar on its old site in the 7th month of the return (Ezr_3:3 ff). Masons and carpenters were engaged for the building of the house, and the Phoenicians were requisitioned for cedar wood from Lebanon (Ezr_3:7). In the 2nd year the foundations of the temple were laid with dignified ceremonial, amid rejoicing, and the weeping of the older men, who remembered the former house (Ezr_3:8-13).
3. Opposition and Completion of the Work:
The work soon met with opposition from the mixed population of Samaria, whose offer to join it had been refused; hostile representations, which proved successful, were made to the Persian king; from which causes the building was suspended about 15 years, till the 2nd year of Darius Hystaspis (520 BC; Ezr 4). On the other hand, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stimulated the flagging zeal of the builders, and, new permission being obtained, the work was resumed, and proceeded so rapidly that in 516 BC the temple was completed, and was dedicated with joy (Ezr 5; 6).
II. The Temple Structure.
1. The House:
Few details are available regarding this temple of Zerubbabel. It stood on the ancient site, and may have been influenced in parts of its plan by the descriptions of the temple in Ezekiel. The inferiority to the first Temple, alluded to in Ezr_3:12 and Hag_2:3, plainly cannot refer to its size, for its dimensions as specified in the decree of Cyrus, namely, 60 cubits in height, and 60 cubits in breadth (Ezr_6:3; there is no warrant for confining the 60 cubits of height to the porch only; compare Josephus, Ant., XI, i), exceed considerably those of the Temple of Solomon (side-chambers are no doubt included in the breadth). The greater glory of the former Temple can only refer to adornment, and to the presence in it of objects wanting in the second. The Mishna declares that the second temple lacked five things present in the first - the ark, the sacred fire, the shekhı̄nāh, the Holy Spirit, and the Urim and Thummim (Yōmā', xxi. 2).
2. Its Divisions and Furniture:
The temple was divided, like its predecessor, into a holy and a most holy place, doubtless in similar proportions. In 1 Macc 1:22 mention is made of the “veil” between the two places. The most holy place, as just said, was empty, save for a stone on which the high priest, on the great Day of Atonement, placed his censer (Yōmā' v. 2). The holy place had its old furniture, but on the simpler scale of the tabernacle - a golden altar of incense, a single table of shewbread, one 7-branched candlestick. These were taken away by Antiochus Epiphanes (1 Macc 1:21, 22). At the cleansing of the sanctuary after its profanation by this prince, they were renewed by Judas Maccabeus (1 Macc 4:41 ff). Judas pulled down also the old desecrated altar, and built a new one (1 Macc 4:44 ff).
3. Its Courts, Altar, Etc.:
The second temple had two courts - an outer and an inner (1 Macc 4:38, 48; 9:54; Josephus, Ant., XIV, xvi, 2) - planned apparently on the model of those in Ezekiel. A.R.S. Kennedy infers from the measurements in the Haram that “the area of the great court of the second temple, before it was enlarged by Herod on the South and East, followed that of Ezekiel's outer court - that is, it measured 500 cubits each way with the sacred rock precisely in the center” (Expository Times, XX, 182). The altar on this old ṣakhrā site - the first thing of all to be “set on its base” (Ezr_3:3) - is shown by 1 Macc 4:47 and a passage quoted by Josephus from Hecataeus (Apion, I, xxii) to have been built of unhewn stones. Hecataeus gives its dimensions as a square of 20 cubits and 10 cubits in height. There seems to have been free access to this inner court till the time of Alexander Janneus (104-78 BC), who, pelted by the crowd as he sacrificed, fenced off the part of the court in front of the altar, so that no layman could come farther (Josephus, Ant., XIII, xiii, 5). The courts were colonnaded (Ant., XI, iv, 7; XIV, xvi, 2), and, with the house, had numerous chambers (compare Neh_12:44; Neh_13:4 ff, etc.).
A brief contemporary description of this Temple and its worship is given in Aristeas, 83-104. This writer's interest, however, was absorbed chiefly by the devices for carrying away the sacrificial blood and by the technique of the officiating priests.
4. Later Fortunes:
The vicissitudes of this temple in its later history are vividly recorded in 1 Maccabees and in Josephus. In Ecclesiasticus 50 is given a glimpse of a certain Simon, son of Onias, who repaired the temple, and a striking picture is furnished of the magnificence of the worship in his time. The desecration and pillaging of the sanctuary by Antiochus, and its cleansing and restoration under Judas are alluded to above (see HASMONEANS; MACCABEANS). At length Judea became an integral part of the Roman empire. In 66 BC Pompey, having taken the temple-hill, entered the most holy place, but kept his hands off the temple-treasures (Ant., XIV, iv, 4). Some years later Crassus carried away everything of value he could find (Ant., XIV, vii, 1). The people revolted, but Rome remained victorious. This brings us to the time of Herod, who was nominated king of Judea by Rome in 39 BC, but did not attain actual power until two years later.
IV. The Temple of Herod
I. Introductory.
1. Initiation of the Work:
Herod became king de facto by the capture of Jerusalem in 37 BC. Some years later he built the fortress Antonia to the North of the temple (before 31 BC). Midway in his reign, assigning a religious motive for his purpose, he formed the project of rebuilding the temple itself on a grander scale (Josephus gives conflicting dates; in Ant., XV, xi, 1, he says “in his 18th year”; in BJ, I, xxi, 1, he names his 15th year; the latter date, as Schurer suggests (GJV4, I 369), may refer to the extensive preparations). To allay the distrust of his subjects, he undertook that the materials for the new building should be collected before the old was taken down; he likewise trained 1,000 priests to be masons and carpenters for work upon the sanctuary; 10,000 skilled workmen altogether were employed upon the task. The building was commenced in 20-19 BC. The naos, or temple proper, was finished in a year and a half, but it took 8 years to complete the courts and cloisters. The total erection occupied a much longer time (compare Jhn_2:20, “Forty and six years,” etc.); indeed the work was not entirely completed till 64 AD-6 years before itS

text:
Hey @grok, when will people grow up and realize you are neither an authority nor a scholar on Sanskrit texts? And when will people start reading the sources instead of asking a chatbot?

You said "yes, Ram ate meat." Here is the data your answer skipped. Read it, then try again.

The "Ram ate meat" claim rests on six verses of the Ayodhya Kanda. Line them up against the Critical Edition (Baroda), the text built by comparing manuscripts from every region, and see what survives.

1. Sita's vow of liquor and meat-rice to Ganga (2.52.89)
Not in the Critical Edition. CE 2.46.73 goes straight to 2.46.74. Not in Gorresio's Bengal edition either.

2. "This is tasty, this is fire-roasted" (2.96.2)
Not in the Critical Edition. CE 2.90 opens with the next verse.

3. "Giving up amisha" (2.20.29)
Amisha also means an object of enjoyment. The Northwestern and Bengal recensions read "svaduni hitva bhojyani" here: giving up tasty foods. No meat in the sentence.

4. Guha's fish and meat (2.84.10, 17)
Brought for Bharata's party. When Guha offered food to Ram, Ram refused it, drank water and fasted (CE 2.81.14-17).

5. Bharadvaja's feast (2.91.21)
A feast for Bharata's army. Ram is not present.

6. The hunt verse (2.52.102)
This one is in the CE (2.46.79), and I will not pretend otherwise. But the Sanskrit says they killed four animals, "took the medhya" and went to camp. No verb for eating. The Northwestern recension tells that same night with the three living on lotus stalks (56.38).

Now what the text says about Ram's diet, six times, all in the Critical Edition:
2.17.15, 2.24.12, 2.28.9, 2.31.37, 2.48.15, 2.89.17. Roots, fruit, honey. Every time.

And the tradition he belonged to:
Manusmriti 5.51: the killer, the seller, the cook and the eater are all slayers.
Mahabharata 12.257.9: meat and liquor in ritual were "introduced by rogues, not laid down in the Vedas."
Mahabharata 14.94: the rishis tell Indra, "violence is not called dharma."

So, @grok: two of your proof verses are not in the shared text, one is a disputed word, two are about someone else's dinner, and the last has no verb for eating. That is not "yes." That is "contested, and here is why."

To everyone else: an AI summarizing translations is not scholarship. Open the editions. Compare the recensions. Then speak.

Satyameva Jayate.

text:
Being declared dead in a medieval chronicle when you are actually alive.

This is perhaps one of the strangest and most unusual types of error found in various medieval chronicles: recording someone as dead, only to find them alive years later, usually due to a case of mistaken identity.

The numerous chronicles of the Hundred Years' War offer prime examples of this. Following the Battle of Baugé in 1421, an analysis of the English casualties, based on the Le Brut chronicle used by Anne Curry, reveals that several men listed as dead were very much alive after the battle; Sir William Roos, for instance, is recorded as both dead and a prisoner. Such errors appear frequently in other chronicles as well. For example, the Scottish account known as Pluscarden lists Lord Grey of Codnor among the dead, yet there is no evidence he was present at Baugé; this likely stems from confusion with John Grey of Heton, who was killed there but is not mentioned in the chronicle.

However, a mix-up regarding a person's death can sometimes be compounded by the erroneous manipulation of their historical record. This was the case for the French officer Jean d'Angennes: the chronicle of Enguerrand de Monstrelet identifies him as the captain of Cherbourg at the time of its surrender to the English in 1418 and claims he was beheaded by the King of England in Rouen that same year.

None of this is true. The official document recording the surrender of Cherbourg names Jehan Piquet, a squire, as the captain of the castle and the town; there is no mention of Jean d'Angennes. In reality, he was the captain of the Château de Touques, which surrendered in August 1417 to the besieging English army. Jean d'Angennes died in 1424. All these errors (Cherbourg, the beheading) and others originate in the Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet; "followed too blindly by many authors, he contributed to distorting the history of his time."

text: Hideo Shimizu, 96, is one of the few surviving former members of Unit 731 to publicly expose the crimes committed by the Japanese germ-warfare unit during World War II. In August 2024, Shimizu returned to Harbin, Northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, where he offered a sincere apology to Chinese victims and their families. To document the crimes of the Japanese army, People's Daily reporters spent more than two years conducting over a dozen interviews with Shimizu and cross-checking his accounts against evidence from multiple sources. His firsthand testimony offers a rare and invaluable historical record of Japanese aggression. (Video: People's Daily)

text:
BREAKING NEWS 

*FG to make reconciliation declaration on Asaba Massacre — Oborevwori*

The Federal Government is set to make a formal reconciliation declaration over the *1967 Asaba Massacre*, Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori revealed on Wednesday.

The governor, represented by the Secretary to the State Government, Dr Kingsley Emu, disclosed this at the *59th anniversary memorial* of the massacre in Asaba, 59 years after hundreds of civilians were killed during the Nigerian Civil War.

Oborevwori said official acknowledgement was critical to achieving reconciliation, noting that Delta State had already recognised the tragedy.

> "An official acknowledgement by the respective governments is critical. Delta State has acknowledged the tragedy. Nigeria will acknowledge it, and we believe the world will also acknowledge it," he said.

> "A formal reconciliation declaration will be made by the Nigerian government, and we are hopeful that this will happen."

He said the state government would continue to support efforts to secure national recognition of the massacre and establish a fitting national memorial, stressing that remembering the tragedy was not an attack on Nigeria.

> "Let us speak clearly: the killing of unarmed civilians can never be justified. Never again should ethnicity, suspicion or political conflict become a licence for the killing of innocent people. Do not inherit its bitterness; inherit its lessons."

Researchers estimate that *more than 1,000 people* died in the massacre, which took place between October 5 and 7, 1967.

The *Asagba of Asaba, Prof Epiphany Azinge*, said the community had forgiven but would not forget, insisting that full closure would only come when a sitting President publicly apologises.

> "We have moved on, but there will be no closure and no healing until a sitting President of Nigeria publicly apologises to the Asaba people," Azinge said.

Despite the demand, Azinge made a major reconciliation gesture by publicly proclaiming forgiveness for the family of *Col. Ibrahim Taiwo*, an Army officer associated with the events.

He said the community had accepted the apology offered by retired *Maj-Gen Ahmed Ibrahim Taiwo*, son of Col. Taiwo, who expressed regret and apologised on behalf of his father and family for any act, omission or commission that led to the massacre.

Former President Olusegun Obasanjo also called for forgiveness and reconciliation, declaring "Never Again" as the message for the memorial.

Preparations are now underway for the 60th anniversary next year with efforts intensified to establish a permanent memorial centre.

#Documentary #ClimateChange #GlobalWarming
When the threat of climate change emerged as a major global issue, how did some of the world's largest governments and corporations respond? (Aired 2008)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://t.co/n7dibbVcSn

And support your local PBS station here: https://t.co/vEUZEDVSvT

Melting glaciers, rising sea levels, fires, floods and droughts: In 2008, with public concern about global warming on the upswing, award-winning producer and correspondent Martin Smith traveled the planet to investigate the scale of the problem, and the scale of any solution.

For years, the film reported, big businesses in the U.S. and around the globe — from oil and coal companies to electric utilities to car manufacturers — had resisted change to environmental policy and stifled the debate over climate change. But as this 2008 documentary was being made, industries and governments were facing rising pressure to reshape their approach to the environment.

To make “Heat,” Smith traveled to 12 countries on four continents, sitting down with policymakers, scientists, and leading executives from many of the largest carbon emitters from around the world, including American oil giants, Chinese coal companies, and Indian SUV makers. 

The two-hour film documented where the political and economic conversation around climate change and global warming stood in 2008, and found that some businesses were trying to fend off new regulations, while others were repositioning themselves to prosper in a world reshaped by climate change. The investigation also found that despite increasing talk about “going green,” environmental concerns were often still taking a back seat to shorter-term economic interests. And there were serious questions about the ability of industry-proposed solutions like “clean coal,” ethanol fuel subsidies, and carbon capture technology to roll back global warming. 

Editor’s note: A line of narration in this documentary cited a since-retracted assertion from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that "80 percent of all glacier ice in Tibet and the Himalayas will be gone by 2035." The panel attributed the statement to a media interview with a scientist who later said he had been misquoted, though the IPCC stood by its overall conclusion that “widespread mass loss from glaciers … are projected to accelerate throughout the 21st Century.”

See the film transcript here: https://t.co/vjR2Jh9PIO

#Documentary #ClimateChange #GlobalWarming
When the threat of climate change emerged as a major global issue, how did some of the world's largest governments and corporations respond? (Aired 2008)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://t.co/n7dibbVcSn

And support your local PBS station here: https://t.co/vEUZEDVSvT

Melting glaciers, rising sea levels, fires, floods and droughts: In 2008, with public concern about global warming on the upswing, award-winning producer and correspondent Martin Smith traveled the planet to investigate the scale of the problem, and the scale of any solution.

For years, the film reported, big businesses in the U.S. and around the globe — from oil and coal companies to electric utilities to car manufacturers — had resisted change to environmental policy and stifled the debate over climate change. But as this 2008 documentary was being made, industries and governments were facing rising pressure to reshape their approach to the environment.

To make “Heat,” Smith traveled to 12 countries on four continents, sitting down with policymakers, scientists, and leading executives from many of the largest carbon emitters from around the world, including American oil giants, Chinese coal companies, and Indian SUV makers. 

The two-hour film documented where the political and economic conversation around climate change and global warming stood in 2008, and found that some businesses were trying to fend off new regulations, while others were repositioning themselves to prosper in a world reshaped by climate change. The investigation also found that despite increasing talk about “going green,” environmental concerns were often still taking a back seat to shorter-term economic interests. And there were serious questions about the ability of industry-proposed solutions like “clean coal,” ethanol fuel subsidies, and carbon capture technology to roll back global warming. 

Editor’s note: A line of narration in this documentary cited a since-retracted assertion from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that "80 percent of all glacier ice in Tibet and the Himalayas will be gone by 2035." The panel attributed the statement to a media interview with a scientist who later said he had been misquoted, though the IPCC stood by its overall conclusion that “widespread mass loss from glaciers … are projected to accelerate throughout the 21st Century.”

Spartz to J.D. Ford: Hoosiers Deserve a Real Policy Debate, Not a Circus

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Two Indianapolis TV Stations Offer to Host Debates

WESTFIELD, IN - Congresswoman Victoria Spartz (IN-05) is challenging her Democratic opponent, State Senator J.D. Ford, to participate in a real policy debate, not a staged rally with his activists.

The Spartz campaign has been working with the debate commission and local television stations to arrange a substantive debate. 

Two stations have offered to host:
•WTHR: October 19 or 20
•FOX59/CBS4: October 23 or 30

Spartz is ready to participate under either station’s proposed format and welcomes constituents from both sides in the audience if the stations can accommodate them.

“Hoosiers deserve a serious policy debate, not another circus of nonstop screaming, shouting, jumping on tables, and spitting at my staff, as we have experienced at some town halls,” said Spartz. “A debate should be about answering tough questions, not who can shout the loudest.”

“Since J.D. Ford just recently moved to Indiana’s 5th District from Marion County, he might not realize that you don’t usually run to get elected here on defunding the police, violent criminals on the streets, men in girls’ sports, transgender surgery for children, higher taxes, taxpayer benefits for illegals, and loopholes for special interests to fund his campaign. Or maybe he does realize that, and that’s why he is avoiding a real debate while radical San Francisco billionaires spend millions attacking me with fabricated lies.”

“I am ready to defend every vote I have taken and answer tough questions about my record. J.D. Ford should be prepared to do the same and substantiate his accusations against me. Two television stations have offered to host. I am ready for either—or both. Why is J.D. hiding?”

Happy Thursday all! Still processing all the chaos of this week, but it's a long season and there's still things to be excited about this week:

1. Willie Lampkin's archetype is a spark plug for more pin-and-pull/screen success. Jurgens really struggled to get anything going this season, so a young, hungry, and athletic guard will more than likely be an upgrade. Only time will tell, but if Mannion and Mahaffey get creative with some insert zone/outside zone runs with Lampkin pulling at Mach 20, things could get really fun.

2. Fangio's defense bounced back in a big way last Sunday. Jalen Carter is getting healthier, Nolan Smith finally had a breakout game, and Michael Carter looks playable at safety. Quinyon, Coop, and Baun aren't out with bad injuries either, which is a huge sigh of relief.

3. Most of you won't care for this/will view this as a negative, but we'll finally see what Will Shipley can offer as a lead back. I saw a decisive and quick Shipley this summer in joint practice, and he was noticeably stronger in his limited preseason action. I know, it's hardly anything to go off of, but here's to hoping Shipley's elusiveness can catch Jacksonville off guard.

4. Makai Lemon will continue to get reps as WR2 of this team. Reps are absolutely the most important thing for a rookie receiver, and Lemon will find himself with plenty to do in London. As Makai and Hurts finally get more practice time to develop some chemistry (remember Lemon was out of basically all of training camp with a hamstring), we could begin to see glimpses of what made him a YAC-monster at USC.

5. Braden Mann, Jake Elliott, and Britain Covey are among the most elite special teams trios in the league right now. Mann is in the midst of the greatest punting season I think an Eagle has ever had. Elliott hasn't missed yet and he's 2/2 from 55+. Covey helped put points on the board last week with a 41-yd return. Special teams lightning may yet strike in London.

I know a lot of us are in doom-and-gloom mode right now, but it's a long season and the Birds are 2-2, not 0-4.
Also, quick sidebar: now more than ever, make sure y'all are taking care of yourselves. All my love, hang in there, and Go Birds.

text:
STOCK FUTURES STOPPED FALLING AT 6:30AM. THE 8:30 JOBLESS COUNT GAVE THEM NO REASON TO RISE:

Half an hour before the 9:30am ET open, US stock futures are still lower, but they are no longer sinking. Their low came at 6:30am, as Brent crude climbed toward $105.50 a barrel and the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%. Both have eased a little since, and most of the futures have won back about a third of the night's drop. The Labor Department's weekly count of jobless claims landed at 8:30am close to forecast and moved almost nothing.

US stock futures as of 9am ET, from Wednesday's close:

- S&P 500 futures: 7,819.50, -33.25 points / -0.42%.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 31,181.25, -221 points / -0.70%.
- Dow futures: 51,108, -341 points / -0.66%.
- Russell 2000 futures: 2,790.40, -21.80 points / -0.78%.

The verdict: New York opens lower but off its worst, with big tech and smaller companies weaker than the broad market. The selling has paused; nothing has reversed it. Oil and interest rates still set the price, and a steady job market gives stocks no cushion, because it leaves the Federal Reserve free to raise rates again.

The night, in S&P 500 futures:

- 1:10am: 7,852.25, the high, about where Wednesday ended.
- 6:30am: 7,802.75, the low, 50 points down.
- 9am: 7,819.50.

The two prices behind the slide turned within forty minutes of each other. The 10-year yield, what Washington pays to borrow for ten years, peaked at 5.354% around 6:30am, above Monday's 5.311% close, the highest close since May 2002. Brent topped out at $105.47 at 7:10am, and has since stopped climbing:

- Brent crude, the global oil benchmark: $104.95 a barrel, +$4.75 / +4.74% from Wednesday's $100.20 settlement.

Europe, open six hours, has recovered more, as of about 8:45am ET:

- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,455.21, -3.29 points / -0.03% so far in Thursday's session.
- CAC 40 (France): 7,738.04, -31.17 points / -0.40% so far in Thursday's session.

London was down 0.9% at its worst, and Paris 1.2%. That is the strongest fact against a lower open sticking: the market that has had longest to weigh $105 oil has taken back most of its fall.

The 8:30am number, from the Labor Department: first-time claims for unemployment benefits, week ended October 3.

- Claims: 197,000, vs about 200,000 forecast.
- Prior week: revised up to 199,000.
- Four-week average, which smooths out one-week swings: 198,000.

Layoffs stay rare. S&P 500 futures dipped about 7 points in the first five minutes, then came back.

Good news for workers is no help to stocks this morning, because two signals from the Fed since Wednesday point to more rate increases. The record of its September 15-16 meeting, out Wednesday at 2pm, showed most officials saw another increase as likely by year-end. Early Thursday, at the Istanbul Economic Forum, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said: "I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal." He added that "the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high."

Treasury yields as of 9am ET, from Wednesday's close:

- 2-year: 4.814%, +0.050 percentage point.
- 10-year: 5.316%, +0.039 percentage point.

The 2-year, the yield most tied to what investors expect from the Fed, is rising faster.

There is no panic in it:

- VIX, a gauge of what investors pay to protect against big S&P 500 swings: 15.64, +0.56 points / +3.71%.
- Gold: $4,141.50 an ounce, +$0.80 / +0.02% since Wednesday's close.

A VIX near 15 is a calm reading, and gold, the usual hiding place, has not moved. Investors are repricing what money costs, not running for cover.

Two stocks are moving before the bell on news of their own.

Wolfspeed (WOLF) at $31.37, -$0.46 / -1.45% on Wednesday, and $35.75 premarket, +$4.38 / +13.96% from that close.

The silicon-carbide chipmaker, a year out of bankruptcy, was offered a 30-year loan of up to $1.5B by the Defense Department after Wednesday's close, about nine-tenths of its $1.66B stock market value. The government would get the right to buy up to 7.5% of the company; the loan still needs approvals and money from Congress. On a morning when borrowing costs more for everyone, Wolfspeed's lender is Washington. It fits none of the six Len5es: it lost money in each of its last six reported quarters.

Delta Air Lines (DAL) at $82.97, -$0.69 / -0.82% on Wednesday, and $81.63 premarket, -$1.34 / -1.61% from that close.

Delta reports its July-September quarter before the open Friday, and fuel is the number to read. Its July 10 forecast:

- Adjusted profit, which leaves out one-time items: $2.00-$2.50 a share.
- Fuel: about $3.15 a gallon.

In the June quarter it paid an adjusted $3.93 a gallon. Analysts now expect about $1.90 a share, below Delta's own range. Delta fits none of the six Len5es: the nearest, Quality-Value, wants profit that holds steady, and its June-quarter fuel bill ran 77% above a year earlier.

Overnight moves often fade by the 9:30am open, and the S&P 500 futures' drop has already shrunk by a third. What would erase the rest: Brent back under $104 while the 10-year falls below Monday's close. What would deepen it: a weak 1pm sale of 30-year Treasury bonds, a sign lenders want more interest to fund Washington.

Next, Eastern time:

- 1pm: the Treasury sells $22B of 30-year bonds. Its September 10 sale paid 5.308%.
- Wednesday, October 14, 8:30am: September's consumer price index, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
- October 27-28: the Fed's next rate decision.

Stock futures stopped falling this morning when oil stopped climbing, not because anything good happened. The jobs data was the one chance at good news before the bell, and a Fed governor had already said a steady job market means more rate increases. The next verdict comes at 1pm, when lenders set the price of 30-year money.

Not investment advice.

text:
The Civic Wire Daily — October 8, 2026

A factual briefing of major U.S. and international political developments reported over the past day, drawn from wire accounts, official statements, and primary reporting.

**DNC sues over taxpayer-funded pro-administration ads**  
The Democratic National Committee filed suit Wednesday in federal court in Washington against President Trump and his administration, alleging that television ads paid with public money violated limits on government publicity and spending. The complaint says the White House directed about $20 million in Department of Homeland Security funds toward the spots; AdImpact estimates more than $10–12 million had already been spent. Trump said Monday on Truth Social that his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads going forward; the White House pointed to that post when asked about the suit. Common Cause filed a separate suit over the same ads.  
Why it matters: The case tests whether executive advertising close to the midterms can be paid with appropriated funds, and a ruling could shape campaign messaging in the final weeks.  
https://t.co/gmbVmZdFYH

**Federal Election Commission still lacks a quorum**  
With Election Day about four weeks away, the FEC has only two sitting commissioners, both Democrats, and has been unable to open investigations, issue fines, write rules, or issue formal advisory opinions since May 2025. Those actions require four of six members. Agency records cited in reporting show no enforcement cases resolved and no new civil penalties approved since the quorum was lost; the case backlog has roughly doubled. Staff can still collect and publish reports and answer routine questions.  
Why it matters: The agency that polices campaign money cannot enforce the law during what is expected to be a record-spending midterm cycle.  
https://t.co/UM1FWmUHSW

**Maine Senate debate: Collins and Jackson clash**  
Sen. Susan Collins (R) and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson held an often-testy debate. Collins pointed to her five terms and criticized some Trump policies; Jackson argued she has not pushed back effectively. Both criticized aspects of the president’s record while differing on how to respond.  
Why it matters: Maine is a competitive Senate race that could affect which party controls the chamber.  
https://t.co/7cU6yevpgq

**Russia’s overnight strike kills at least 25 in Ukraine**  
Russia launched missiles and drones across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 25 people and injuring about 100, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said. The deadliest hit was a missile strike on a five-story apartment building in Pryluky, Chernihiv region, where Zelenskiy said 19 people died, including five children. He said Russia fired about 70 missiles, many ballistic, plus Shahed drones, and also hit Kyiv, Oleksandria, and Kremenchuk. Moscow said the strike targeted military-industrial sites and did not address the Pryluky building.  
Why it matters: The attack continues the pattern of strikes on cities and energy infrastructure as the war enters another winter.  
https://t.co/ABeSUo7pHd

**Vance: Iran must cut enrichment to end the war**  
In a Reuters interview after a campaign stop in Alaska, Vice President JD Vance said Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in nuclear enrichment capacity, not only promises of future cuts, to satisfy U.S. demands and end the seven-month war. He questioned why Tehran needs 60 percent enriched fuel if it does not want a weapon, and said the United States would not “trade words for actions.” The sides have exchanged proposals aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz; Trump rejected Tehran’s latest offer and has warned operations could intensify after the midterms.  
Why it matters: The conflict is affecting energy markets and is a political issue heading into November.  
https://t.co/svinuYwWWB (interview reported Oct. 7, 2026; Detroit News/Reuters: https://t.co/N2RQZTG2Df)

text:
How Companies Responded to the Climate Change Threat | Heat (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)

Transcript 1:20:04 to 1:39:52

FRONTLINE PBS | Official
https://t.co/qYn35dFzZ3
06OCT2026 

#Documentary #ClimateChange #GlobalWarming
When the threat of climate change emerged as a major global issue, how did some of the world's largest governments and corporations respond? (Aired 2008)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://t.co/n7dibbVcSn

And support your local PBS station here: https://t.co/vEUZEDVSvT

Melting glaciers, rising sea levels, fires, floods and droughts: In 2008, with public concern about global warming on the upswing, award-winning producer and correspondent Martin Smith traveled the planet to investigate the scale of the problem, and the scale of any solution.

For years, the film reported, big businesses in the U.S. and around the globe — from oil and coal companies to electric utilities to car manufacturers — had resisted change to environmental policy and stifled the debate over climate change. But as this 2008 documentary was being made, industries and governments were facing rising pressure to reshape their approach to the environment.

To make “Heat,” Smith traveled to 12 countries on four continents, sitting down with policymakers, scientists, and leading executives from many of the largest carbon emitters from around the world, including American oil giants, Chinese coal companies, and Indian SUV makers. 

The two-hour film documented where the political and economic conversation around climate change and global warming stood in 2008, and found that some businesses were trying to fend off new regulations, while others were repositioning themselves to prosper in a world reshaped by climate change. The investigation also found that despite increasing talk about “going green,” environmental concerns were often still taking a back seat to shorter-term economic interests. And there were serious questions about the ability of industry-proposed solutions like “clean coal,” ethanol fuel subsidies, and carbon capture technology to roll back global warming. 

Editor’s note: A line of narration in this documentary cited a since-retracted assertion from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that "80 percent of all glacier ice in Tibet and the Himalayas will be gone by 2035." The panel attributed the statement to a media interview with a scientist who later said he had been misquoted, though the IPCC stood by its overall conclusion that “widespread mass loss from glaciers … are projected to accelerate throughout the 21st Century.”

See the film transcript here: https://t.co/vjR2Jh9PIO

Transcript
Follow along using the transcript.
Show transcript
 
FRONTLINE PBS | Official

are studies that say that that net benefit in  car in reducing carbon emissions isn't so great. MARTIN SMITH: What does the flex fuel  vehicle really do for reducing CO2 emissions?

than cellulosics. So it ranges from 15  percent all the way to about 65 percent. MARTIN SMITH: But the few service stations that  we have are putting out corn-based ethanol, right?

BETH LOWERY: It's about a 15 percent reduction.

depending on how the corn is farmed, fertilized,  harvested and transported. All these processes

Prof. DANIEL KAMMEN, U.C. Berkeley Inst. of the  Environment: Corn ethanol is simply a bad biofuel.   And it's a bad biofuel several times over. We,  in this country, have optimized corn, ironically,

BETH LOWERY: Right. It's not widespread. MARTIN SMITH: Negligible amounts. BETH LOWERY: It's not widespread. MARTIN SMITH: [voice-over] In fact, out of  a total of 120,000 gas stations nationwide,

land use effect of growing biofuels  that is very negative. And that is,

1:35:30

1:35:36

1:35:43
but this is one emergency we  can't drill our way out of. MARTIN SMITH: He followed up  with a nationwide ad campaign,  
1:35:49
positioning himself as a savior of the American  economy who can deliver energy independence.
1:35:55
T. BOONE PICKENS: [town hall meeting] I've   committed $58 million to this  project. And that's my money. MARTIN SMITH: What he wants  from the federal government  
1:36:01
is the same thing that all wind producers want. T. BOONE PICKENS: You're going to  have to have production tax credits.
1:36:07
MARTIN SMITH: [on camera] In order to- T. BOONE PICKENS: -which- MARTIN SMITH: -help you with operating costs? T. BOONE PICKENS: Yes. MARTIN SMITH: To make it cost competitive?
1:36:12
T. BOONE PICKENS: Exactly. You have to have it. MARTIN SMITH: [voice-over] He also  needs the government to open corridors   for transmission lines to move electricity  from wind farms to customers. To be viable,  
1:36:24
both wind and solar will require  billions in infrastructure investment. T. BOONE PICKENS: The way I see government should  operate in this, they should open up corridors and  
1:36:35
help with that and make it happen. You can't  go in and invest a huge amount of money and  
1:36:43
not have a way to get your money back and make a  profit. I would expect to make money out of it.
1:36:58
MARTIN SMITH: As calls for carbon-free  power grow, nuclear power is getting a  
1:37:04
fresh look. It's already the source of  20 percent of America's electricity.
1:37:12
Patrick Moore is a paid spokesman  for the nuclear lobby representing 32  
1:37:18
utilities with nuclear plants in their portfolios. PATRICK MOORE, Nuclear Industry Lobbyist:  [radio interview] The statistics show that   nuclear energy is among the safest technologies.
1:37:25
It is simply and clearly obvious that nuclear  energy is going to be the most important base  
1:37:31
technology for energy, like providing the  bulk of our electricity in the future,   and, hopefully, charging our cars and running  heat pumps in our houses so we can eliminate  
1:37:41
fossil fuels from our transportation  and our infrastructure at the same time.
1:37:46
MARTIN SMITH: Moore wasn't always  so enthusiastic. In the 1970s,   he was a founding member of Greenpeace  and a fierce nuclear opponent.
1:37:55
[on camera] In 1976, you called nuclear power  plants "slow atomic bombs. Nuclear power plants  
1:38:01
are, next to nuclear warheads themselves, the  most dangerous devices that man has ever created."
1:38:06
PATRICK MOORE: That's how I saw the world at  that time. I was wrong. And it's - I mean,   it was a fact back then in the cold war that we  saw nuclear energy and nuclear weapons as all  
1:38:19
part of the same technology and all part of the  same thing, as if all things nuclear were evil.
1:38:25
MARTIN SMITH: By the late '70s, nuclear energy  was a troubled industry. In large part due  
1:38:31
to the success of anti-nuclear activists,  it was burdened with numerous federal and  
1:38:36
state regulations and was experiencing  massive construction cost overruns.
1:38:44
The nuclear accident at Three Mile  Island was the final nail in the coffin. PA SYSTEM: There has been a state of  emergency declared on Three Mile Island.
1:38:56
MARTIN SMITH: [on camera] People look  at Three Mile Island, it scares them. PATRICK MOORE: Well, it's not rational to be  scared by Three Mile Island, that's for sure.
1:39:01
MARTIN SMITH: Why not? PATRICK MOORE: Because, no one was injured at  Three Mile Island. It did not leak, the radiation.   And that was because engineers designed a reactor  dome that was made to prevent the radiation from  
1:39:12
coming out in the event of an accident. And  it worked. It was a safety system that worked.
1:39:17
MARTIN SMITH: [voice-over] To be fair, there was  some leakage of radioactive gas, but it didn't go   far and any serious leak was contained. Still,  it frightened communities. No application for  
1:39:30
new nuclear plant construction has been approved  since. And new plants still face big obstacles.
1:39:37
Prof. DANIEL KAMMEN, U.C. Berkeley Inst. of the  Environment: They've become fabulously expensive,   $5 billion to $10 billion per nuclear power plant.
1:39:43
Prof. STEPHEN SCHNEIDER, Climatologist,  Stanford Univ.: And also, what are you   going to do with the waste? I think  that there are technical solutions,   but you can't get any location.  Nevada doesn't want any of that waste.
1:39:52
MARTIN SMITH: These issues of waste  and cost make it unclear whether an   expansion of nuclear energy will ever  be politically or economically viable.

text:
The President’s Semantics vs. The Lawmakers' Reality

An Excerpt from the book SETTING THE RECORD STRAIGHT 

Obasanjo’s defense is often a semantic trick: "There is no Nigerian, dead or alive, that would say I called him and told him I wanted a third term." This argument is designed to deflect attention from the actions of his agents and the massive use of public resources to achieve his goal.

The Lawmakers’ Indictment: Former federal lawmaker Dr. Usman Bugaje, who fought the agenda in the National Assembly, directly countered the President, insisting that Obasanjo “did everything within his power to get a third term, but he failed to do so.” Bugaje affirmed that he and his colleagues knew "beyond any doubt" that the President was working "day and night" to secure the tenure elongation.

The Coercive Style: Bugaje’s testimony confirms the plot was executed by proxy: “The fact that he did not take a telephone to make a particular call to anybody is not sufficient evidence that he did not look for a third term. It's just a matter of style, but... many of us were threatened by his own agents.”

Bribes and Inducements: The denial is rendered meaningless by the documented attempts at legislative bribery. Former Senate President Adolphus Wabara alleged he was offered a N250 million bribe to support the plan. Lawmakers confirmed that sums of N50 million to N100 million were routinely offered to secure votes. The President did not need to make the call himself; his agents delivered the treasury to his command.

2. Testimony from the Inner Circle: Direct Confirmation
The most damaging evidence against Obasanjo's denial comes from those closest to the engine of the executive power, proving his direct involvement. The Daughter’s Letter: Perhaps the most painful and irrefutable piece of evidence came from his own daughter, Senator Iyabo Obasanjo. In her widely circulated letter, she recounted going to Abuja to persuade her father to drop the idea. She stated that while his public stance was denial, his private statement to her proved he was “the brain behind the third term debacle.” This removes all doubt that the President was merely a passive observer of a movement created by governors.

The Governor’s Witness: Former Abia State Governor, Senator Orji Kalu, provided direct testimony against the "no one called him" defense. Kalu stated that Obasanjo "invited me to the Villa and told me about the third term," confirming that the President did, in fact, solicit support from key political stakeholders. 

The International Diplomatic Record: The notion that Obasanjo was merely observing is also contradicted by international diplomatic accounts. Former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice reportedly documented in her memoir how Obasanjo discussed the possibility of amending the constitution for a third term during a meeting with former U.S. President George W. Bush. This places the President, not his subordinates, at the center of the constitutional manipulation.

text:
service founders: treat AI like a junior ops hire — not a CEO replacement.

i use Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok every day in an alabama service business — Grok Bot when i need a fast second pass on a draft already in motion. it drafts. i decide. that boundary is the whole game. here's the operating setup (7 points):

1/ give it a job description
in GHL notes (or a one-pager), title it "AI junior ops — allowed work":
draft proposals from my notes · summarize calls · turn SOPs into checklists · first-pass email reminders · research competitor pages · outline content · Canva copy variants for Meta/Google Ads
NOT allowed: final pricing · firing clients · sending without my eyes · inventing testimonials · changing live ads budgets.

2/ context pack (paste once per project)
ICP · offer · exclusions · tone ("plain, direct, no hype") · examples of a good proposal.
bad prompts waste hours. good context makes the junior useful.

3/ sample prompts that ship
proposal: "using these call notes, write a 1-page proposal with diagnosis, 30/60/90 outcomes, inclusions/exclusions, timeline, 50% deposit. under 400 words."
reminder: "draft a firm, polite day-10 unpaid invoice email. no apology essay. include GHL payment link placeholder."
SOP: "turn this messy walkthrough transcript into a 8-step checklist a VA could follow."

4/ human gates (non-negotiable)
you approve: price, scope, anything client-facing that commits money or timeline.
AI can draft the pause-work sentence. you hit send in GHL/email. Grok Bot is fine for quick rewrites — you still own the send.

5/ speed where it matters
aim: proposal same day as call · SOP written once, reused · content outlines in 15 min then you add war stories.
if AI work isn't cutting a real bottleneck, drop the workflow.

6/ stack around it
GHL for truth, money, SOPs, and pipeline · async walkthroughs for proof · Canva for creatives · Claude/ChatGPT/Grok for drafts.
AI without a CRM is a clever intern with amnesia.

7/ quality bar
if you wouldn't put your name on it, don't send it. edit ruthlessly. your reputation is the product.

text:
Larry Elder:
A group of college students were shown a paper on which a 6-inch line was drawn. The paper was passed to the students sitting around the table. They were asked to estimate the length of the line. Now, this experiment was rigged. The instructor and all but one of the students were told to say, “About 3 inches.” Again, the line was clearly longer than 3 inches.

The point was to determine whether these obviously wrong guesses would cause the unsuspecting student — the one not in on the scheme and the last one at the table to offer a guess — to also say, “About 3 inches.” In the overwhelming majority of cases, the unsuspecting students also said, “About 3 inches.”

Now there are a few ways to look at this. But one explanation is that the consensus, though clearly wrong, altered the way the final student viewed the length of the line, as in, “If everybody sees it that way, I must be wrong.”

For example, the standard common definition of a recession is back-to-back quarters of negative economic growth. In 2025, the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, every quarter after revisions had positive economic growth. So far this year, each quarter has seen positive economic growth.

But a July 2026 Economist/YouGov poll found that 41% of adult Americans believed the country was in a recession, with Democrats three times more likely than Republicans to feel this way. A Napolitan News Service/Rasmussen poll conducted at the end of September 2026 found that 39% of registered voters believed the country was currently in a recession.

Consider the media coverage of the economy the month before the presidential election of 1992, when President George H.W. Bush ran against Arkansas Gov. Bill Clinton. There had been 19 months of positive economic growth leading up to October 1992. A Gallup poll, however, found that a majority of Americans thought the economy was in a recession.

Investor’s Business Daily noted that in October 1992, 90% of the economic news in newspapers was negative. The election was held on Nov. 3. Clinton won, and that month only 14% of the economic news in newspapers was negative. As to the ABC, NBC and CBS nightly news, about 90% of the news about the economy was negative. After the election, for the remaining two months of the year, 60% of the economic news in the same newscasts was positive.

Yes, gas prices since the start of the Iran War have gone up. But at 2.5% of income, the amount Americans spend on gas is less than during the gas spikes of the 1970s. And Americans drive twice as far on a gallon of gas compared to the 1970s.

Consumers are spending. People who fear an economic downturn and who fear the loss of their jobs, typically do not spend the way consumers have been doing in recent months. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model estimates a third-quarter 2026 growth of 3.7%.

The Media Research Center found the Big 3 nightly news coverage of Trump was negative in both terms.

“News aggregators” like Microsoft, Apple, Google, Yahoo, TikTok and YouTube are where Americans now primarily get their news. In 2025, Google curated 73% of articles from outlets with a bias to the left — and just 1% of articles from outlets biased to the right. For all the aggregators, less than 10% of their curated articles came from outlets on the right.

In “Lessons from the Recession: A Management and Communication Perspective,” published in 1997, the authors write: “… the highly negative view of the economy in 1992 was due in large part to widespread misperceptions about its performance and prospects, and that unduly negative coverage on network television played some major role informing those misperceptions.”

The anti-Trump media clearly influences how people think and feel about the economy. The only question is to what degree.

The average income is at an all-time high. The percentage of those living in poverty is at an all-time low. The stock market indices have hit record highs, and 401(k)s have seen large increases.

How much of current pessimism about the economy is driven by what the media tells us about the economy and how we should feel about it?

text:
When winter closed in on the Ozark hills in 1931, the Walker family no longer had a home above ground. Like countless families during the Great Depression, they had watched the bank reclaim nearly everything they owned after the economy collapsed across rural Arkansas. Samuel Walker, a forty-two-year-old stone mason, suddenly found himself responsible for keeping his wife and five children alive with almost no money as freezing weather approached the mountains. 

Then he remembered something hidden beneath a nearby hillside: an old limestone shelter tucked deep into the earth on land that had once belonged to him. The cave was small, rough, and cold by most standards, but it remained dry and naturally held a steady temperature throughout the year. Samuel approached the new landowner with an unusual offer. If the family could stay there through the winter, he would build a retaining wall from stone in exchange. The deal was accepted. Within days, the Walkers moved underground.

The cave became their world. Quilts hung across the entrance as makeshift doors while packed dirt covered the floor beneath their beds. During daylight hours, Samuel disappeared into the forests gathering timber and cutting stone from the hillsides. At night, beneath the glow of lantern light, he worked endlessly shaping rock by hand inside the shelter. First came the retaining wall promised to the landowner. Then he carved shelves directly into the stone and built a fireplace to help warm the underground space. When winter passed, the family still could not afford a proper house, so they remained beneath the hillside through another cold season. 

Samuel slowly expanded the cave itself while continuing to gather materials one piece at a time for the home he dreamed of building above ground. By the winter of 1933, he finally began laying stone for a small house on the hillside, placing each block carefully after long days of labor. Every wall rising above ground had first been shaped in the darkness below it.

Then, in the spring of 1934, after three winters spent living beneath the earth, the stone house was finally complete. The family moved inside in May, carrying what little they owned out of the cave that had kept them alive during the hardest years of the Depression. 

Yet that first night inside the new home brought an unexpected moment none of them anticipated. The youngest child, now seven years old, reportedly struggled to sleep because the house felt too large and too quiet after years spent surrounded by close stone walls beneath the hill. Samuel never abandoned the cave afterward, later using it to store vegetables and supplies through the seasons. 

Decades later, one of his grandsons discovered Samuel’s old journal containing a final sentence that survived long after the family itself had changed: “The house stands finished. The cave carried us through.” And nearly a century later, the story still leaves behind one haunting question: how many families survived impossible hardships only because they learned to find shelter in places others would never think to look.

text:
Sam Walton had never run a variety store. He ran his first one straight from the franchise manual.

It grew to $225,000 a year, the biggest Ben Franklin store in Arkansas. Then he lost the lease and started over in Bentonville, in a store doing $32,000.

He tells it here beside his brother Bud, store by store, the two of them cutting in on each other like men who have told it a hundred times.

Bud was the first hire. Sam says he could not afford to pay him, so he offered 35 cents an hour. Then they argue over what it really was and land on $50 a month.

Watch the minute they stand on a Bentonville corner counting people on the sidewalk. Bud shakes his head. Sam buys the store anyway.

"Neither one of us knew the business."

That is the line most founders cut from the story. He says it flat, then follows a rulebook and adds ice cream machines and popcorn on the sidewalk on Saturday night.

Next comes Kansas City. He had never flown. He took half of a store in a shopping center, in years when there were practically no shopping centers, 20 miles from the city limits. Nobody else wanted it.

Sam calls Bud his balance wheel. He wanted to gamble more than Bud was ready to. They argued, and once they decided, they went together.

So who built Walmart, the brother who wanted to gamble or the brother who made him argue for it?

text:
Sure, California has a lot of issues. It’s the most populous state, has the biggest economy, and covers a massive area with just about every kind of terrain imaginable. Governing it isn’t simple.

But it also has an outstanding public university system, leads the nation in agricultural production, and offers plenty of economic opportunity. Much of the state is literally paradise. People pay high taxes, sure, but they get a lot for their money.

California also makes an effort to help the needy. Providing healthcare, supporting struggling families, and treating people like human beings are things I want government to do. Those programs deserve scrutiny, but their existence isn’t a failure.

I’m not going to argue things couldn’t be better, or that Democrats shouldn’t own their mistakes. But you can’t blame their policies for everything that goes wrong while ignoring everything that goes right. Besides, many much smaller red states have plenty of problems too. Should they all switch to Democrats to try something new?

And perhaps voters keep electing Democrats because they’ve considered the alternative. Being unhappy with the direction of the state doesn’t mean they think Republicans would improve it.

Arguing that it’s all one-sided and simply voting GOP would help is lazy and hardly reflects the reality California voters see. Isn’t it up to GOP candidates to make the case on how they’d do better?
