text:
Women and underrepresented minorities have higher tenure-track placement rates in the political science job market | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

Getting a tenure-track faculty position is often the primary goal for doctoral students, but the odds of landing one are notoriously low. A recent analysis of the political science job market suggests that while the prestige of a candidate’s university is linked to the type of academic institution they end up at, it does not actually predict whether they will secure a professorship. The research, published in PS: Political Science & Politics, indicates that having a strong publication record, studying a high-demand field, and being a female or an underrepresented minority candidate are stronger predictors of finding a tenure-track academic job.

A tenure-track professorship is a university teaching and research position that can eventually lead to a permanent, lifelong appointment. In many academic fields, the competition for these roles is intense, with far more new graduates than available openings.

Past research analyzing this system has pointed to a rigid prestige hierarchy. For instance, a 2022 study of faculty hiring across the United States found that a small minority of elite universities supply the vast majority of professors. Similarly, a 2025 analysis of political science departments indicated that the top 20 percent of programs produced 75 percent of tenure-track faculty at U.S. doctoral departments, while the bottom half produced less than 5 percent.

These past studies tend to imply that graduating from a top-tier university is the only reliable way to get a job in academia. But that approach relies on looking backward at the people who already secured positions at major research universities. This method can introduce bias.

First, it ignores the fact that elite universities often have much larger graduate programs, meaning they naturally produce more job applicants. Second, it overlooks professorships at the thousands of colleges and universities that only offer bachelor’s or master’s degrees. About 17,000 people teach political science in the United States, but only about 3,000 work at doctoral departments, meaning studies that look only at those departments miss more than 80 percent of faculty jobs.

“Existing work has claimed that where one earns the PhD is critical to whether they find a professor job, and some even suggested closing more than half of PhD programs,” Scott W. Desposato, the Simón Bolívar Chair of Latin American Studies and a professor of political science at the University of California, San Diego, told PsyPost.

“But this body of work assesses placements by looking at professors at PhD-granting programs. Thus, they don’t control for the size of the PhD program (bigger programs should have more placements, even if their training is the same as smaller programs) and they ignore the many professor jobs at small liberal arts colleges, community colleges, and other universities that don’t have phD programs.”

“As I write in the paper, it’s like studying fitness by seeing which country won the most medals in the Olympics and concluding that the best way to be healthy is to move to that country,” Desposato continued. “That would be a crazy way to study fitness, and it’s the wrong way to study the academic labor market.”

“Faculty are full of advice about what students should do to succeed on the job market,” he said. “But their recommendations are based on anecdotal observations. We try to be systematic and scientific in our research – so why wouldn’t we want some real evidence from which to make recommendations to our PhD students?”

To get a more accurate picture of how hiring works, Desposato identified a group of active job seekers and checked on their outcomes a year later. The researcher collected data on 413 political science candidates who were actively on the academic job market during the 2023 to 2024 hiring cycle. The candidates were identified from the “Job Market Candidate” pages on various university websites in the fall of 2023. The sample only included candidates who were either finalizing their dissertations or had recently graduated, excluding anyone who already held a tenure-track job or had graduated before 2023.

Using the candidates’ websites and resumes, the researcher recorded a variety of details. These included the rank of their university, their specific field of study, their teaching experience, any awards they had won, and their publication record. To assess publications, the study tracked both the number of articles and the prestige of the journals in which they were published.

The researcher also coded the candidates’ perceived gender and underrepresented minority (URM) status based on names, pronouns, identity-specific awards, personal statements, and appearance. Candidates perceived as Black, Latino, or Native American were classified as URM, a measure meant to approximate how hiring committees might see them.

In the fall of 2024, the researcher checked back to see what types of jobs the candidates had secured. By that time, about 26 percent of the candidates had accepted tenure-track professorships. Surprisingly, the prestige of the university where a candidate earned their degree had virtually no bearing on whether they secured one of these positions.

Placement rates showed no consistent pattern by rank: the top 10 departments placed 25 percent of their candidates, while departments ranked 71st or lower placed 35 percent. The results suggest that graduating from an elite institution does not guarantee a job, nor does graduating from a lower-ranked program automatically disqualify a candidate. However, lower-ranked programs were thinly represented in the data, as only 13 of the 60 lower-ranked departments listed candidates online. The lowest-ranked group’s 35 percent placement rate largely reflected the University of Missouri, which placed nine of its 16 candidates; the rest of that group placed just five of 24 candidates.

While institutional rank did not predict if a candidate got a job, it did predict what kind of job they got. Candidates from top-ranked programs were much more likely to secure postdoctoral fellowships, which are temporary research positions that often serve as stepping stones to tenure-track jobs. When elite candidates did land tenure-track roles, they mostly went to universities that also grant doctoral degrees. By contrast, candidates from lower-ranked programs were more likely to find tenure-track positions at smaller colleges and universities that do not have doctoral programs, or they took temporary teaching positions.

More than 70 percent of candidates held some kind of academic job a year later. Among candidates who were already postdoctoral fellows when the study began, 30 percent landed tenure-track jobs, compared with 15 percent of those working as visiting lecturers.

Publishing was among the strongest predictors of landing a tenure-track job. Candidates without any published research had a placement rate of just 16 percent, compared with 32 percent for those with one to three publications. In statistical models, the researcher compared hypothetical candidates to a baseline: a non-minority man studying American politics at the 30th-ranked department who had not yet finished his degree and had no publications. That baseline candidate had an estimated 27 percent probability of landing a professorship.

If that same candidate had co-authored an article in the American Political Science Review, a top journal, the probability rose to 41 percent. A solo-authored article in that journal was associated with a probability of roughly 52 percent, nearly double the baseline, though this estimate was less statistically certain. Only about 5 percent of candidates had published in a top journal at all. Teaching experience, on the other hand, did not seem to help: candidates with seven or more teaching roles had a lower placement rate of 18 percent.

The candidate’s field of study and demographic identity were also linked to their job market outcomes. Applicants specializing in American politics were the most successful, with nearly 40 percent finding a tenure-track position, compared with 20 to 24 percent in other fields. That year, there were about as many job listings in American politics (118) as American politics candidates (118), whereas comparative politics had 189 candidates for 71 listings.

When looking at demographics, the study found no evidence that female or URM candidates faced hiring disadvantages. In fact, these identities were associated with higher placement rates. The raw placement rates for tenure-track jobs were 19 percent for non-minority men, 32 percent for non-minority women, 36 percent for URM women, and 39 percent for URM men. In the researcher’s statistical models, a baseline non-minority male candidate had a 27 percent probability of securing a tenure-track job.

By comparison, a URM male candidate had a 47 percent probability, and female candidates sat at roughly 44 percent. However, this advantage only appeared for positions at doctoral universities; for jobs at colleges without doctoral programs, gender and minority status were not significantly linked to placement. These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that women applying for tenure-track faculty positions in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines experienced hiring equality or advantages compared to men with matching qualifications. Desposato’s own analysis of the American Political Science Association’s placement survey data from 2017 to 2025 found the same advantages for female, minority, and American politics candidates.

“The effect sizes for URM/female were particularly large,” Desposato pointed out. “Members of those identities had a much higher placement rate than white/Asian males.”

“The most striking finding was that departmental rank had so little effect on placements, whereas both female gender and minority status had such large effects compared to the other predictors,” Artur Nilsson, a professor of personality psychology at the University of Bergen who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “That publications and research topics matter too is not surprising.”

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study provides an observational snapshot of a single hiring cycle, meaning it cannot demonstrate that specific factors directly caused people to be hired. For example, a strong publication record might improve a candidate’s chances by impressing a search committee, or it might simply be a byproduct of writing a very good dissertation, which the committee also recognizes.

The models accounted for broad subfields, such as American or comparative politics, but not for narrower research specialties that might have been in higher demand. “These are observational data with tons of selection issues,” the researcher explained. “For example, why are URM candidates placed at double the rate of non-URM males? This might simply be that those candidates were studying more popular fields.”

“Or, it may be that non-URM candidates have better alternatives to academia and are leaving for those positions,” he continued. “Or, it may be that there is discrimination based on identity. It could be all of these! This is just one year’s worth of data, from a unique moment of racial reckoning, but it deserves some consideration.”

There are also many unmeasured variables that influence hiring decisions, such as a candidate’s interview skills, the strength of their recommendation letters, and the overall quality of their research. Additionally, the data collection relied on which candidates academic departments chose to list on their public websites. This means some job seekers were likely missed, especially those from programs outside the United States or those whose departments do not maintain such directories.

It is also unclear whether the hiring trends apply to other countries or disciplines. “The main caveat is that these findings represent a specific job market at a particular point in time, subject to the idiosyncrasies of the U.S. system,” Nilsson said. “Their generalizability is difficult to estimate.”

Because the academic job search often takes several years, tracking outcomes after a single year may not capture the full trajectory of a candidate’s career. Looking ahead, Desposato hopes to apply the same approach to other fields and follow candidates for several years. He noted that upcoming experimental studies on hiring by other scholars will also help address these limitations.

He argued that graduate programs should release hard numbers on how their students fare, since many advertise an “excellent placement record” to prospective students without backing it up. “It’s not clear what ‘excellent placement record’ can mean when 75% of candidates did not have professor jobs after a year on the job market,” he added. “We owe it to our PhD students and prospective students to be honest about the job market and what they are signing up for when they start a PhD program, and we should make sure there are non-academic pathways for our PhD students.”

“This is especially true given demographic change,” Desposato concluded. “Many small colleges are going to close as enrollments decline. Most of those colleges offer political science or government as a major, and those professor jobs just won’t exist anymore. I expect a difficult academic job market for PhD candidates for the foreseeable future.”

text:
Player Spotlight of the Week! 🌀

Zaven Collins was born May 19, 1999, in Tulsa and played at Hominy High School in Hominy, Oklahoma (Class A, town of about 3,500 people, and about 45 miles from Tulsa).
He was lightly recruited. Tulsa was the only FBS school to offer him a scholarship. He has said bigger programs told him his school was too small and the competition level too low, even though he was the class valedictorian with a strong ACT and no off-field issues.
Commitment: August 15, 2016 National letter of intent: February 1, 2017
His true freshman year, 2017, was a redshirt. He did not appear in a game. Philip Montgomery said Collins spent that season on the scout team at multiple spots while learning linebacker, a position he had not played in high school. He arrived listed around 6-foot-3 or 6-foot-4 and about 213 to 220 pounds. By the next fall Tulsa was listing him at 6-foot-4, 250.
2018 as a redshirt freshman, He played in all 12 games. Started 10, moving into the lineup in the third game. Zaven finished with 85 tackles (second on the team), a team-high 9.5 tackles for loss for minus-31 yards, 1.5 sacks, three quarterback pressures, three pass breakups, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery, and one blocked kick. Also listed is one interception.
2019 Zaven Collins was named Preseason All-AAC team as an honorable-mention linebacker. He started all 12 games. Zaven finished with 97 tackles, 8 tackles for loss for minus-27 yards, 2 sacks, three pass breakups, and one fumble recovery. After the season he was second-team All-AAC.
2020 the Maxwell Football Club put him on the Chuck Bednarik Award preseason watch list, one of 90 players. Tulsa went 6-3 under Philip Montgomery, 6-0 in the AAC, then a 27-24 loss at No. 6 Cincinnati in the conference championship on December 19, then a 28-26 loss to Mississippi State in the Armed Forces Bowl on December 31. Collins started all eight regular-season and championship games he played. He declared for the draft and did not play in the bowl.
The conference announced him unanimous AAC Defensive Player of the Year, the first unanimous player-of-the-year selection in league history, and unanimous first-team All-AAC. He was the first Tulsa player to win the AAC’s defensive player of the year award.
Bronko Nagurski Trophy, The Oklahoman called him the first Tulsa player to win a national performance award since Howard Twilley was UPI lineman of the year in 1965.
Chuck Bednarik Award, Finalists included Notre Dame’s Jeremiah Owusu-Koramoah and Alabama’s Patrick Surtain II.
Lombardi Award, CFB on FOX Defensive Player of the Year, and Runner-up for the Butkus Award. Zaven was a 2020 consensus All-American, earning first-team honors on all five NCAA-recognized teams: the Associated Press, AFCA, FWAA, Sporting News, and Walter Camp. He was also named first-team All-America by USA Today, CBS Sports, Pro Football Focus, The Athletic, and Phil Steele. The FWAA selection was automatic as the Bronko Nagurski Trophy winner. He was a unanimous first-team All-AAC selection and the unanimous AAC Defensive Player of the Year, and he was Tulsa’s first consensus All-American since the great, Jerry Ostroski in 1991.
On April 29, 2021, the Arizona Cardinals selected him in the first round of the NFL Draft with the 16th overall pick. He was the first Tulsa player taken in the first round since guard Steve August, selected 14th overall by the Seattle Seahawks in 1977. Collins signed a four-year rookie contract worth just over $14 million on June 8, 2021.
Since turning pro, Zaven has stayed tied to the program. On August 24, 2026, Tulsa Athletics announced an impactful gift from Collins to Tulsa Football to support the student-athlete experience and the program’s future. The university did not disclose the amount. Zaven said Tulsa was the foundation for his success and that the gift was about giving back to the place that invested in him.
Zaven ended up being one of my favorite TU players of all time.

text:
The Difference Between Leadership and Empathy Is Showing Up. ✊🇳🇬

Let’s be brutally honest for a moment.

When tragedy strikes, genuine leaders don’t just stay in the comfort of air-conditioned rooms at Aso Rock, issuing official press releases, declaring three days of national mourning, and ordering flags to fly at half-mast while remaining completely detached from the people’s suffering.

When the tragic Nigerian Air Force crash occurred—taking the lives of our brave military personnel and civilians—where was President Tinubu? Flying flags at half-mast from a distance is easy. Issuing statements through aides is easy. But physically showing up to look grieving families and military leadership in the eye? Apparently, that’s too much to ask.

Meanwhile, look at Peter Obi. A private citizen. Not in power, holding no official office, yet he personally went straight to the Nigerian Air Force Headquarters in Abuja to offer his condolences, sign the condolence register, and share in the grief of the fallen heroes' families. He demonstrated that true leadership isn't about titles; it’s about empathy, presence, and genuine care.

Remember when US service members lost their lives, and world leaders—even former US President Trump—met the fallen soldiers at the tarmac, stood in respect, and saluted them as they arrived home? That is what respect for fallen heroes looks like.

If a leader cannot even travel down the road in Abuja to honour those who laid down their lives for this country, what message are we sending to our men and women in uniform?

Leadership is not a title; it’s an action. People don't care how much you know or what press statement you sign until they know how much you care.

What are your thoughts on this? Does empathy still matter in Nigerian leadership? 👇

#Dendias’ Strategic Move: Meeting with the #Indian Ambassador – Defense Cooperation Takes Center Stage as #Athens and #NewDelhi Forge a Powerful Defense Partnership 

A new geopolitical reality is taking shape in the Eastern Mediterranean as Greece and India deepen their military and strategic cooperation, laying the foundations for a defense partnership that could influence regional security calculations from the Aegean Sea to the Indian Ocean.

The meeting between Greek Minister of National Defense Nikos Dendias and Indian Ambassador Ravi Shankar on October 8, 2026, represents another step in the steadily expanding relationship between Athens and New Delhi.

At a time of growing international instability, both countries recognize the importance of strengthening defense cooperation, military interoperability and strategic dialogue.

The emerging Greece–India partnership carries particular geopolitical significance because of Turkey’s extensive military relationship with Pakistan, India's longstanding strategic rival.

Although Athens and New Delhi have not established a formal military alliance against Ankara, their growing cooperation creates new opportunities for strategic coordination.

Dendias–Ravi Shankar: A New Chapter in Greek–Indian Defense Cooperation

The meeting at Greece’s Ministry of National Defense focused on regional security challenges and opportunities to deepen bilateral defense relations.

Both sides emphasized the importance of maintaining close communication and expanding military cooperation.

For Greece, India represents an increasingly important strategic partner with significant military capabilities, advanced technological ambitions and growing international influence.

For New Delhi, Greece offers a valuable connection to the European Union, NATO and the strategically important Eastern Mediterranean.

The relationship reflects a broader convergence of interests involving maritime security, regional stability and defense technology.

The February 2026 Agreement: Building a Five-Year Defense Roadmap

A major milestone occurred on February 9, 2026, when Nikos Dendias met Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh in New Delhi.

During that visit, the two countries signed a Joint Declaration of Intent on defense industrial cooperation, establishing the framework for a proposed five-year roadmap.

They also exchanged their bilateral military cooperation program for 2026.

The initiative connects Greece’s defense modernization agenda with India's Aatmanirbhar Bharat, its national strategy for developing domestic industrial and technological capabilities.

The potential significance extends beyond arms procurement: Both countries could explore joint research, technological development, industrial partnerships and specialized military systems.

The challenge now is transforming the institutional framework into concrete programs.

Greek F-16 Fighters in India – Indian Su-30MKI Aircraft in Greece

Military cooperation has already moved beyond diplomatic declarations.

In 2024, the Hellenic Air Force deployed four F-16 Block 52+ Advanced fighter jets from its 336 Squadron to participate in India's multinational Tarang Shakti exercise.

Greek pilots operated in a demanding multinational environment, gaining experience in complex air combat scenarios and coordination with foreign air forces.

A year later, India participated in Greece’s Iniochos 2025 exercise at Andravida Air Base, deploying Su-30MKI fighter aircraft, an IL-78 aerial refueling aircraft and a C-17 transport aircraft.

These exercises provide important opportunities for Greek and Indian aircrews to exchange operational knowledge and improve interoperability between different military platforms.

They also demonstrate that geographical distance is not necessarily an obstacle to sustained defense cooperation.

Indian Warships Enter the Aegean: The Naval Dimension

The maritime component of the partnership is equally significant.

In September 2025, the Indian Navy's INS Trikand participated in bilateral naval exercises alongside the Greek frigate HS Themistocles and submarine HS Pipinos.

The exercises covered anti-submarine warfare, air defense scenarios, surface operations and maritime situational awareness.

The presence of Indian naval forces in the Aegean demonstrates New Delhi's interest in strengthening military engagement beyond the Indian Ocean.

For Greece, cooperation with the Indian Navy offers access to valuable operational experience developed across the Indo-Pacific.

For India, exercises with Greek naval forces support greater familiarity with Mediterranean operating conditions and NATO-member naval procedures.

Drones, Electronic Warfare and Defense Technology: The Next Frontier

One of the most promising areas for future cooperation concerns defense innovation.

India has invested heavily in indigenous missile technology, unmanned systems, electronic warfare and advanced military production.

Greece is simultaneously seeking to strengthen its domestic defense industry through modernization initiatives and the Hellenic Center for Defense Innovation.

Potential cooperation could include drones, counter-drone technologies, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, electronic warfare and advanced naval systems.

These remain prospective opportunities rather than confirmed new procurement contracts.

Nevertheless, the February 2026 defense industrial framework offers a foundation for more structured cooperation between research institutions, defense companies and military organizations.

Turkey–Pakistan: The Geopolitical Factor Behind the Partnership

The expanding relationship between Greece and India cannot be examined without considering the strategic connections between Turkey and Pakistan.

Ankara and Islamabad maintain substantial military ties involving defense technology, training and equipment programs.

Pakistan is also India's longstanding strategic rival.

Against this background, closer Greek–Indian cooperation introduces an additional dimension to regional strategic calculations.

Athens and New Delhi share an interest in maintaining regional stability and protecting maritime security.

Their cooperation may strengthen diplomatic coordination and diversify defense partnerships.

However, it should not be interpreted as an officially established anti-Turkish military alliance. Neither country's defense relationship is exclusively defined by its differences with Ankara or Islamabad.

Greece–Cyprus–India: A Strategic Connection Across Two Regions

The growing relationship between India and Cyprus adds another dimension.

In May 2026, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides advanced their bilateral strategic relationship, including a defense cooperation roadmap for 2026–2031.

This opens possibilities for closer coordination among Greece, Cyprus and India.

A deeper trilateral relationship could connect the Eastern Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean through maritime security, defense technology, energy infrastructure and commercial connectivity.

The India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor, known as IMEC, further reinforces the importance of regional transport networks and secure maritime routes.

For New Delhi, the Eastern Mediterranean offers strategic access to European markets.

For Athens and Nicosia, India's expanding international role creates opportunities for diplomatic and economic engagement.

The Strategic Outlook: From Military Exercises to Long-Term Cooperation

The Dendias–Ravi Shankar meeting should be viewed as another step in the gradual institutionalization of Greece–India defense relations.

The immediate priorities include expanding joint exercises, encouraging defense industrial partnerships and creating sustainable channels for technological cooperation.

Longer-term opportunities could involve maritime domain awareness, advanced training, cybersecurity and emerging military technologies.

Success will depend on practical implementation, funding, industrial participation and the ability of both countries to identify complementary military requirements.

From Greek F-16 fighters operating over India to Indian warships conducting exercises in the Aegean, Athens and New Delhi are building a defense relationship with increasingly important strategic implications.

The partnership does not represent a formal military bloc. It does, however, offer both countries additional options in a rapidly changing geopolitical environment.

As Turkey strengthens its defense relationship with Pakistan, Greece and India are developing their own strategic cooperation—one that could become an increasingly significant element of Eastern Mediterranean and Indo-Pacific security over the coming decade.

text:
(Part 5)

As with other addictions, listeners may develop a tolerance and begin demanding something stronger. The music becomes louder, more jarring, and more discordant. A person may start with soft rock, progress to rock and roll, and eventually move into heavy metal.

Dr. Bell also noted mood swings among adrenaline addicts, including people addicted to hard music. After the fight-or-flight response comes a period of recovery, followed by a crash. The addict tries to maintain the high, but it cannot last. The longer the high continues, the deeper the crash may become.

He also described despair and an increased tolerance for dangerous activities among music and adrenaline addicts. Danger can produce a similar high, making reckless behavior feel familiar or even comfortable. The brain system designed to protect a person from danger may begin leading that person toward it.

The answer is not to take the same drug and place a Christian label on it. Doing so would be like printing John 3:16 on a bottle of liquor and calling it acceptable. There is no such thing as “Christian cocaine.”

If rock music functions like a drug, then offering a softer version with Christian lyrics may still serve as a gateway into the culture the music was created to express. Research and testimony suggest that some people who begin with Christian rock also listen to secular rock and become deeply influenced by it. The lyrics may change, but the sound keeps the audience.

At times, the sound and presentation of Christian rock appear virtually indistinguishable from secular culture. If Scripture commands Christians to prove all things and hold fast to what is good, something cannot be accepted as Christian merely because it carries a Christian label.

Time reporter and music critic Christopher Farley once wrote that Christian rock sometimes sounds like the Devil. He described “howls, whoops, shrieks, stomping feet” and “menacing bass licks,” along with physical and musical expressions that would appear sinful if they were not being performed in the name of the Lord.

Doing something in the name of the Lord does not automatically make it holy.

When Moses went up the mountain, the people of Israel sacrificed to a golden calf. They worshipped the calf and called it the LORD. The name was right, but the golden calf was not the Lord. Every generation faces the temptation to blend the worship of the god of this world with the worship of the God of Heaven.

Cain offered a sacrifice, but God rejected it because it was not the sacrifice He required. A person can be sincere and still be wrong. Many people involved in contemporary Christian music may be sincere, but sincerity is not the final standard. Scripture is.

Psalm 29:1–2 says:

“Give unto the LORD, O ye mighty, give unto the LORD glory and strength. Give unto the LORD the glory due unto his name; worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness.”

It would be wrong and unbiblical to deny Christian liberty. Musical preferences exist, and culture must be considered. The proper application is not that a Christian must listen only to classical music or sing only hymns written in the seventeenth century.

The proper response is to hear the Spirit of God through the Word of God, which commands believers to prove all things and hold fast to what is good.

We must admit there is an element of culture and subjectivity in this matter. What Joshua thought was “the sound of war in the camp (Exodus 32:17)” Moses knew to be “the noise of them that sing (Exodus 32:18.)” We must remember that the Hebrew music of Christ’s day with joyous tambourines differed greatly from the style and sensibility of austere European classical music. 

Christians possess liberty, but Galatians 5:13 gives an important qualification:

“For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.”

text:
The full speech of Secretary of State Marco Rubio

-----

SECRETARY RUBIO:  There are great ruins all across the world.  In many cases, they are places where history seems to have exhausted itself: remnants of distant cultures that have long passed beyond living memory.

But the Acropolis is different.

For thousands of years, the civilization that built what stands behind me has captivated the imagination of the Western world.  Generations of our statesmen, artists, and philosophers have looked to it – they’ve looked to it with wonder and they’ve looked to it with awe.

Now time has a tendency to dull the senses: great victories and catastrophic defeats, they seem to  shrink to becoming like a footnote in a textbook, another fact for our schoolchildren to memorize and forget.  But the Greeks of antiquity, they seem to have an almost mystical hold on our memory.  They call us back to them, again and again.

480 years before Christ, the armies of Xerxes arrived in this city and they put its sanctuaries to the torch.  Most Athenians had by then evacuated by ship to a nearby island.  But there was a handful of them that refused to leave their home.  So instead, they barricaded themselves in the rocky fortress of the Acropolis to fight an extraordinary last stand, heaving massive stones down the cliffs onto the Persian invaders and holding the greatest empire of the age at bay for days.  They were eventually overwhelmed.  The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood.  And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon.

For 25 centuries since, the Parthenon has stood.  Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow.  And the progeny of the men who built it – the sons of Athens and Rome – have carried their civilization with them to the ends of the Earth.

Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish.

The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity.  Greece is literally carved into the architecture of our government: in the towering columns, in the domes and the monuments across our capital city.  The city where our Constitution was born – Philadelphia – is itself a Greek name.

The men who founded my country were fascinated by the heritage we inherited from yours.  They were exceptionally well-read in history – they were vividly aware of their unique place in it – but no other age of the past held their attention or their imagination quite like that of antiquity.  Many, many people are surprised to learn that the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was not an Enlightenment philosopher or political theorist.  No, the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was Plutarch, the Greek biographer of Greece and Rome’s great men.

Now, much has been written and said about the influence of ancient Greece on the ideas of the American Founders – and, for that matter, on all of the Western philosophers and statesmen that preceded them.  Most of us are familiar with the basic history.  Athens gave us democracy.  Plato and Aristotle gave us Western philosophy.  Our ideas of law, of virtue, of citizenship, and republican government were shaped in the Greek city-states.  Even much of our political vocabulary – words like democracy, tyranny, the word “politics” itself – found its origins here.

Now, all of that is true.  But the things we owe to this place – as Americans, and as Westerners – are actually far far deeper.  These institutions and ideas – these institutions and ideas were the outward expression of more fundamental qualities we see in the ancient Greeks – qualities that can’t be reduced to any particular political system or theory.

Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West: fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory.  An insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates, a hunger to know the mysteries of nature and grasp the secrets of the cosmos.  An impatience with the notion of impossibility, chafing at all boundaries and limits, straining to peer into the depths of the unknown.

These were not just the formulas or precepts of a particular school of philosophy.  They were the characteristic of a people – expressed in their traditions, their stories, their imagination; in the qualities they demanded of their citizens; in the things they lived and fought and died for.

To know them is to know ourselves.

What blossomed here in this place was the Western desire to uncover all that ignorance, darkness, and distance had kept hidden from the mind of man.  The Greeks did not just shape history; the Greeks gave us history itself. Much about – much of what we know about many ancient civilizations comes almost entirely from the records of Greek explorers and historians, explorers and historians who didn’t just chronicle the histories of their own people, but ventured outwards to observe and record the sagas of foreign peoples and cultures all across the world.

Where others looked inward, the Greeks were the first to direct their focus outward, to chase the thrill and glory of seeing all that was strange and new.  It was this trait – it was this trait that would push the West to create and build things that others could not, marking us out from so many other cultures and civilizations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life.

But it is not just the ambition to explore the unknown that we inherit from the Greeks; it is the conviction that the unknown canbe known.  The confidence that the world can be charted and measured and mapped and understood – and that there is a rational order to the cosmos, governed by certain fundamental laws, laws that men can observe and the mind can come to understand.

This was the foundation of the Western mind: our math, our science, our medicine.  Our philosophy, ethics, and religion.  It paved the way for the gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom. It was the foundation of the riches of Christian theology – of Augustine and Aquinas and the whole tradition of natural law.

It gave birth to a civilization marked not just by a common culture, it was marked by a common anthropology – a common view of man and his place in the universe.  Its descendants would share not just the idea of a natural order, but a distinctive understanding of virtue; of destiny and fate; of truth, goodness, and beauty; of a code that dictates how men ought to live; of objective standards and ideals to strive towards.

For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence.  They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft.  The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle – to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.

Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel.  The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat.  Too often these days, we build downwards. We design our standards to ensure no one will lose; we preoccupy ourselves more with the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best.  We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.

The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things.  The ancient Greek city-states were filled.  They were filled with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict.  But from that constant struggle for distinction – from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.

The thumos, as the ancient Greeks called it – the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride – is the heart of great civilization.  And without it?  Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive.

Today, too much of the West has forgotten this quality.  Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional.  We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world.  Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt.  We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness.

The word “nationalism” became a dirty word.  And so we tore down our monuments; we condemned our own history.  And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.  In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay.

And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control.

But others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left – the vacuum left behind by our weakness.  And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead.

And now, today, we find ourselves at a crossroads.  Because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century.  The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.  We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.

Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice.  We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.

We choose to reach for new frontiers: in advanced manufacturing and super intelligence; in drones, weapons, and warfare; in chips, minerals, cyber, and every other domain of human possibility.  To unleash our energy, to rebuild our factories, to return our astronauts to the moon and launch a new age of exploration in space.

Now for all their lofty ideals, the ancient Greeks were not naive.  They understood that nations have interests.  They understood that statecraft requires prudence and diplomacy, but they also understood that it requires the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail.  They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.

This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim – reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization.

We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.

There are already signs.

Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift: skyrocketing defense spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programs, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defense commitments made last year in The Hague.

Greece has been at the center of this shift.  The people of this nation have proved themselves once again to be an indispensable friend to Europe and to the United States alike, on everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally.

And it’s our sincerest hope that all of Europe will follow your example.

Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.  Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age.

And we can.  Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum.  Quite the opposite: our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts.  It is a vision we saw in action just last month, in an unprecedented new agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland – an agreement that will reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO.  All three partners in that deal emerged victorious.  All of Europe – and NATO and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.

We want to win together.  We must win together.

Now it’s has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people.  And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else.

They believed – fiercely – in the ideal of the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds.  But they believed that glory and fame, those things were won through striving, sacrificing and achieving greatly for something larger than yourself.  The recurring hero of the ancient Greek world was the man who was willing to pay any cost for a cause worthy of his loyalty.

We see this in Socrates, who refused to abandon the inquiry into truth even at the cost of his own life.  We see it in the legendary stand of 300 Spartans – surrounded and hopelessly outnumbered by the vast armies of Persia – who refused the chance to save themselves, choosing to fight to the last man rather than abandon their post or abandon their duty.  And we see it in the epic myth of Achilles, who is offered the choice to return home and live a long and peaceful life – but chooses instead to remain at Troy and perish in pursuit of eternal glory.

These – these are the qualities that would shape the Western moral imagination.  From the Christian martyr who refused to betray his faith to the patriot who gave his life for his country; from Saint Thomas More to the Battle of the Alamo, running through the immortal closing words of the Declaration of Independence of the United States which says, “We mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country.  Our heroes, the heroes of the West are those who choose to remain faithful to their duty precisely when it is most difficult and painful to do so: the man who is bound by his word, the soldier who will not abandon his post, the captain, the proverbial captain, who goes down with his ship.

This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.

Our heroes – our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but our heroes do not worship death.  It is precisely because we value life that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles.  Now, we take the West’s conception of these things – heroism, honor, duty – we take these things for granted.  We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places.  They are not.  They are the product of a distinct character, a distinct character which arose here and shaped the whole story of the civilization that came after it.  A civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.

The men who built the Parthenon were succeeded by the architects of European Christendom, who raised the cathedrals of Milan, Cologne, and Florence.  The quest to perfect the human form that moved the ancient Greek sculptors found a new expression in Michelangelo.  The Greek philosophers’ search for the structure of the universe was inherited by Copernicus, and then Galileo, then Kepler, and in Newton.

The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’ discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon.  And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.

And in America, that same tradition rediscovered itself anew.  An open and wild land became the site of a great revival of Western imagination and ambition.  The Greek aspiration for new horizons became the American frontier spirit.  The civilization of Athens and Rome transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire.

The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world.

Together, we must now rediscover that spirit.  We are at an inflection point – an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization.

The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity.

National interests did not vanish in the face of international institutions.  War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace.  Other states continued to arm, to seek influence, to compete for territory, and technology, and resources, and markets, and energy, and power.

And now, there is war again.  There is new competition between great powers again.  There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again.

And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together – understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them.  And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.

We have built a model of that with our partners here in Greece.  In our defense partnerships, in energy and technology, in our shared ambition to secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration.

Our friendship dates back to the earliest years of my nation.  When Greece rose in 1821 to recover its independence after centuries of Ottoman rule, Americans recognized something familiar in that struggle.  Three years later, the great American statesman Daniel Webster, he delivered a famous address to Congress, helping bring the cause of the Greek Revolution before the representatives of the young American republic.

And he began by calling their attention to everything around them.  This is what he said in his speech; he said:  “This free form of government, this popular assembly… this practice of free debate, and public discussion, the contest of mind with mind… even the edifice in which we assemble, these proportioned columns, this ornamented architecture, all remind us that Greece has existed, and that we, like the rest of mankind, are greatly her debtors.”

Those words are as true today as they were when he said them.  And all of us – not just Americans, but Europeans and our friends across the West – must relearn the lessons our forefathers took from this place and from its history.

The history of Greece – the history of Greece does not just offer us a glimpse – it does not offer a glimpse of our institutions in their earliest forms.  The history of Greece shows us an image of ourselves.

It shows us that ours is the inheritance of great heroes, and that we should be proud – that we should be intensely proud – of where we come from.  We should marvel at what our forefathers carved out of this countryside.  The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man.  And it began here, with the first men and women of the West.  From them – from them – we can rediscover the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time.

Thank you.

Study Notes - (Pulpit Version Explained) (PART B) 

Every Christian will join in saying, "Grace be with all them who love cur Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity and in truth."
II. SPIRITUAL UNITY IS THE UNITY OF A COMMON INTEREST. And that interest for Jews was the honor of Jehovah, the nation’s God; it is for Christians the honor of Jehovah-Jesus, the manifested God. How a common interest blends men together is seen in societies, clubs, conferences, etc. It is the secret of the unity of Churches.
III. SPIRITUAL UNITY IS THE HARMONY OF VARIED FORMS. Different-shaped hills made up the unity of Jerusalem. Different-colored flowers make up the unity of the garden. Different moods in worshippers make up the unity of a religious service. Different mental apprehensions of truth make up the unity of the Christian doctrine. Reunion of mere samenesses is not a pleasing thing either to God or man. We do not care for things cut to an exact pattern, or pressed into one mould. In variety lies charm; and variety is not only consistent with unity, it is a condition of unity if the unity is to go deeper than mere appearances. "That vast society in whose ample bosom the souls of Christian men from generation to generation find shelter and warmth and nourishment, is the reality of which the old Syrian city was a material type. This is the Jerusalem of the Christian Creed, ’I believe in one holy Catholic and Apostolic Church.’ There may be controversies among Christians as to the exact extent and direction of its walls, just as there are controversies among antiquarians as to the extent and direction of the walls of its material prototype, but as to its place in the thoughts and affections of the true Christian man there should be no room for controversy. No other association of men can have such claims on the heart of a Christian as the Church of God." "The true remedy for disappointment and sorrow on the score of shortcomings and differences within the sacred city is to be found in such prayers as we offer in our holiest service to the Divine Majesty, beseeching him to inspire continually the universal Church with the spirit of truth, unity, and concord."—R.T.
Psa_122:4
The mission of the great feasts.
"The pre-Mosaic festivals were pure nature-festivals. In the changes of the seasons, and of the phenomena of heaven, nature always displays a gracious adaptation to the needs of man, giving him special opportunities and intervals when he may rest for a considerable while from his ordinary toil, and devote himself unreservedly to higher thoughts." The work of Moses in developing, and adapting to a purpose, these nature-festivals needs to be carefully studied. He gave them precisely historical and religious relations and suggestions. The "tribes of Israel" is a phrase belonging to the old times of Israel’s glory. (For the three assemblies, see Exo_23:17; Exo_34:23; Deu_16:16.) These annual pilgrimages are spoken of as the subject of a Divine testimony or precept to Israel. Without attempting to discuss elaborately the mission of these feasts, there are four things to which attention may be directed.
I. THEY WERE DESIGNED TO PRESERVE THE NATIONAL UNITY. It should be kept in mind that Israel was not so much a tribe as a set of tribes, and there was always the danger of jealousies producing divisions. The times of the judges reveal how easily the national life could be broken up. Something in which the unity of the nation could be publicly recognized was absolutely necessary. This something must be in the nature of a command from the central authority; and it must take a regular and systematic form. Compare pilgrimages to Mecca, and even the country fairs and national holidays, which have their distinctly national uses. Show the moral influence of such blendings of people from different parts of the country; and explain that the preservation of the unity of Israel as a nation bore direct relation to the testimony it made for Jehovah among the nations. Statesmen still make it their supreme aim to secure the essential unity of the composite sections that make up the nations they govern. Their mottoes always are, "United we conquer; divided we fall." "Union is strength." A constantly repeated united national act is an important help to preserving national unity.
II. THEY WERE DESIGNED TO PRESERVE THE RELIGIOUS UNITY. Unity is the key-note of the Jewish religion. It expresses the conception of God. "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord." So unity must be the idea everywhere and in everything. The primary idea of the religion must get representation in every conceivable form. A multiplicity of conceptions of God is condemned. A variety of altars is regarded as distinctly mischievous. And even an extension of sacrifice and service beyond Jerusalem was not permissible. The whole nation was required to join in the most solemn acts of worship—the Passover, Day of Atonement, etc. Subject to all kinds of disintegrating influences in their tribal associations, the nation was recalled to what may be termed its doctrinal and ecclesiastical unity three times a year. The formal religious unity so jealously preserved for the Jews should not be thought of as requiring our formal imitation. It was the outward and pictorial illustration of that spiritual unity which is the true religious unity, the family unity of those who have one Father.
III. THEY WERE DESIGNED TO CONSERVE THE GREAT NATIONAL TRUST. Israel, or the Abrahamic race, was called out from other nations to be the depositories of those primary truths concerning God which were imperiled by man’s being left to his self-development. "To them were committed the oracles of God," which include the threefold conception of God as one, spiritual, holy; and only to be served by righteousness. This was the national trust; and it must be kept ever before the minds of the people. In the most solemn way they were reminded of it at the great feasts.
IV. THEY WERE DESIGNED TO SANCTIFY THE NATIONAL HOLIDAY-TIMES. The feasts of heathen religions are times of moral license, only suggested by the drunkenness and immorality of country fairs. Israel must realize that all life and relations are consecrated to God. They must see that the true relations and pleasures of life must be sanctified, must be kept within the holy restraints of religion. Their feast-times were their great holiday-times, and in them joy must blend with self-restraint, and freedom with purity.—R.T.
Psa_122:5
The blending of the civil and religious.
This subject need not be treated controversially. All are agreed that a vital union of the civil and religious, of Church and State, is desirable, and even necessary. There may be differences of opinion as to the formal ways in which such union may be represented. If we look for its realization in the ancient Jewish nation, we must bear in mind that it was based on the theocratic notion. The unseen Jehovah was as truly the Head of the State as he was Head of the Church. Modern difficulty arises from the apparent necessity for making an ordinary human being at once the head of both State and Church. What was possible when men could look past all delegated authorities to one unseen, spiritual, and supreme Being, in whom absolute authority rested, may not be possible under modern conditions. We must fully recover the theocratic sentiment before we can safely blend the civil and religious. Jerusalem was first the civil metropolis before it became the "city of God." It became the religious capital of the nation because it was already the civil capital (Deu_17:8, Deu_17:9). Israel, as the people of the revelation, was at once a civil society and a Church—the two were not then essentially distinct, as has been and is the case in Christendom.
I. THE CIVIL AND RELIGIOUS ARE THE TWO SIDES OF MAN’S RELATIONS. There is no conceivable antagonism between them ideally, whatever there may be actually. Man is a being who is set in relations with God and with his fellow-man. And one set of relations is as right and as necessary as the other. A man’s relations with God are the concern of religion. A man’s relations with his fellow-man are the business of civil governments. No man can meet his natural obligations by exaggerating the importance of either one of those relations and neglecting the other. No man can be truly religious and neglect his civil duties. And this the apostles clearly taught the early Christians.
II. THE CIVIL AND THE RELIGIOUS CAN BE HARMONIOUSLY BLENDED. They always have been in the most manly and most Christian man. They have been in the representative nation of Israel. They have been in the healthiest and best periods of modern nations. They can be when the sense of God dominates both.—R.T.
Psa_122:6, Psa_122:7
Peace, prosperity, and prayer.
Emphatically a pilgrim-song, and by a poet who usually lived in the country. Describes the pleasure felt at invitation to join a party who were going up to one of the feasts. We have the joy and music of the journey; then the impressions on arrival, the first passionate delight of being in the holy city—a city beautifully built, well compacted, adorned with palaces, and strongly fortified. Observe the intense feeling with which Jerusalem was regarded by Jews. Beautifully situated, it was the center of national and religious interest. Relics of the national feeling remain in the desire of modern Jews to die within its walls, and in the scenes at the "Place of Wailing." Many of us can understand this. We have a Jerusalem round which our thoughts entwine—the church of our fathers and of our childhood. What associations we have with it! Three words are here connected—Peace, prosperity, and prayer.
I. PEACE VERY LARGELY DEPENDS UPON PROSPERITY. "Peace" is a word with an extensive, beautiful, and suggestive connotation. We, perhaps, cannot fully realize it by any aid of memory; we can only enter into it with the help of the familiar engravings of ’War’ and ’Peace.’ It is not possible to overrate the value of peace for nations, or for Churches, or for families. But it largely depends on prosperity. This may be illustrated by the inward life of the religious man. Devotion and work are allowed to flag, soul-prosperity fails, and at once doubts and fears come to spoil the soul’s peace. It may be illustrated in the life of the Church. When work and zeal and spiritual life—the signs of Church prosperity—fail, then differences are sure to come, roots of bitterness spring up.
II. PROSPERITY VERY LARGELY DEPENDS UPON PRAYER, Show the natural influence of prayer. It lifts into strength the better nature. Show the supernatural influence of prayer in bringing to us spiritual power. Plead for renewal of interest in private and individual prayer; and for more frequent and earnest united prayer. Secret forces are the mighty ones. Men take little count of the atmosphere, but it holds up the clouds. Who is it, then, upholds the prosperity of the Churches? Who are the peacemakers and the peace-keepers? Look below the surface, and you will be sure to see the men and women of faith and prayer. They gain for us prosperity, which leads in peace.—R.T.
Psa_122:8
The religious value of the patriotic spirit.
"For my brethren and companions’ sakes, I will wish thee prosperity." This may be the expression of a pilgrim on leaving Jerusalem to return to his home. The love of the psalmist for his country was patriotism. Perowne says, "The last four verses of the psalm breathe a spirit of the noblest, most unselfish, patriotism. Not for his own sake, but for the sake of his brethren—the people at large—and for the sake of his God, his temple, and his service, he wishes peace to Jerusalem, and calls upon others to wish her peace. With love to Israel and love to Jehovah there is naturally united a warm affection for Jerusalem, a hearty interest in her welfare.
I. THE PATRIOTIC SPIRIT IS KIN WITH THE RELIGIOUS. The moral value of both is the same, and it lies in taking a man out beyond himself, and interesting him in something other than himself. The patriotic spirit interests him in other people, the religious spirit interests him in God. They are also alike in their power to arouse and culture emotion, and to inspire self-denying acts.
II. THE PATRIOTIC SPIRIT NOURISHES THE RELIGIOUS. According to the principle laid down by St. John, "If a man love not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" It is a delusion that religion claims isolation; it is both expressed and nourished through the temporal. Religion separated from life and its common claims and obligations is but weak and deluding sentiment. Patriotic Moses is pious Moses. The separation of Christian men from political, civil, and social interests is entirely a sectarian delusion. The noblest and the healthiest Christian lives have always been, and are always sure to be, in the truest sense patriotic.
III. THE PATRIOTIC SPIRIT QUALIFIES THE RELIGIOUS. For while it is quite true that man is not all body and human relations, it is also quite true that he is not all soul and soul-relations. The religious side of man’s nature can be exaggerated, and often is. The unworldly may become a snare as well as the worldly. It is helpful to qualify the heavenly by the duties of the earthly.—R.T.
Psa_122:9
Piety blessing national life.
"Yea, because of the house of the Lord our God, I will seek to do thee good" (Prayer-book Version). Piety is seen in the tender, almost pathetic, interest the man has in the temple, where the worship of God is conducted; the temple which is so rich with hallowed associations. That interest fills the psalmist with admiration for the city, and concern for the well-being of those who dwell in it, and the nation of which they all form parts. There is a possible injurious selfishness of piety, which all sectarianism tends to nourish. It localizes and narrows the interest; encourages a kind of tribal jealousy. The sect should never be permitted to take our concern from the nation, whose moral and spiritual well-being should ever be the subject of our prayer and our service. The psalmist "prays for Jerusalem because of Zion. How the Church salts and savours all around it! The presence of Jehovah our God endears to us every place wherein he reveals his glory."
I. PIETY GOES WITH GOOD CITIZENSHIP, AND THAT BLESSES NATIONAL LIFE. Character is power in city and in national life, and even the higher possibilities of human character belong to the religious life. The peace-loving and peace-seeking citizens are the truly religions. Those who plead for righteousness in business relations, and charity in human relations, are the truly religious. The examples of good citizenship—not of noisy citizenship—are the truly pious. Of old the blessing of a nation was conceived to be its numbers; we know better than that now. "Righteousness exalteth a nation," and righteousness depends on righteous men, and righteous men are they who have the fear and love of God before their eyes. The heavenly citizens are the best earthly ones.
II. PIETY GOES WITH SACRIFICING MINISTRY, AND THAT BLESSES NATIONAL LIFE. It should never be lost sight of that the two key-notes of Christianity are righteousness and service. A Christian cannot be content without doing good. And so the Christian citizen is an active force for good. Wherever he is, he is doing some good, lifting some burden, helping some struggler, and his ministry therefore becomes a national benediction.—R.T.
HOMILIES BY C. SHORT
Psa_122:1-9
Worship.
"I was glad when they said unto me," etc. This beautiful ode is supposed to have been by one dwelling in the country, who had been invited to join, and had joined, a company of pilgrims on their way to one of the feasts at Jerusalem; on his return, this ode embodied the sentiments that had been inspired.
I. THE JOY OF WORSHIP. The delight of anticipation. (Psa_122:1.) The brooding gladness which dwells on some anticipated great occasion. His imagination would draw pictures of Jerusalem and the temple on the way thither, and all their sacred historical and religious associations; as we try to think of heaven and of the scenes in which our nature shall be perfected.
II. THE JOY OF RETROSPECTION. (Psa_122:2-5.)
1. He remembers with what awe and delight he was spellbound within the gates of the city and temple. Think how a Mohammedan would feel at Mecca, or a Roman Catholic at St. Peter’s in Rome, or a modern Christian in visiting Calvary, or Bethlehem, or the sepulcher where Christ lay. But the awe and delight of spiritual worship transcend all the emotions inspired by hallowed places—"in spirit and in truth."
2. He was greatly moved by the sight of the stateliness and beauty of the city, which had been rebuilt after the Exile. (Psa_122:3.) The restoration of a national structure, or of the nation itself after forfeiting its glory, or of a human life and character after loss and shame, greatly moves all sympathetic minds. The transition from darkness into light is very great.
3. The tribes gathered on such occasions, came up in obedience to the Divine law, to worship God with a national thanksgiving. (Psa_122:4.) The author of the psalm was a grateful participant in the worship. The law of grateful worship is the law of all reasonable spiritual beings, the very necessity of their nature, and therefore full of delights.
4. The "thrones of judgment" for the civil law were under the shadow of the throne of mercy, or "the mercy-seat." The supreme tribunal was to be in the same place as the sanctuary (Deu_17:8, Deu_17:9). Law and mercy, both in God and in the best man, are always closely related.
5. The highest result of true worship is to produce the spirit of peace. (Psa_122:6-9.) Between God and man, among nations and Churches, and between man and man.—S.
