text:
Anastas Mikoyan (1895–1978) was an Armenian-born Soviet statesman and Old Bolshevik who survived five decades of high-level Soviet politics, serving under every leader from Vladimir Lenin through Leonid Brezhnev. He served on the State Defense Committee (GKO), orchestrating critical military supplies, food logistics, and transport for the Red Army. While he participated in Stalinist structures and loyalty tests, he managed to navigate the terror alive—a feat that earned him the title of the ultimate "survivor" in Soviet politics. Anastas Mikoyan Moscow joke centers around his legendary reputation as the ultimate survivor of Soviet politics. One afternoon, Anastas Mikoyan is leaving a meeting inside the Kremlin. As he steps out into Red Square, a sudden, torrential downpour begins.

A fellow Politburo member notices he doesn't have an umbrella and runs after him, shouting:

"Comrade Mikoyan! Wait! Let me get you an umbrella, or at least a raincoat! You'll get completely soaked!"

Mikoyan turns back with a knowing smile, waves his hand, and calmly replies:
"Don't worry, Comrade. I'll just walk between the raindrops."

Mikoyan is remembered as a master political survivor who transitioned from a revolutionary in the civil war era to a reform-minded administrator in the Cold War. His brother, Artem Mikoyan, co-founded the famous MiG fighter jet design bureau... 

A popular Moscow joke insisted that Anastas Mikoyan could walk across Red Square in a torrential downpour without an umbrella and reach the Kremlin completely dry, simply darting between the raindrops. For more than five decades, the sharp-featured Armenian Bolshevik performed an even more miraculous feat: he survived the bloodiest political labyrinth of the twentieth century. While the Russian Revolution devoured nearly every one of its founding fathers in execution cellars and arctic gulags, Mikoyan remained near the summit of Soviet power. From the civil war battlefields alongside Vladimir Lenin to the paranoia of Joseph Stalin, through Nikita Khrushchev’s volatile thaw and into the stagnation of Leonid Brezhnev, Mikoyan became the Kremlin’s ultimate survivor.

Mikoyan’s uncanny talent for outliving catastrophe began in the crucible of the Russian Civil War. In 1918, serving as a young commissar in Azerbaijan, he was captured by British-backed interventionist forces. When twenty-six Bolshevik leaders—the legendary 26 Baku Commissars—were rounded up and executed by firing squad in the Turkmen desert, Mikoyan inexplicably escaped the death list due to an administrative paperwork omission. Joining the ruling circle in Moscow during the 1920s, he tied his fortunes to Joseph Stalin, rising to the Politburo and managing the Soviet Union's domestic trade and food supply. In 1936, Mikoyan traveled to the United States on a three-month industrial tour, fascinated by American efficiency. He returned to transform the Soviet kitchen, introducing mass-produced ice cream, canned goods, factory bakeries, and mass-market hamburger patties that Soviet citizens dubbed "Mikoyan cutlets."

Yet survival in Stalin’s Moscow demanded absolute moral compromise. When the Great Terror decimated the Bolshevik leadership in the late 1930s, claiming old comrades like Bukharin, Rykov, and Zinoviev, Mikoyan survived by rubber-stamping execution orders and conducting purges in Armenia. Even then, proximity to Stalin offered no permanent safety. In October 1952, at the 19th Party Congress, an increasingly paranoid Stalin delivered a venomous speech accusing Mikoyan and Vyacheslav Molotov of right-wing deviations and disloyalty. Mikoyan knew the script; his arrest and liquidation were imminent. He was saved only by the calendar: in March 1953, Stalin suffered a fatal stroke, leaving Mikoyan alive while rivals scrambled to consolidate power.

text:
Since I’m not able to respond to your later post quoting this one (comments are restricted), I’ll respond here. This charge against paedobaptists is absurd. In Hebrews 6, the author’s fuller point is that once you abandon Christ, there remains no further sacrifice for sin—that is, there is no other way of salvation apart from Christ. Who the author is writing to must be kept at the forefront: he is writing to Jewish Christians, likely in Jerusalem (debated ikik), and evidently some of the audience were returning, or at least tempted to return, to the old covenant order (cf. Deut. 4:29–31; 30:1–10; Num. 15:30–31). But one cannot return to that order and its sacrificial system and expect to be restored to Yahweh through the blood of animals, because—as the author will later expound on—Christ is, and always has been, the substance of those sacrifices. The author later states categorically that “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Heb. 10:4; cf. Lev. 4:13–14; 16:21–34); those sacrifices were shadows pointing to Christ, whose blood alone takes away sin (Heb. 9:15; cf. Rom. 3:25). Therefore, to abandon Christ and return to the old sacrificial system is to reject the very substance from which those sacrifices had ever derived any salvific meaning. In that sense, further sacrifice is to “crucify again the Son of God” (Heb. 6:4–6; cf. 9:24–28; 10:26–29)—to repudiate the once-for-all sacrifice and return to the shadows as though Christ the substance still needed to be offered (Heb. 7:27; 10:1–2, 11–14; 12:25). The impossibility in view in 6:4–6, then, is not necessarily that a truly repentant apostate who returns to Christ would be refused by God, but that one cannot be restored to repentance and reconciliation with the Father while repudiating the Son and returning to that old sacrificial order, as though reconciliation with the Father could still be found in animal blood pointing to the very crucifixion of the Son (cf. Heb. 3:12–14; 6:1; 9:14; 10:10–14, 26; 12:17, 25, 28). There is much irony here. Their supposed repentance of the Son would, in fact, be a repudiation of the only means by which genuine repentance and reconciliation with the Father is possible. The present active participles in the Greek of verse 6 seem consistent with this interpretation, insofar as they can be understood temporally, describing a continuing repudiation of Christ. Therefore, I do not think the author must be saying that true repentance back to Christ is impossible. Moreover, the agricultural imagery immediately following in verses 7–8 appears to echo Deuteronomy's covenantal blessings and curses (Deut. 11:11–17, 26–28; 29:22–28). Yet Deuteronomy explicitly anticipates repentance and restoration even after covenantal judgment (Deut. 4:29–31; 30:1–10). Significantly, Hebrews describes the unfruitful land as “near” to being cursed (Heb. 6:8), and whose end is to soon be burned (which did happen not much long after in A.D. 70; cf. Heb. 8:13; 10:25, 26–31; Matt. 10:23; 24), before encouraging its recipients toward perseverance and expressing confidence in better things concerning them (Heb. 6:9–12). Thus, the covenantal imagery need not imply that every instance of covenantal apostasy renders subsequent restoration categorically impossible. Paul explicitly says concerning unbelieving Jews, who had already been broken off from covenantal participation through unbelief, that “if they do not continue in their unbelief, [they] will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again” (Rom. 11:23). These were not strangers to Yahweh's covenant, but members of the covenant people to whom belonged the covenants and promises (Rom. 9:4). Yet, having rejected Christ—the very fulfillment and substance of those covenants—they were broken off through unbelief and faithlessness. Nevertheless, Paul explicitly affirms the possibility of their restoration. Thus, covenantal apostasy does not, in itself, establish the categorical impossibility of subsequent repentance and restoration (cf. Jas. 5:19-20; Acts 8:13, 18–22; 2 Tim. 2:12–13, 24–26; Gal. 2:14; 5:4, 7–10; 6:1). If the Jews, already being broken off in their unbelief (Rom. 11:17, 19–20), can then be restored, true repentance cannot be said to be impossible. This, of course, does not attempt to dodge the other apostasy passages (Heb. 10:26–39; 2 Pet. 2:20–22; 1 John 2:19; et al.)—and rightly so. Apostasy remains a real danger for those who are in covenant with Yahweh, including these unbelieving Jews, but I do not believe this particular passage in Hebrews 6 must be read to say that true repentance after apostasy is categorically impossible. As you yourself noted, that interpretation does not seem to align with the reality concerning those within the Church who do fall, yet are eventually restored. Rather, I interpret Hebrews 6—which is an incredibly hard passage to understand—as a particular warning to Jews against abandoning the Son and seeking restoration to the Father through the vanishing old order (Heb. 8:13). Of course, there remains much work to fully develop this thesis, and perhaps I'm wrong, but this is where I'm currently at. F. W. Farrar has a similar exegesis of the text, though not exact. Regardless, the apostasy in 6:4–6 seems to be of a particular kind.

text:
@Kalshi is breaking the law in Iowa, we've researched - @BrennaBird @KimReynoldsIA please look into this 

Count 1 — Unlicensed gambling, Iowa Code ch. 99F and 725.

Kalshi sells a contract that pays $1 if Sand is inaugurated and $0 if he is not. That is a wager on a future contingent event. Iowa treats that as gambling unless it is licensed. Kalshi has no Iowa racing-and-gaming permit. Locher already held that the Commodity Exchange Act does not clearly preempt Iowa gambling law. The Iowa case is therefore: election contracts offered to Iowans are illegal wagers, and the Sand market is one of them.

Count 2 — Deceptive act, Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, Iowa Code § 714.16.

The actionable statement is not the trade. It is the label. Kalshi tells the public Sand has an “87% chance” or “89% chance,” and its politics account posts that figure as an all-time-high probability. A contract price is not a probability. Research on Kalshi’s own markets finds favorite-longshot bias: expensive contracts are not clean probability estimates. On this race the platform puts an 89% figure next to a 51–43 poll split. That is a misleading representation of the chance Sand wins, capable of moving donors, press, and turnout. Disclaimers in small type do not cure a banner that says “chance.”

Count 3 — Failure of an orderly market, used as the factual predicate.

As a CFTC-designated contract market, Kalshi must list contracts not readily susceptible to manipulation and must police abusive trading. This book is only about $1.4 million. A motivated buyer can hold an elevated price. Kalshi then republishes that price as the race’s official chance. The Iowa use of Count 3 is not a private CFTC lawsuit. It is evidence for Counts 1 and 2: an unlicensed wager whose published “odds” are not a reliable probability and can be supported by concentrated money.

text:
WHO PAYS FOR $105 OIL? DELTA $DAL GIVES THE FIRST ANSWER BEFORE FRIDAY'S OPEN:

Delta Air Lines (DAL) at $82.41, -$0.56 / -0.67% today.

Oil jumped more than 5% this morning on reports that President Trump is weighing new large-scale strikes on Iran. Delta is the first US airline to report on July through September, tomorrow before the opening bell, and fuel is the cost that swings its profit most. Investors already expect a soft quarter. What this morning puts at risk is Delta's forecast for the whole year, which needed a strong finish even before Brent crossed $105.

- Brent crude, the global oil benchmark: $105.31 a barrel, +$5.11 / +5.10% from Wednesday's settlement price.
- Heating oil futures, the usual stand-in for jet fuel: $4.84 a gallon, +$0.21 / +4.64% from Wednesday's settlement price.
- S&P 500: 7,779.07, -22.70 points / -0.29%.

People familiar with the discussions told NBC News that no decision has been made. Trump said late Wednesday: "I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop." The broad market is taking that in stride. An airline cannot, because its fuel is refined from the same crude.

Delta wrote its summer forecast on July 10. It assumed fuel would cost about $3.15 a gallon, everything included, based on market prices for future delivery as of July 2. The timing helped: June was jet fuel's cheapest month since February. Then the price climbed in every month of the quarter. Jet fuel for immediate delivery on the Gulf Coast, the main US refining hub, by the US Energy Information Administration's count:

- June: $3.04 a gallon.
- July: $3.40.
- August: $3.72.
- September: $4.39.

Each measured against its own earlier quarter:

- Delta's July-September assumption: 78 cents a gallon under the $3.93 it paid in April-June.
- The Gulf Coast price: about 20 cents a gallon higher in July-September than in April-June.

Delta's forecast had fuel getting cheaper. The market made it dearer.

What a dime is worth, from Delta's April-June quarter:

- Fuel bill: $4.4B at $3.93 a gallon, about 1.1 billion gallons.
- Each 10 cents a gallon: about $110M a quarter, near 8% of the $1.4B Delta earned before taxes and one-time items.

Wall Street has done that math for the summer. Analysts' average forecast is about $1.88 a share of adjusted profit, the measure that leaves out one-time items. That is below the $2.00-$2.50 Delta gave in July, so a miss on the quarter would surprise no one.

The year is different, because the full-year forecast Delta reaffirmed in July still stands:

- 2026 forecast: $6.50-$7.50 a share.
- January-June, already reported: $2.20 ($0.64 + $1.56).
- Still needed from July-December to reach the bottom of the range: $4.30.

If the summer lands where analysts expect:

- October-December would need about $2.42 a share to reach $6.50.
- The same quarter of 2025 earned $1.55.

That quarter is eight days old, and Brent settled above $100 on every one of its trading days before this morning's jump.

The case against a cut is that Delta has two cushions the fuel price does not show. The first is fares. In April, Delta said it was meaningfully slowing the growth in the seats it flies until fuel costs improve, and fewer new seats keep planes full and fares firm. Premium revenue, the money from its pricier seats up front, rose 17% in April-June. Delta forecast total revenue growth in the mid-teens for the summer.

The second is a refinery. Delta owns one through its Monroe Energy unit, and it earns more when refined fuel prices run ahead of crude. It made $351M of operating profit in April-June, against a $10M loss a year earlier. Per gallon, the help is small: 11 cents in April-June, on fuel that cost 75% more than a year before. An outage that began in mid-June cut its expected help to about 5 cents a gallon for the summer.

The stock has priced some of this. Delta touched $95.68 on July 2, its high for the past year, on the same day its fuel assumption was set. It now sits 11.1% below that day's close.

United Airlines (UAL) at $107.84, -$2.33 / -2.11% today.

United owns no refinery and has fallen 19.1% since its own July 2 close. It reports on October 20, after the close, so whatever fuel price Delta assumes for October-December tomorrow becomes the yardstick United's forecast gets read against. The Growth Len5 is watching United, #11 of 30, because about 10 times its past year of profit is a price that leans on little further growth.

Delta is on none of the six Len5 watchlists. The nearest is Growth, which looks for profit that keeps rising at a price that does not already assume it. Delta has the price half, at about 14 times its past year of profit. It lacks the rising half: analysts' full-year averages all sit under $6 a share, against $5.82 in 2025. What would put Delta on the Growth Len5: a full-year forecast kept at $6.50 or better tomorrow, then earned with fares that carry the fuel bill.

Tomorrow, read three things before the quarter's profit: whether the $6.50-$7.50 range survives, what fuel price Delta now assumes for October-December next to the $3.15 it used for the summer, and whether revenue still grew in the mid-teens. A range kept near its floor with fuel assumed near today's prices would say travelers are absorbing the bill. A cut toward the analysts' averages would say Delta's owners are. The key risk sits outside any forecast: a decision in Washington to resume the strikes that moved oil this morning.

Delta set its summer fuel price coming off jet fuel's cheapest month since February. Tomorrow it sets the next one with Brent past $105, and the size of any cut to the year is the first hard measure of who pays for this morning's news.

Not investment advice.

text:
⚡️Washington is beginning to discover that American corporate success can become economically hostile to American workers.

That is where this is heading.

For decades, the bargain was straightforward. Help American technology companies dominate global markets, and their success produces American jobs, higher wages, tax revenue, and national prosperity.

AI is breaking the employment side of that bargain.

Microsoft can become substantially more profitable while employing fewer people. Its revenue can accelerate while its demand for domestic analysts, developers, administrators, and middle managers contracts. The company can contribute enormously to GDP while distributing a declining share of its economic value through ordinary wages.

A country can become richer while a growing share of its educated population becomes economically less necessary.

That possibility has enormous political consequences.

Trump is now operating under two increasingly incompatible objectives. He wants American technology companies to win the global intelligence race. He also wants American workers protected from displacement.

The first objective rewards automation. The second eventually requires confronting its consequences.

Immigration enforcement offers an immediate political instrument. Washington can restrict labor certification, punish employers accused of abusing visa programs, and claim to be protecting American jobs.

But suppose Microsoft eliminates 20,000 positions because automated systems can perform the underlying work. Preventing the company from hiring 5,000 foreign workers does not restore those 20,000 positions. The demand for that labor has disappeared.

And that exposes the next phase.

The political fight over immigration will increasingly become a political fight over who receives the economic gains from automation.

The pressure will migrate toward corporate tax treatment, government procurement, subsidies, domestic employment obligations, workforce displacement, and eventually the distribution of AI-generated wealth.

The companies most responsible for American technological supremacy will simultaneously become targets of American economic resentment.

That is the conflict taking shape.

The likely sequence through 2027 and 2028 is increasingly aggressive enforcement against foreign labor substitution, selective protection for genuinely scarce AI talent, and growing political scrutiny of technology companies whose profits rise while employment falls.

The larger fight over automation itself comes later, as the employment effects become harder to attribute to immigration or cyclical weakness.

Reasons to Visit Uganda 🇺🇬 

Known as the "Pearl of Africa," Uganda packs an extraordinary range of landscapes, wildlife, and cultural depth into a compact country. 

Here are ten top reasons to visit:

​Mountain Gorilla Trekking in Bwindi: 
Bwindi Impenetrable National Park and Mgahinga Gorilla National Park are home to over half of the world’s remaining endangered mountain gorillas. Spending an hour walking in the presence of a habituated gorilla family is consistently ranked among the world’s top wildlife experiences.

​World-Class Chimpanzee Tracking: 
In Kibale National Park—known as the primate capital of East Africa—you can track wild chimpanzee troops through dense tropical rainforest alongside colobus and red-tailed monkeys.

​Rare Tree-Climbing Lions: 
Queen Elizabeth National Park’s remote Ishasha sector is one of only two places on Earth where resident lion prides regularly spend their afternoons lounging in massive fig trees.

​The Raw Power of Murchison Falls: 
In Murchison Falls National Park, the entire Victoria Nile forces its way through a narrow, 7-meter rocky gap before plunging 43 meters into the "Devil's Cauldron," creating one of the most powerful natural water surges on the planet.

​Big Game Safaris Without the Crowds:
 Across parks like Murchison Falls, Queen Elizabeth, and the rugged, remote Kidepo Valley in the north, you can encounter elephants, lions, leopards, Rothschild's giraffes, and cape buffalo with a fraction of the safari vehicle traffic seen in neighboring regional parks.

​Whitewater Rafting and Adventure in Jinja: 
Located at the historical source of the Nile, Jinja is East Africa’s adrenaline hub, famous for Grade 5 whitewater rafting, kayaking, bungee jumping, and quad biking along the riverbanks.

​Hiking the "Mountains of the Moon" (Rwenzoris): 
The UNESCO-listed Rwenzori Mountains feature dramatic alpine trekking with jagged peaks, giant heather forests, and equatorial glaciers—offering one of Africa’s most diverse high-altitude trekking routes.

​A Birdwatcher's Paradise: 
With over 1,060 recorded bird species, Uganda is a premier global birding destination. Highlights include searching for the prehistoric-looking Shoebill stork in the papyrus wetlands of Mabamba Swamp.

​Tranquil Island and Crater Lake Escapes: 
From the 29 scattered islands of serene, bilharzia-free Lake Bunyonyi to the secluded beaches of the Ssese Islands in Lake Victoria and the crater lakes near Fort Portal, the country offers peaceful retreats surrounded by lush, terraced hills.

​Vibrant Culture, Food, and Warm Hospitality: 
Uganda is celebrated for its exceptionally welcoming culture across more than 50 distinct ethnic communities. 

Beyond the wildlife, you can experience Kampala's lively nightlife, traditional Ndere dance performances, and street food staples like the iconic "Rolex" (an omelette rolled inside fresh chapati).

Uganda ❤️🇺🇬 
By Robert Phoenix

text:
Eli Junior Kroupi: The Arsenal Fit #AFC

Could Kroupi be the next major signing to bolster Arsenal's somewhat thin attacking depth? 

At just 20, the Frenchman already possesses one of the most unique attacking profiles in the Premier League

With Arsenal lacking a reliable and consistent goal threat at the moment, Kroupi feels like the type of high ceiling profile worth exploring in serious detail.

I thoroughly enjoyed writing this article and I would appreciate any tactical nuances and feedback on my analysis. 

I have also attached a compilation of some of his shooting actions, chance creation actions and all his goals from last season for a simpler visual understanding. I have also attached a player scout report in A4 format and two very basic tactical image for those who prefer a shorter analysis structure.

Kroupi Summarised:

Kroupi’s fit at Arsenal is interesting because his "9.5" profile gives Arteta several different ways of using him. He can operate as a lone #9, drop underneath a focal point, start slightly deeper before attacking the box as a second striker, or play from the left of the front three as an inside forward. I would not view him as somebody who requires one specific role to function. The main attraction is the flexibility of his movement and the fact that his strongest quality (snapshot finishing and spatial awareness) can translate across several attacking structures and sequences, including the left side where Arsenal have lacked a consistent goal threat in recent years.

The most obvious starting point is Kroupi as the lone #9. Arsenal's current options already offer two very different interpretations of the role. Most common actions:
- Havertz regularly drifts away from the defensive line, often towards the RHS, where he can receive underneath, combine with Saka and Odegaard, create overloads and vacate central space for runners such as Calafiori before attacking the box again.
- Gyokeres is much more of an aggressive focal point against settled blocks, pinning and occupying the CBs close to goal. By keeping the defensive line deep and central, he naturally creates more space for Arsenal's creative players in the half spaces and around the edge of the box.

Kroupi would offer something different again. He is smaller and considerably weaker physically than both Havertz and Gyokeres, so his role would rely far less on direct occupation of the CBs. Instead, he can operate a few yards below the CBs, drop into zone 14, avoid physical battles, receive on the half-turn and immediately attack the defence facing forward. His ability to play quick bounce passes, recognise one twos and understand third man combinations also makes the idea particularly interesting. Rather than consistently pinning the defensive line, Kroupi could manipulate it through his movement, dragging defenders away from their positions before combining and immediately attacking the space created.

Key USPs

Shooting
Kroupi’s standout trait is obviously his shooting and according to @Gradient_Sports he had the highest shooting grade in the entire Premier League last season despite being just 19. He scored 13 Premier League goals from 8.35xG last season, overperforming by +4.65 while boasting an incredible 25% goal conversion rate from 52 shots. His 0.70 goals per 90 ranked in the 99th percentile against other Premier League forwards, alongside 2.78 shots per 90 (89th percentile) and 1.18 SOT per 90 (94th percentile). The numbers clearly illustrate a forward who doesn’t only score at an exceptional rate but someone who is consistently able to get dangerous attempts away.

He also scored 2/2 penalties which suggests he scored 11 non-pen goals from just 6.77 non-pen xG. +4.23xG overperformance.

His 9.79xGOT suggests his shot placement adds value beyond xG, but 13 goals is still well above that, so some regression is likely even if the underlying skill is real.

Snapshot Finishing
The speed of his execution is one of the most impressive parts for me. 10/11 of his non-pen goals were finished in 2 touches or less, including 5 first time goals. He rarely needs several touches to set himself. His short backlift, rapid balance adjustment and ability to strike from awkward body positions allow him to shoot before the defender has completely set himself. 6/11 non penalty goals were also volleys, half-volleys or headers, which demonstrates how quickly he can adapt his body to bouncing, dropping and aerial deliveries even with limited space.

Body Manipulation and Balance
IMO his body manipulation and separation abilities are equally quintessential as he ranked in the 88th percentile for creating his own shots, but the data and eye test suggests he is not a strong isolation/1v1 dribbler. He completed only 0.80/2.00 dribbles per 90 (41% success) and averaged just 0.95 progressive carries per 90. His dribbling/carrying is far more purposeful and direct. He aims to use his first touch, a shoulder movement or a small body feint to shift the defender before immediately attacking the defender's wrong side. I saw this clearly in his goal against Forest, where he manipulated Milenkovic's body position, carried into the vacated space and finished brilliantly from distance.

To put it simply, Kroupi’s primary objective is normally to create enough separation to shoot. That is why the combination of his body manipulation and rapid shooting style is so difficult to defend, especially when facing recovering defenses.

Running In Behind 
While he thrives dropping deep, data tracking highlights Kroupi as a standout threat as a runner. According to @SkillCorner, he ranks exceptionally high for making diagonal, high speed channel runs that split CBs and FBs. His explosiveness over short distances allows him to get off the mark quickly, using transition phases (in particular) to sprint into central lanes or half spaces in behind. This verticality usually leads to a retreating backline, creating the exact space in zone 14 he operates so lethally in.

He averaged 5 channel runs per 30 minutes, which is extremely efficient. The timing can still improve, as 2 further goals were ruled out for offside.

Low Touch Efficiency
The final USP is his low-touch efficiency as he averaged only 39.68 touches per 90 (8th percentile), but still produced 4.49 touches in the opposition box (11%), 2.78 shots, 1.18 SOT and 0.70 goals per 90. He clearly does not need to constantly be involved in play to remain dangerous. The key thing is his movement as he combines well with one twos and third man combinations by moving into dangerous open spaces like a “9.5” does.

Kroupi as the lone #9: Basic Demands - Refer to Image 1

Kroupi’s basic role as Arsenal’s #9 would be relatively simple to explain:
- Occupy the CBs without constantly engaging them physically
- Move between the lines when the shooting opportunity appears
- Continuously work towards receiving in pockets where he can face the target and shoot quickly
- Shown in his goals vs Wolves, Arsenal and Forest

He will obviously not be asked to become a traditional target man because physically he does not meet the standards. The data supports this as he had a low 32% ground duel success rate (3rd percentile) and 26.7% aerial duel win rate (27th percentile). The simple tactical objective is to keep him close enough to the CBs that they remain pinned to him whilst using micro movements to avoid the actual contact.

I believe his movements need to work in cycles. Start high enough to occupy the CBs, drop into the pocket to open a passing lane, combine or turn and then immediately attack the open space whilst facing the target. I think that Kroupi should not drop into the midfield and remain there as we would then lose that central occupation. The movement away from goal needs to eventually coincide with a movement back towards it after a quick combination.

Note: With him replacing Havertz or Gyokeres up front we do lose that aerial support during defensive set-pieces. A small trade-off but not one I could ignore.

Explained Through The Phases

In Build-Up
During the first phase of possession Kroupi can peel away from the CBs into either half-space (depending on the overload priority) and offer himself as a vertical option. His first touch and awareness will allow him to receive, play a quick bounce pass and immediately continue his movement forward rather than taking multiple touches or attempting to dictate.

This is where I’d suggest his “9.5” profile becomes useful:
- If a CB follows him when he drops, we could attack the space created behind
- If the CB stays attached to the defensive line, Kroupi can receive in between the lines and turn
- I particularly enjoy watching him as the second or third in third man combinations which allows the team to beat the first lines of press and progress forward quickly.

Progression
Once we settle into our 3-2-5/3-1-6, Kroupi can alternate between occupying the defensive line and dropping into zone 11. He tends to remain central but naturally gravitates towards the left channel (See Left Inside Forward Section) which could lead to a strong relationship with Calafiori and Tzolis. It could also lead to one of the two having to remain wider to avoid an unnecessary channel overload.

This could create some interesting rotations. If Kroupi moves between the opposition RB and RCB, the RCB has to decide whether to follow or stay.
- If the CB follows a late/box crashing runner like Calafiori, Rice or Bruno G can attack the central space (during transitions or high tempo moments).
- If the CB holds position Kroupi can receive freely in space between the lines before turning and carrying/combining in zone 11/14 areas (most likely scenario).

His passing numbers also provide useful context as despite only completing 19 passes per 90 (76% acc.), he ranked in the 73rd percentile for both progressive passes and passes into the final third, along with ranking in the 68th percentile for forward passes. He is a low volume player but naturally vertical.

Note:
Despite his left channel preference, he is also extremely capable at combining on the right and using movement to drag a play before manipulating a defender and attacking the space in a third man combination (Goal vs Arsenal at the Vitality). Connections with Saka and Odegaard could be interesting with all of them being able to play strong bounce passes. An upgrade in tempo perhaps?

To counter the strengths, there is also an important factor of adaptation that has to be analysed. Bournemouth operate at a much higher attacking tempo and regularly attack extremely vertically, whereas Arsenal spend far more time circulating patiently around settled blocks. Kroupi will therefore have fewer chaotic spaces to immediately exploit and will need greater patience when Arsenal circulate. There is a chance that he may become impatient and drift to get on the ball and speed up tempo. It is something that can’t be ignored with his age profile too.

At Arsenal, his off the ball concentration will be extremely important:
- Remain relatively uninvolved between the lines
- Constantly adjust between CBs
- Explode once the passing lane appears

Final Third
Kroupi’s first thought when receiving in the final third is usually to create a shooting angle immediately. As I mentioned earlier his 88th percentile ranking for creating his own shots is very useful against low blocks because defenders often allow attackers only fractions of a second before closing them down.

Arsenal also create cutback situations from both sides and Kroupi’s box movement fits these sequences well because he does not exclusively attack one zone:
- He can run across the CB towards the front post (He particularly repeats these diagonal movements)
- Arrive centrally
- Ghost to the back post
- Delay his arrival around the pen spot
- All movements were shown last season.

His finishing technique will translate very well to these types of low and fast deliveries as he is a very confident one touch finisher. A first time cutback or loose second ball around the box is exactly the type of situation where his rapid release becomes valuable.

He can also combine well when runners move into the channels beyond him and he is also very capable at using quick bounce passes before moving from deeper positions to receive the return as the third man.

Note: His goals also came across a useful variety of attacking situations: 
- 5 from controlled possession
- 3 in transition
- 3 from set-piece situations
- 2 penalties. 
That variety matters because it shows his scoring threat is not exclusively dependent on open-field or transition moments.

The obvious weakness in Kroupi’s final third profile is his aerial ability. We would lose the ability to consistently target the striker with high crosses or long balls, specifically when compared to Havertz. Arsenal would have to emphasise low deliveries, combinations and cutbacks a lot more if Kroupi led the line

Attacking Transitions

Kroupi is extremely dangerous when the game becomes more transitional. He recorded one of Bournemouth’s highest sprint speeds (34.6 kmph) and understands exactly how and when to occupy the free space created when defenders retreat.

His off the ball verticality is crucial here, as he is incredibly sharp at making diagonal channel runs to stretch recovering defences. He aggressively exploits gaps between CBs and FBs the moment high regains occur, forcing the defence to drop deeper and open up his favoured central zones. 

However, he does not always need to lead the transitions himself. That's what makes this profile so interesting. I like him as the second attacker. If the winger or midfielder carries/makes a run ahead of him and attracts a defender, Kroupi can arrive underneath the backline in a dangerous area and receive. His ability to rapidly adjust his feet and shoot suits these sometimes awkward or wayward transition deliveries.

His carrying is also a very dangerous tool as he is strong at receiving whilst moving or pushing off from a standstill. He uses body feints and his balance to attack whichever side the defender has exposed rather than repeatedly attempting 1v1s.

To repeat, Arsenal will naturally provide fewer of these sequences than Bournemouth because opponents simply defend deeper against us. The question that can only be answered if he joins is whether he can transfer the same decisiveness into a slower tempo environment and be ruthless when "rare" transition opportunities do arrive.

Kroupi as a Left Inside Forward

Given his natural pull towards the left channel, a simpler option than the shadow striker idea is to start him on the left of a front 3. From there he can cut inside onto his stronger right foot, attack the half space and shoot. 

It keeps Gyokeres or Havertz central as the focal point, protects the midfield structure, and puts him in a role where his weaker aerial and physical profile matters less. The trade-off is that he'd likely see less of zone 14 and would need to be coached to hold width when Calafiori overlaps or underlaps. 

The left wing is where Arsenal's attack has lacked a consistent goal threat. Used as a left inside forward, Kroupi could change that. His ability to cut inside and shoot gives them a goalscorer in a zone that has produced too little. 

Risk and Solution
The main risk in this role is his 41% dribble success, as he is not an isolation winger and shouldn't be asked to beat a FB in wide areas 1v1. Arsenal can reduce those situations through structure. Calafiori underlapping from LB would pull the FB inside and open the touchline, while Odegaard or Bruno could rotate into the LHS to give Kroupi a quick bounce pass option. 

That lets him receive on the move, pass or combine, and attack the inside channel rather than isolating the FB. His 1v1 dribbling still needs to improve, but the role can be built to limit how often he has to beat a man - similar to what we're seeing with Tzolis now.

Kroupi as a Shadow Striker: The Theory - Refer to Image 2

Another potential, (although unlikely) spot we could see if he joins is Kroupi starting from the LCM base but effectively operating as a shadow striker.

Kroupi x Gyokeres (Similar to Kroupi x Evanilson but less technical)
The logic is very clear. Like what Evanilson does at Bournemouth, Gyokeres can occupy both CBs and force the defensive line deeper, creating space in zone 14. Kroupi can then operate dangerously in that zone without constantly dealing with the physical contact he may otherwise struggle with when playing as a lone #9.

Theoretically:
- If Gyokeres remains centrally, Kroupi can receive underneath
- If Gyokeres runs into a channel, Kroupi can fill the vacated central space.
- If Gyokeres receives to feet he can combine with Kroupi through a bounce pass before attacking the defender's blindside with vertical or diagonal movements.

This could be useful against low blocks as Gyokeres provides that fixed box occupation while Kroupi becomes another genuine scoring threat operating off his back. It is important to note that I would not expect Kroupi to operate as a creator as his 0 assists from 1.53xA and 1.18 chances created per 90 suggest he is primarily a shooting threat.

Kroupi x Havertz
By contrast, the partnership with Havertz would be a lot more fluid. Kai naturally drops away from the defensive line to take part in right sided overloads and combine. The key would be to stagger their movements and provide a clear fluid central partnership.

Theoretically:
- If Havertz drifts and drags, Kroupi should take up the vacated space.
- If Kroupi drifts to the right/left, Havertz needs to remain central and occupy the CBs
- Having both players in wide or deeper central areas would allow the opposition defensive line to step forward and close down the space between lines.
- Note: His channel/half space running could be ruthless with the technicality of Havertz (only really works if both remain close in proximity which is unlikely due to Havertz's drifting tendencies)

The technical relationship could be excellent. Havertz operates at an extremely high technical level compared to the average CF and is comfortable playing quick one touch bounce passes before immediately moving into space (Raumdeuter). Kai also retains the aerial threat and physical security that Kroupi lacks, which also somewhat fits the Evanilson comparison I mentioned earlier.

I think their different instincts could naturally balance the partnership as Havertz is more likely to connect possession and operate as a clear and safe progression outlet, whilst Kroupi is generally more shot focused. If (unlikely) Arteta adapts the system to suit this Kai could become the forward operating as ball to feet whilst Kroupi operates more so as a runner. We saw this on occasion last season with Trossard as a LCM.

Key Weakness with Kroupi as a Shadow Striker
The key and obvious trade-off is defensively. Starting another forward from LCM reduces our midfield security and would likely require a stricter rest defence behind him. Players like Timber would likely have to remain slightly more conservative alongside Rice, whilst Kroupi could move next to Gyokeres/Havertz in a 4-4-2 OOP shape meaning a less physically capable Odegaard drops into the midfield line and we lose his press leading qualities. If Bruno G starts instead it could work much better in settled defensive phases.

Out of Possession

In his first season at Bournemouth Kroupi averaged only 0.48 tackles per 90 (2nd percentile) and won just 32% of his ground duels, yet recorded 0.48 interceptions per 90 (49th percentile) and 1.07 final third possessions won per 90 (95th percentile).

That fits the eye test. He appears much stronger anticipating passes and loose touches than directly tackling opponents. His high intensity pressing can therefore be built around curved runs, screening the opposition #6 and cutting passing lanes to force the opposition to go long or reset.

As the lone #9, he could lead the first line alongside pressing leader Odegaard in the 4-4-2 shape. Alternatively, if he plays underneath a Gyokeres or Havertz he is likely to again be the leader or work in an interdependent relationship as he has done for majority of his career.
- Pressing followers: Mohamed Bamba/Aiyegun Tosin at Lorient
- Work alongside another capable pressing leader (Evanilson).

As mentioned earlier, Odegaard/Bruno would then likely drop to #8 and allow Kroupi to defend in the first line.

Main Concerns

The most obvious weakness is physicality. Standing at 5”10 and 70kg he cannot physically impose himself on Premier League CBs or provide the same direct outlet we see with Gyokeres or Havertz.

There is also a translation risk. Kroupi, if he joins, will move from a high tempo Bournemouth side to a low tempo Arsenal side. He will have to adapt and become more patient as his touches will likely decrease unless he performs a similar combination role to Havertz (Gyokeres - 26 touches per 90, Havertz - 44 touches per 90 last season).

Finishing regression is also something to watch out for as scoring 13 goals from just 8.35xG and boasting an incredible 25% conversion rate is exceptional but unlikely to remain at that level forever. However, I do think his snapshot shooting ability, balance and body manipulation to create separation provide legitimate technical reasons that would allow him to sustain the ridiculous numbers he achieved last year.

Finally, his decision-making can at times resemble “selfishness”. He recorded 0 assists from 1.53xA and there are moments where he could have easily released a better positioned teammate. I personally wouldn’t want to completely coach that “selfishness” out of him because his shooting mentality is arguably his biggest strength, but adding that layer of creation would make him very complete. We must remember he is only 20.

Final Thoughts

Kroupi is my personal favourite out of the names currently being thrown out for attacking alternatives because I feel he provides something genuinely different to our existing striker options:
- Havertz offers fluidity, technical security and aerial ability
- Gyokeres gives us direct channel running and physical occupation of CBs
- Kroupi would offer spatial and body manipulation, elite in behind movement and efficient quick finishing

As a lone #9 there is a clear benefit of embedding his “9.5” profile directly into the system and allowing him to alternate between occupying the CBs and dropping into zone 11/14 before attacking the space again. Against mid blocks in particular, his ability to receive comfortably on the half turn could be crucial.

Against low blocks, the physical limitations become more relevant. That is where using him with a focal point becomes interesting. Gyokeres would give him that fixed player to play around (similar to Evanilson) and Havertz would provide a more fluid relationship based on interdependent movement.

The left inside forward role is the most realistic alternative. It keeps Gyokeres or Havertz as the central focal point, places Kroupi in the area where his shooting and cut inside tendency fit best, and addresses the left side's lack of goals. It does depend on how well Arsenal can protect him in 1v1s, but with Calafiori's underlap and a rotation with Odegaard or Bruno, that is a structural problem Arteta can solve.

The biggest unknown for me is if he can adapt from Bournemouth’s high tempo environment to the slow and more controlled tempo under Arteta. He will definitely have less space to operate in and far more situations where he has to remain patient against stubborn defensive units. That's where his most transferable skill of snapshot shooting comes into play.

To summarise, at only 20 years old, Kroupi’s profile is understandably still open to significant development. His physicality, creation and decision-making can improve, however, elite finishing is one of the hardest qualities to find and Kroupi already combines it with incredible spatial awareness, movement and excellent abilities to create space for his own shots.

Personally it is a no brainer. Pay the money before a young player of immense quality joins a different elite club in Europe. £100m player in my humble opinion.

Thank you for reading my article on how Eli Junior Kroupi can fit into Arsenal. What are your thoughts? Since the market is depleted of available elite talent, why not develop a player with a clearly unbelievable skill set?

text:
ITS STILL A MESS 
Drinking water at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune in Jacksonville, North Carolina, was contaminated with industrial solvents for decades, roughly from the early 1950s until the mid-to-late 1980s. The period used for VA benefits and federal claims is August 1, 1953, through December 31, 1987.
What contaminated the water
Two treatment plants supplied the affected water:
•  Tarawa Terrace mainly had perchloroethylene (PCE, also called tetrachloroethylene), used in dry cleaning. The primary source was improper disposal at ABC One-Hour Cleaners, an off-base dry cleaner that became a Superfund site. ATSDR water modeling estimated PCE above the current EPA maximum contaminant level (5 μg/L) from about November 1957 to February 1987. The highest measured level in finished water was 215 μg/L.
•  Hadnot Point mainly had trichloroethylene (TCE), a metal degreaser, plus benzene, vinyl chloride, and dichloroethylene. Sources included on-base leaking underground storage tanks, industrial spills, and waste disposal. Finished water at Hadnot Point reached TCE levels as high as 1,400 μg/L (current MCL is 5 μg/L). Hadnot Point also supplied the base hospital and, at times, housing on the Holcomb Boulevard system.
Contaminated wells were shut down in late 1984–early 1985 after testing began in 1982. The Tarawa Terrace plant closed in 1987. ATSDR and base reports state that notable VOC contamination has not been detected in the drinking-water systems since the mid-1980s; current supplies are tested separately from the historical systems. Groundwater under parts of the base remains a longer-term cleanup issue.
Health findings
ATSDR cohort studies comparing Camp Lejeune Marines, Navy personnel, and civilian workers with personnel at Camp Pendleton have reported elevated risks of several outcomes, including:
•  Kidney, esophageal, and female breast cancer mortality among Marines and Navy personnel
•  Chronic kidney disease, Parkinson’s disease, and female breast cancer mortality among civilian workers
•  Higher incidence of certain leukemias and lymphomas, and cancers of the lung, breast, larynx, esophagus, thyroid, and soft tissue
Earlier work also examined associations with birth defects and childhood cancers linked to in-utero exposure. Evidence strength varies by disease; ATSDR has published assessments integrating Camp Lejeune data with occupational and environmental studies of TCE, PCE, vinyl chloride, and benzene.
The VA treats several conditions as presumptive for disability compensation and health care if the person served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 days in the 1953–1987 window and was not dishonorably discharged: adult leukemia, aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, liver cancer, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and Parkinson’s disease.
Claims and litigation
The Camp Lejeune Justice Act (Section 804 of the 2022 PACT Act) created a federal cause of action for people who lived or worked on base for at least 30 days during the exposure window and later developed related injuries. Administrative claims had to be filed with the Navy by August 10, 2024.
As of a September 14, 2026 court filing, about 408,500 administrative claims had been submitted. Under the government’s Elective Option (fixed payments generally from $100,000 to $550,000 based on disease tier and time on base, plus an additional amount for death), approved offers totaled about $1.08 billion and payments made totaled about $872 million. Roughly 3,780 lawsuits were pending in the Eastern District of North Carolina. Bellwether trials were scheduled for late 2026, and the court had pressed the parties toward a global settlement framework by October 30, 2026.

text:
CASE 04 | CHILDREN CAUGHT IN A REFUGEE INTERVIEW: WHO IS HOLDING USCIS ACCOUNTABLE?
REAL PEOPLE. REAL FAMILIES. REAL STORIES.
@POTUS @SecRubio @DeputySecState @VP @Jim_Jordan @SenTedCruz @SenJohnKennedy 
Imagine living in a country where you believe you are being persecuted because you are white, or simply because your skin color makes others identify you as white. Imagine fearing for your life and the lives of your family members because of your racial identity. You cannot change your skin color. You cannot change your ancestry. And no human being should have to live in fear because of either.

THIS IS THE FEAR ONE SOUTH AFRICAN FAMILY BROUGHT TO THE UNITED STATES REFUGEE PROGRAM.

This applicant and their spouse sought refuge in America because they believed their lives were in danger in South Africa. They described fears of racial persecution, threatening political rhetoric directed at white South Africans, and uncertainty surrounding their future and property rights. They feared that their government was unwilling or unable to protect them.

They were not asking to be exempt from American immigration laws. They were asking for an opportunity to explain why they believed remaining in South Africa placed their family at risk.

According to their testimony, what happened during their USCIS interview left them devastated. Multiple family members were brought into the interview together despite having separate living arrangements. The applicant describes the interviewer as rude, dismissive, and unwilling to allow them to fully explain their fears of persecution. They say the questioning focused heavily on one political organization rather than the broader circumstances behind their application.

BUT THE ALLEGATION INVOLVING THE CHILDREN DESERVES PARTICULAR ATTENTION.

The applicant alleges that children accompanying the family were told to remain quiet because the interviewer would determine whether they would ever see relatives already living in America again.

CHILDREN WERE ALLEGEDLY TOLD THAT THE PERSON CONDUCTING THE INTERVIEW WOULD DECIDE WHETHER THEY COULD SEE THEIR FAMILY AGAIN.

These children were not responsible for South Africa's political situation. They were not responsible for their family's decision to seek refuge. They were children accompanying adults who hoped the United States might offer their family protection.

If this account is accurate, it raises serious questions about how the interview was conducted and how children were treated during the process.

The applicant described the experience as one of the worst their family had endured.

Then came the decision.

INELIGIBLE.

After months in the refugee process, the family received a notice of ineligibility. According to the applicant, they were not given enough information to understand why their application had been rejected.

They report having no criminal records. They do not know whether the decision involved their testimony, their eligibility under refugee law, security considerations, or another issue.

THEY STILL DO NOT KNOW WHY.

And now they remain in South Africa, the very country they were trying to leave.

Consider what that means. A family believes it is facing persecution because of racial identity. They approach another country seeking protection. They disclose personal information and describe why they are afraid. They participate in interviews, hoping their circumstances will be fairly considered.

Then they receive an ineligibility notice without enough information to understand the decision.

Their fears have not disappeared simply because their application was unsuccessful.

There is also the question of what could happen if their identity as refugee applicants becomes known. We cannot establish that the South African government is targeting this family for applying, but publicly identifying them could create additional risks.

THAT IS WHY THEIR IDENTITIES WILL REMAIN PROTECTED.

The United States has every right to establish refugee eligibility requirements, conduct security screening, and determine who qualifies for admission. An applicant's fear of persecution must be assessed under the applicable legal standards. No one is entitled to automatic approval.

But those responsibilities do not eliminate the need to examine credible allegations of inappropriate interview conduct.

Were the applicants allowed to fully explain their fears? Were the children treated appropriately? Was the family's claim individually assessed? What was the actual basis for the ineligibility decision?

These questions deserve answers.

NO PERSON SHOULD FACE RACIAL PERSECUTION BECAUSE OF THE COLOR OF THEIR SKIN, WHETHER BLACK, WHITE, OR ANY OTHER COLOR.

This family says they sought protection because they feared persecution. They describe an interview that left them feeling humiliated and unheard. They were subsequently found ineligible, and they still do not understand why.

REAL PEOPLE. REAL FAMILIES. REAL STORIES.

This testimony has been anonymized to protect the applicant and family. The allegations concerning the interview reflect the applicant's account and have not been independently verified.

REJECTED BY POLICY. NOT BY WORTH.

text:
In Sanatan Dharma, lighting a Deepak before the Divine is not merely a ritual. 🪔

It is traditionally considered a powerful way to invoke divine blessings, focus the mind and pray for the fulfilment of one’s wishes.

But did you know that the oil, ghee, wick and even the form of the Deepak can differ according to the deity and intention?

1. For Wealth & Prosperity
A pure ghee lamp may be lit in the home temple.

2. For Shani Dev
A mustard oil lamp is traditionally used for Shani worship.

3. For Surya Dev
A ghee lamp is traditionally offered during Surya worship.

4. For Rahu & Ketu
A flaxseed oil lamp is traditionally associated with their worship.

5. For Durga & Saraswati
A two-wick lamp is traditionally used during their worship and for knowledge-related intentions.

6. For Lord Ganesha
A three-wick ghee lamp is traditionally associated with Ganesha worship.

7. For Bhairava
A four-wick mustard oil lamp is traditionally used in Bhairava worship.

8. For Lakshmi Ji
A seven-wick ghee lamp is traditionally associated with prosperity and abundance.

9. For Lord Vishnu
A sixteen-wick lamp is traditionally associated with Vishnu worship.

10. For Hanuman Ji
A triangular lamp with jasmine oil is traditionally associated with Hanuman worship.

Where should the Deepak be placed?
For regular home worship, it should be kept in the puja area, before the deity, on a stable and safe surface.

The exact practice may vary according to the deity, sampradaya and family tradition.

A Deepak is not just a flame. 🪔
In Sanatan tradition, it represents light, devotion and the intention behind your prayer.
